#1315. O'Neill reiterates support for Trusty as Celtic boss slams McAvennie's comments about defender's absence

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 17:48 EDT, 4 November 2026

Martin O'Neill has stressed that Auston Trusty has the full backing of everyone at Celtic — after describing Frank McAvennie’s comments about the defender’s ongoing absence as being ‘in poor taste’.

Trusty remains with his family in the US on compassionate grounds following the recent passing of his father Walt.

Speaking on his Let me be Frank podcast this week, former Parkhead striker McAvennie questioned why Trusty wasn’t back playing — describing it as ‘nonsense’ perpetuated by ‘the woke brigade’.

‘I’ve got every respect for that, but how long do you want off?’ McAvennie said. ‘Martin (O’Neill) says he’s away to celebrate the life of his dad.

‘Celebrate the life? You’ve got football. You’re getting paid and we’re in trouble. How long is it going to be?

‘It’s the woke brigade now, isn’t it? It’s nonsense. My dad was the best man, the only man I looked up to when he died, but you’ve got to get on with it.’

Trusty has missed Celtic's last four games after returning home following his father's passing

Those remarks brought a huge backlash with McAvennie later forced into a public apology, claiming he meant no disrespect to Trusty or his family.

‘I should have chosen my words more carefully,’ said McAvennie, who scored 37 goals in 85 games across two spells with Celtic. ‘I can understand why people feel my comments were insensitive. Everyone deals with grief differently and I certainly meant no disrespect.

‘Celtic need the big man back and that’s what I was clumsily trying to say. I wish him and his family all the very best.’

Evidently unimpressed with that attempt to backtrack, O’Neill made it clear that his player, who’s been absent for four matches — against Celta Vigo, Hibernian, Dundee United and Falkirk — should take all the time he needs before returning to Glasgow.

‘That’s really poor taste. That’s really poor,’ said the Celtic boss. ‘I know I’ve said some things and ended up backtracking. But that’s a family bereavement.

‘And that’s making someone’s mind up about how long they should be grieving and stuff like this here. That’s not on.

‘Trusty asked me for some time (off). Even if it’s a celebration (of his late father’s life) it doesn’t matter.

McAvennie has been widely criticised for comments he made on his podcast

‘The father’s been in poor health for quite some considerable time. And I know there was a stage where he thought that he wasn’t going to see it through.

‘But I’m with Trusty the whole way there. Because I wouldn’t want anybody to tell me that I had to grieve over a brother or sister dying. And I’ve had that.

‘He’s 28 years of age. And he’s taken it badly. He has taken it badly. Honestly.

‘I’ve afforded him all the time he wants.

‘At some stage, obviously, he’ll come back. But, at the end of the day, I’ve given that time because I know that we might be talking about different eras or whatever the case may be. That’s nothing to do with it.

‘This is a family thing. And that’s not right.

‘So, Trusty has got the time and he’s got the backing of myself and he’s got the backing of the club.’

#1313. Champions League: Supercomputer Predicts Final League Phase Table

With the 2026/27 Champions League season now underway, a supercomputer has tried its hand at predicting how the opening stage of the competition will pan out.

French giants Paris Saint-Germain are, once again, the favourites for glory as they pursue a third successive triumph in Europe's premier competition. But they will face stiff opposition from the likes of Premier League champions Arsenal, as well as Bayern Munich, Barcelona and Real Madrid.

For many clubs, however, the league phase could make or break their Champions League campaign. Now in its third iteration following UEFA's overhaul of the old group-stage format ahead of the 2024/25 season, every result could have a significant bearing on a team's route through the competition.

While some sides have been handed a tougher set of league phase opponents than others, Opta's data analysts have put together a predicted final table, with statistics, fixture difficulty and thousands of simulations helping to paint as accurate a picture as possible of how the first stage could unfold.

The wooden spoon is reserved for Slovan Bratislava, who have never reached the knockout stages and are predicted to collect just 3.4 points.

Unfortunately for Azerbaijani side Sabah FK, there is little reason to take issue with their predicted position just off the bottom of the table. Not only are they competing in the Champions League for the first time in their history, but they have also been handed the toughest set of opponents of any club in the competition. As a result, analysts expect them to have a tough time getting points on the board, but they aren't tipped to come last.

Lille have lost three of their opening four games (3-2 at home to Real Betis, 3-0 away to Arsenal and 4-2 at home to Galatasaray), which has done serious damage to their hopes of progressing.

Napoli, Lens and Feyenoord are all in danger of finishing in the bottom segment of the table.

Porto, like Lille, have surprisingly lost all three of their opening games. They are now being predicted to pick up just seven points and crash out of the competition in the League Phase.

Shakhtar Donetsk, who have agreed to play their home games at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge, are currently on course to finish on just eight points after one win, one draw and two losses.

AEK Athens and Slavia Prague are also expected to bow out in the League Phase.

Supercomputer Predicts UCL League Phase Table (36-28)

Villarreal, Porto and PSV are all tipped to only hit just over eight points, but that's not expected to be enough to advance.

Viking FK will be hoping Norway's growing reputation in European football can help them punch above their weight and replicate Bodo/Glimt's surprise run to the knockout stages last season. They are predicted to join RB Leipzig in scraping into the top 24.

Bodo/Glimt were a breath of fresh air last season, as they got wins over Man City, Atletico Madrid and Inter before falling at the Round of 16. The Norwegian side, as well as Roma, Fenerbahce and LASK, should get another shot at the knockouts.

Supercomputer Predicts UCL League Phase Table (27-19)

Diego Simeone's Atletico Madrid and Turkish giants Galatasaray are predicted to finish 18th and 17th, respectively.

Manchester United started their campaign off with a convincing win over Sabah, but suffered defeats to Atletico Madrid and Como. A stunning comeback against Roma on matchday four has seen their chances of progressing increase dramatically.

Just above them are Inter Milan and VfB Stuttgart, who have the easiest fixture list based on opponent ratings. Inter will hope to recover and have another shot at the big-eared trophy after reaching the final twice over the last five seasons, where they were left heartbroken at the last hurdle against Man City in 2023 and PSG in 2025.

Spanish side Real Betis have surprisingly won three of their opening four matches, beating Lille, Porto and Feyenoord. The Supercomputer thinks they'll finish just outside the top 10 with Borussia Dortmund.

Como have one of the most inspirational stories in European football in recent memory, with their meteoric rise under the management of former Arsenal and Chelsea midfielder Cesc Fabregas making them very difficult not to love. They are now predicted to finish 10th after big wins over Manchester United and Lens.

Supercomputer Predicts UCL League Phase Table (18-10)

Club Brugge could be this season's surprise package, especially if they match the supercomputer's prediction and finish in the top nine. The Belgian outfit have claimed nine points from a possible 12 so far.

Just ahead of them are Europa League holders Aston Villa, who would be very happy with avoiding the play-off round.

Liverpool had a tricky tie against Atletico but were able to come from a goal behind to win 2-1 at Anfield. They then thrashed LASK 6-3 in Austria and scraped past Villarreal. However, a disappointing collapse has given them less room for manoeuvre if they want to make the top eight.

Manchester City are being tipped to finish sixth. Enzo Maresca's team's tally of 16.4 expected points suggests a continuation of the impressive Pep Guardiola era.

Bayern Munich will look to translate their domestic dominance into continental superiority as they are expected to finish fourth, just ahead of Barcelona.

Man Utd feature, while PSG still aren't top despite retaining their Champions League title.

Arsenal are tipped to come third. The reigning Premier League champions have beaten Napoli, Lille and Slavia Prague, as well as playing out an entertaining 2-2 draw with Bayern at Allianz Arena.

Spanish giants Real Madrid are predicted to come second. Jose Mourinho's side have a perfect record so far, having beaten Inter, Roma, RB Leipzig and AEK Athens.

Finally, Paris Saint-Germain, who are looking to win the Champions League for a third time in a row this season, are tipped to finish first. They have shown that they are the team to beat once again with League Phase victories over Manchester City and Barcelona.

#1312. Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR–Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal–fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

The proteomics data have been deposited into the ProteomeXchange Consortium (identifier PXD067722; http://www.proteomexchange.org/) via the jPOST partner repository (JPST004036; https://jpostdb.org/)61. The FASTQ files for CRISPR–Cas9 screens have been deposited into the DNA Data Bank of Japan (accession number DRA022489). The statistical analysis data for the proteomics and CRISPR–Cas9 screens have been appended as Supplementary Tables. Gene expression data used for candidate selection were obtained from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (https://sites.broadinstitute.org/ccle). Subcellular localization data were obtained from the COMPARTMENTS database (https://compartments.jensenlab.org/). All other data supporting the findings of this study are available in the paper and its Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.

Y. Mori, S.T., Y. Matsuura and A.R. conceived the project. Y. Mori, M.S., Y.N., T.H., Y.K., H.K. and A.R. designed the experiments. Y. Mori and Y.I. performed the proximity biotin labelling experiments using APEX2–VLPs. Y.I. and Y.K. performed LC–MS/MS and data analyses. Y. Mori, M.S. and M. Nagai performed CRISPR–Cas9 screening, viral attachment and internalization assays. Y. Mori, M.S. and Y.N. performed RuV infection experiments. Y. Mori and M.S. performed VSVpv infection, subgenomic replicon and inhibitor addition assays. Y. Mori, S.S., H.H., K.M. and E.N.K. prepared and purified recombinant proteins. Y. Mori, S.S. and M. Nagai performed ELISA-based binding assays. Y. Mori, K.F., H.A. and M.I. conducted SPR experiments. Y. Mori, M.S. and M. Kakizaki performed flow cytometry and cell sorting. M.S., M. Kawase, M. Kakizaki and K.S. prepared ALI-cultured respiratory epithelial cells and performed infection experiments. M. Nishi performed immunohistochemistry. Y.N., M.S. and T.H. prepared differentiated trophoblasts and performed infection experiments. T.O., T.T., W.K. and K.S. prepared recombinant RSV. Y. Mori, M.S., Y.N., Y.I., T.H., K.F., H.A., S.S., S.T., M.I., Y.K., H.K., Y. Matsuura and A.R. interpreted the experimental data. Y. Mori, Y.I. and A.R. wrote the original manuscript. Y. Mori, K.M. and A.R. wrote the revised manuscript. Y. Mori, M.S. and Y.N. generated figures. All authors read, edited and approved the final version of the manuscript before submission.

(a) Schematic diagram illustrating the preparation of subgenomic RNA-containing VLPs or empty VLPs with DogTag inserted into the envelope proteins. BHK-SGR-NL cells were transfected with a plasmid expressing the structural protein precursor CE2E1 to produce VLPs containing SGR (SGR-VLP). Plasmids encoding C-DTE2-E1, which contains an in-frame DogTag insertion between Gly1 and Leu2 of the E2 protein, and C-E2-DTE1, which contains an in-frame DogTag insertion between Asn213 and Gln214 of the E1 protein, were also expressed. Expi293F cells were utilized to produce large quantities of empty VLPs. (b) A series of SGR-VLPs encoding NanoLuc as a reporter were inoculated into Vero cells to assess infectivity. As a negative control, culture medium collected from BHK-SGR-NL cells expressing mCherry instead of CE2E1 was used. Infectivity was determined by measuring the relative activity of NanoLuc (n = 3 biologically independent cultures). (c) Western blot analysis to detect the E2 (left panel) or E1 (right panel) protein of SGR-VLPs. SGR-VLPs were incubated overnight at 4 °C in the presence or absence of DC-APEX2. SDS-PAGE samples were prepared by adding SGR-VLPs to SDS-PAGE sample buffer containing 2-mercaptoethanol and incubating at 95 °C for 5 min. Arrows indicate the original bands of viral proteins with an inserted DogTag, while arrowheads indicate those covalently bound to DC-APEX2. (d) Infectivity analysis of SGR-VLP mixed with PBS or DC-APEX2. SGR-VLPs were incubated overnight at 4 °C with PBS or DC-APEX2 and subsequently inoculated into Vero cells to analyze infectivity. As a negative control, culture medium collected from BHK-SGR-NL cells expressing mCherry instead of CE2E1 was used. Infectivity was determined by measuring the relative activity of NanoLuc (n = 4 biologically independent cultures). (e) Electron microscopic images of VLPs and APEX2-VLPs visualized by negative staining. (f) Following treatment of JAR4-SMS1KO22 cells under the indicated conditions, biotin-labeled proteins were detected by western blotting using HRP-conjugated streptavidin. (g) Fluorescence staining images of JAR4-SMS1KO22 cells treated with biotin labeling in the presence or absence of APEX2-VLP. RuV E1 protein, biotin, and nuclei are visualized in green, magenta, and blue, respectively. Images in left and upper right panels were obtained by confocal microscopy and are shown as z-stack projections. The boxed area in the left panel is magnified in the upper right panel. The cross-section obtained by cutting along the dotted line in the left panel is shown in the lower right panel. The plasma membranes stained with WGA are shown in gray in only the cross-section image. Data are mean ± s.d. Statistical analyses were performed using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc multiple comparison test (b) and two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s post hoc multiple comparison test (d). Statistical significance is indicated by asterisks: ****P < 0.0001; ***, P < 0.001; **, P < 0.01; ns, not significant. Exact P values are provided in Supplementary Table 5.

(a) Lysates of Raji-derived cells were analyzed by western blotting using antibodies against Nectin-4 (EPR15613-68), MOG, DYKDDDDK-tag (for FLAG-tagged SeV C protein), and GAPDH. (b) Lysates of Raji-derived cells were analyzed by western blotting using antibodies against ADAM9, DYKDDDDK-tag (for FLAG-tagged SeV C protein), and GAPDH. (c) RajiSC-EV or RajiSC-hNectin-4 cells were stained with anti-Nectin-4 goat polyclonal antibody or normal goat IgG, followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry. (d) RajiSC-EV or RajiSC-hMOG cells were stained with anti-MOG mouse monoclonal or mouse IgG1 monoclonal antibody (isotype control), followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry. (e) Jurkat or Jurkat-hNectin-4 cells were stained with anti-Nectin-4 human monoclonal (Enfortumab) or human IgG1 monoclonal antibody (isotype control), followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-human IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry. (f) Jurkat or Jurkat-hMOG cells were stained with anti-MOG mouse monoclonal or mouse IgG1 monoclonal antibody (isotype control), followed by PE-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry. (g, h) Cells were stained with anti-Nectin-4 human monoclonal (Enfortumab) or human IgG1 monoclonal antibody (isotype control), followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-human IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry. Dead cells were excluded from analyses by staining with 7-Aminoactinomycin D. All cells were analyzed using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer. (i) Expression of Nectin-4 and α-tubulin in NCI-H358-NT, NCI-H358-Nectin-4KO, and NCI-H358-N4KO-N4OE cells was analyzed by western blotting using anti-Nectin-4 human monoclonal (Enfortumab) and anti-α-tubulin polyclonal antibodies.

(a) Schematic diagram of the measurement of replication, transcription, and translation activity by the RuV subgenomic replicon (SGR). SGR-RNA, in which the structural protein gene of RuV was replaced by a fusion protein gene of puromycin-N-acetyltransferase (PAC), an FMDV 2 A protease cleavage site, and NanoLuc (NLuc), was generated by in vitro transcription. SGR-GND is an RNA replication-deficient mutant generated by substituting amino acids in the active center of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of p90 (GDD to GND). SGR-WT RNA or SGR-GND RNA was transfected into RajiSC-EV or RajiSC-hNectin-4 cells together with mRNA for RuV C protein and Firefly Luciferase (FLuc), and incubated at 35 °C. At 72 h post-transfection, the NLuc and FLuc activities were measured. (b) Results of a reporter assay following RuV-SGR RNA transfection. SGR activity was determined as NLuc activity normalized by FLuc activity (n = 9 biologically independent cultures derived from three independent experiments). Statistical analyses were performed using two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s post hoc multiple comparison test. No significant differences (ns) were detected. Exact P values are provided in Supplementary Table 5.

(a) Flow cytometry analysis of cell surface expression of the Nectin family in RajiSC-EV, hNectin1-, hNectin2-, or hNectin3-overexpressing RajiSC cells. (b) RajiSC cells expressing each Nectin member were inoculated with pseudotyped VSV strains encoding the firefly luciferase gene: VSVpv-G (VSV-G), VSVpv-ΔG (∆G), and VSVpv-RuV-CE2E1 (RuV-CE2E1). After incubation for 20 h at 37 °C, relative light units (RLU) were measured (n = 3 biologically independent cultures). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviations. Statistical analyses were performed using two-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc multiple comparison test. Statistical significance is indicated by asterisks: ****, P < 0.0001; ns, not significant. Exact P values are provided in Supplementary Table 5. (c) CBB-stained image of the SDS-PAGE gel of purified human IgG1-Fc domain-fused ectodomains derived from Nectin family members. In each lane, 1 µg of protein was loaded. (d) ELISA-based binding assay. Purified Fc domain-fused Nectin ectodomains were added to wells coated with RuV particles at the indicated concentrations. Bound proteins were detected by immunochemistry (n = 3 biologically independent experiments). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviations.

(a) Confocal microscopy of VLP binding on the cell surface. NCI-H358 cells were labeled with anti-RuV E1 (green) and anti-Nectin-4 (magenta) antibodies after 2 h of VLP binding on ice. Slice-1 (apical) and Slice-2 (mid-section) are shown. Lower panels are magnifications of the dotted regions in Slice-1. (b) Confocal microscopy of VLP internalization into cells. NCI-H358 cells were incubated with VLPs on ice for 2 h for binding, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h to induce internalization. Cells were labeled with anti-Rab5 (green), anti-RuV E1 (cyan), and anti-Nectin-4 (magenta) antibodies. The nuclei were shown in blue. The main image shows a representative mid-section slice. Right panels represent magnified views of the regions enclosed by dotted boxes 1 and 2. (c) Proposed model for RuV cell entry mediated by hNectin-4 receptor. (1) RuV initially attaches to cholesterol- and sphingomyelin-rich membrane domains, which are abundantly distributed on the target cell surface, through calcium ion-dependent interactions involving fusion loops within the E1 protein. (2) RuV subsequently binds to hNectin-4 at the cell surface via the E2E1 heterodimer, which (3) induces endocytosis of the virus–receptor complex. (4) pH-dependent conformational changes in the E1 protein within the acidic endosomal compartment trigger membrane fusion between the viral envelope and the endosomal membrane, facilitating the release of the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm.

(a) The amino acid sequence of hNectin-4 from position 340 onward is shown. Transmembrane domains and linear amino acid motifs were predicted using SOSUI and ELM, respectively. For hNectin-4, the putative transmembrane domain is underlined, putative binding motifs for the sigma (ELME000526) and mu subunits (ELME000120) of the adaptor protein complexes are shown in pink and blue, respectively, and binding sites to the Afadin PDZ domain are shown in gray. The amino acid sequence shown in green for hN4-GPI is the GPI anchor attachment signal derived from human CD55. (b) RajiSC-EV, RajiSC-hNectin-4, or RajiSC-hN4-GPI cells were stained with anti-Nectin-4 human monoclonal (Enfortumab) or human IgG1 monoclonal (isotype control) antibodies, followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-human IgG, and analyzed by flow cytometry using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer. (c) Western blot analysis of Nectin-4 expression in RajiSC-EV, RajiSC-hNectin-4, and RajiSC-hN4-GPI cells. Nectin-4 and GAPDH were detected using anti-Nectin-4 rabbit monoclonal antibody and anti-GAPDH mouse monoclonal antibody, respectively. Asterisks indicate non-specific signals.

(a) Schematic diagram of hNectin-4 structure. Nectin-4 is a single-pass type I transmembrane protein of the immunoglobulin superfamily and contains one V-set (V) and two C2-set (C2) domains in the ectodomain. TM, Transmembrane domain; CT, Cytoplasmic tail. (b) Schematic diagram of a series of soluble hNectin-4 ectodomains fused with the human IgG1 Fc domain. The recombinant Nectin-4 proteins consist of either one V domain, two C2 domains, or both, with the interleukin-2 signal sequence (IL2ss) fused to the N-terminus and the human IgG1 F domain fused to the C-terminus, designated hN4-VCC-Fc, hN4-V-Fc, and hN4-CC-Fc. Manchester United, Chelsea and Liverpool are reportedly interested in signing Eintracht Frankfurt defender Nnamdi Collins as Premier League clubs look to strengthen their defensive options.

The 22-year-old has attracted considerable attention with his performances in Germany, and several English clubs are closely monitoring his development ahead of future transfer windows.

According to a report from Fussball News, Manchester United, Chelsea and Liverpool are all keeping tabs on the German defender, having been impressed by his performances for Frankfurt and the German U21 national team.

The three English clubs are understood to have sent scouts to follow Collins, who has established himself as an exciting defensive prospect.

The German youngster offers considerable versatility, having shown he can play both centre-back and right-back. His adaptability could make him a useful addition for clubs looking to improve their defensive depth.

Furthermore, his impressive pace, physical strength and ability to compete in individual duels make him an attractive prospect for the Premier League. He has also caught scouts’ attention through his performances for the German U21 side, including their recent encounter against Georgia.

However, no concrete negotiations have taken place so far, and interested clubs are still assessing his suitability.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Meanwhile, Eintracht Frankfurt are unlikely to sanction his departure in the January transfer window. The Bundesliga outfit considers Collins an important part of their long-term plans and have secured his future with a contract running until June 2030.

Although his current market valuation is considerably lower, Frankfurt are reportedly looking for offers around €35 million before considering a sale.

The German club could also seek additional performance-related bonuses and a percentage of any future transfer fee.

It remains to be seen whether Manchester United, Chelsea or Liverpool will formalise their interest with an offer. However, Collins’ versatility and physical attributes make him an exciting defensive prospect, and a move to the Premier League could represent an important next step in his career.

#1310. Danny Dyer Would Let Jarrod Bowen Leave West Ham For Two Clubs

Jarrod Bowen has been nothing short of incredible since joining West Ham United from Hull City in January 2020. The Englishman has been an extremely loyal servant at the club, even after the Hammers were relegated from the Premier League and into the Championship.

Since his £22 million transfer six years ago, Bowen has netted 94 goals in over 297 appearances and has become the talisman at the London Stadium. His place in history is already sealed, after he netted a dramatic late winner in the UEFA Europa Conference League final in 2023.

That delicate chipped effort secured the east London club's first piece of major silverware since the 1980 FA Cup. Bowen hasn't just racked up strong achievements on the pitch, but he's gained family ties to West Ham off it, too.

It certainly makes leaving a lot more difficult. But given the continued struggles the Iron find themselves in, he may be tempted to go against his father-in-law's ideals in search for a career more attuned to his quality.

Bowen married into one of the most well-known east London families he possibly could've when he tied the knot with reality TV star Dani Dyer in 2025. Of course, that now means Bowen calls notorious actor Danny Dyer his father-in-law.

Dyer is a massive West Ham fan and has often spoken about his delight at the Hammers' captain now being part of his family. Adding to that, the entire Dyer clan live in east London, and Bowen would have to think hard about relocating.

There was one big player who stood out as the hardest for Danny Dyer...

Speaking to talkSPORT in 2025, The Football Factory star was quizzed over whether he'd accept the West Ham captain jumping ship to any other club. At first, he shut down the idea of an Arsenal move, saying: "He’s never going to do that. Why would he? What’s in it for him?"

The prospect of another cross-London switch was quickly denied, too. This time, Dyer ruled out Chelsea as a possible option: "Why would he go there?"

However, two teams did come up in the conversation that Dyer claimed he could 'suffer' seeing his son-in-law join. First was European giants, and possibly the biggest club in the world, Real Madrid: "Real Madrid? Yeah, for sure."

Interestingly, it appears only one Premier League club would leave Dyer 'over the moon' for Bowen. Manchester City were given as the other acceptable destination. Dyer said:

"Listen, it’s his career. City? I wouldn’t mind that, I’d suffer that.

"I’m not going to lie, it would hurt, but he’s a grown man and he makes his own decisions. It would obviously hurt, but of course I would be over the moon for him."

With West Ham suffering relegation under Nuno Espirito Santo in 2026, Bowen and his teammates had to face the reality that they would be lining up in the second-tier of English football. However, the winger has stayed loyal to the Irons so far, despite the demotion, and the subsequent poor form to start the new campaign.

However, there will continue to be no shortage of clubs interested in the forward, who can play across the frontline. Reports over the summer suggested London rivals Chelsea were among the front-runners to secure his signature.

The Blues would likely be another team on Dyer's no-list. But with Bowen having racked up 22 England caps, he will surely have a pick of the club he desires should he decide to part ways with the east London side.

#1309. The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour–nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour–nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

Legends and additional references for Supplementary Tables 1–6.

Behaviour statistics. Summary information for all behavioural tests for each manipulation. Values are reported to 1 decimal place. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). In cases in which a Benjamini–Hochberg correction was made for multiple comparisons, an adjusted P value (p′) is shown (where p′ = P × m/i, where i is rank and m is number of cohorts tested; Methods). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For self-stimulation, ‘presses’ means the number of inactive lever presses has been subtracted from the number of active lever presses. In flavour conditioning experiments in which mice began the test with >90% preference for one flavour, statistics are also provided (in parentheses) with these mice excluded. Permutation (perm.) tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note: this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Dopamine imaging statistics. Summary information for all recordings of dopamine release in each brain region. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For photometry traces, dF′/F′ means the dF/F values seen during sham infusion have been subtracted. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. For fall times, s′ means that the time is relative to the end of the infusion. For peak times during licking, s′ means that the time is relative to the start of the first licking bout. The baseline is defined as the first 10 min of the recording for GI and post-GI measurements, or 0–20 s before the start of the first licking bout for oral measurements. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n >9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Single-cell imaging statistics. Summary information for all 1- and 2-photon miniscope recordings. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. The number (n) of animals and number of cells are reported separately. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to either the onset of the licking bout or to the approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. Population-weighted activity (pop-z) is calculated for a group of neurons (for example, activated or inhibited neurons) by multiplying activity by the fraction of neurons belonging to that group. Linear-mixed models (LME) treat mouse differences as both a fixed random effect and covariate (Methods). The relative contribution of mouse differences to total variance is reported by ICCs. Note that, for PCA, the number of PCs is equal to the number of cells. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means that the lowest calculable P value for those tests is 1 × 10−5).

fMRI imaging statistics (n = 38). Activity from left and right BLA clusters binned every 2 min (20 min total), as shown in Extended Data Figs. 10f and 11n. For PET statistics, see ref. 56. Each of the ten time bins after glucose intake was contrasted against the baseline (2 min before glucose intake), representing the change in brain activity after glucose intake relative to the baseline. The contrast for the first effect was [ones(1,10)], and for the following contrasts [1], corresponding to the different time bins. The significance threshold was P < 0.05, FWE-corrected for multiple comparisons at the voxel level within the left or right BLA mask, respectively, with initial peak-level threshold set to P < 0.05 uncorrected.

Pseudorabies statistics. Regional labelling (load) was normalized to VTA load to control for injection efficiency. From the 1,328 annotated CCFv3 regions, only grey-matter areas were retained (372 total), with cortical layers collapsed into single structures. Regions smaller than 100 × 100 × 100 pixels were excluded to remove small nuclei with high variance from few labelled cells, yielding 131 analysed regions.

Brain connectivity tables. Connectivity matrices were generated manually, with each pair given a number indicating bidirectional projection strength from 0 (no known direct connection) to 5 (strongest projection known from this area). The connectivity strength between an area and itself was assigned a value of 5. For deciding what strength to assign a projection, large databases like the Allan Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (ref. 1 of the Supplementary References) were preferred, supplemented by additional sources comprising reviews and anatomical tracing studies (refs. 2–32 of the Supplementary References).

#1308. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

Matt Law has turned his attention to how the player has embraced his role, and who contributed to his success, including former boss Liam Rosenior.

Others have struggled, but, “Pedro, though, has been so comfortable as Chelsea’s No 9 at the start of this season that he not only wears the number on the back of his shirt. Having taken his tally to five goals with two cool finishes against Bournemouth, the £55m signing this week showed off a custom-made necklace that features a large nine.”

Everton could go as high as third today. They would need to put 10 past Chelsea to equal Brighton’s goal difference.

Chelsea, would need 11, if they were to move from sixth to leapfrog Brighton. That would be a busy liveblog.

Matchweek 6 ✅ How the table stands 👇 https://t.co/tJF9PhdCje

The Chelsea social media team have taken some 1990s TV background music and created a happening montage.

Today's setting. 📍 #CFC | #EVECHE https://t.co/PK0onwYMr8

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1307. Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.

Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.

Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.

Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.

Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time. This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type). To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) and throughout vascular development. In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig. 1b). This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.5 and E12.5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO. However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

The absolute fold change of the ratio of Vegfr2KO ECs versus the ratio of control Tomato+ cells is indicated in red. c, Representative gating scheme for the ratiometric analysis (see also Extended Data Fig. 1a). d, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 retinas immunostained for Tomato, YFP and ERG (which labels EC nuclei). Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing the zonal distribution and percentage of Tomato+Cre+ cells when equal numbers of randomly selected YFP+ and Tomato+ cells were plotted (see method in Extended Data Fig. 3a). Right, log2 ratio of Tomato+/YFP+ cells detected in whole-mount retina immunostainings, showing an overall competitive disadvantage of Vegfr2KO cells in the mapped retinas. e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for ERG at P7, from pups injected with 4-OHT at P1. Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing distribution of MTomato+ERG+ (wild-type, Vegfr2HET or Vegfr2KO) cells in space in relation to MTomato−ERG+ (wild-type) cells. f, Bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of the indicated cells in the indicated areas and genotypes. g, log2 fold change of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 cells relative to the respective control wild-type cells. Numbers indicate fold change (×) between the two groups. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm. A, arteries; AF, angiogenic front; dist., distance; freq., frequency; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; LE, leading edge; MA, mature area; V, veins; WT, wild type.

VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).

To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.

Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.

We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).

a, Representative confocal micrograph of a control P7 retina immunostained for the proliferation marker Ki-67 and the EC nuclear marker ERG. The chart shows the frequency of Ki-67+ERG+ (pink pseudocolored) nuclei in different vascular zones. b, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 mice at P7, immunostained for YFP, Tomato, ERG and Ki-67. Yellow arrows indicate YFP+Ki-67+ cells and magenta arrows Tomato+Ki-67+ ECs. c, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 retinas induced at P1 and analysed at P20. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing that Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 ECs grow in veins and surrounding capillaries. d,e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 and respective quantification charts, showing increased apoptosis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 but not Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs. f, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice induced at P4 and analysed at P7. Arrows indicate recombined ECs (Tomato+) that are Ki-67+ (yellow) and Ki-67− (white), respectively. Chart shows the percentage of Tomato+ ECs positive for Ki-67. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,c–e), 50 μm (b,f). Cap., capillaries; CC3, cleaved caspase 3; Ctrl, control; DCap, distal capillaries; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; PCap, proximal capillaries. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods of time and later to form most of the perivenous capillary vessels and the deeper vascular plexus that developed during a second wave of VEGF-independent angiogenesis from P7 to P20 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This was consistent with previous findings showing that the tip cells that dive to form the deeper vascular plexus in the retina lack expression of the VEGFR2 signalling target gene Esm1; instead, their migration is dependent on other pathways such as Alk or TGFβ and WNT signalling25,26,27.

Together, these data show that VEGFR2 function is essential for the initial sprouting angiogenesis driven by high VEGF levels in hypoxic embryos and organs but not for the development of veins and perivenous capillaries or the subsequent steps of capillary angiogenesis and remodelling that occur after the first vascular plexus is formed in various organs. Thus, by forming veins, which are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis23, Vegfr2KO ECs can continue to proliferate and participate in subsequent steps of vascular development for long periods of time.

We previously observed that the distribution of Vegfr2KO ECs in the retina plexus at P7 differed between animals with long-term (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) and short-term (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7) mosaic deletion of Vegfr2. Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front than Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs (Fig. 1f,g). Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs also proliferated normally (Fig. 2b). Therefore, we hypothesized that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs might be genetically rewired and adapt over time to loss of the most important receptor for VEGF.

To assess the early response of ECs to loss of VEGFR2, we first analysed apoptosis markers in growing retina vessels, as VEGFR2 has been shown to regulate EC survival. Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice showed a very significant increase in the number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase 3 positive) ECs (Fig. 2d). This apoptosis was a reaction to the acute loss of VEGFR2, as Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 or even Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 mice did not show any apoptotic ECs (Fig. 2e), suggesting adaptation of the surviving cells over time. When the acute loss of Vegfr2 was induced in all ECs, we observed an immediate depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs from the VEGF-high angiogenic front, but not from veins or more mature vessels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Therefore, even though many ECs in the retina plexus showed upregulation of the apoptosis marker in the first days after Vegfr2 loss (Fig. 2d), only the angiogenic ECs that were exposed to high VEGF levels at the time of Vegfr2 deletion died (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

We also found that Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs were significantly less proliferative than control cells only in the heart and kidney (Fig. 2f), whereas the proliferation of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was similar to that of controls (Fig. 2b). This suggests that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time and are later able to proliferate in these organs. In the newborn retina, deletion of Vegfr2 did not affect the proliferation of surviving ECs in any segment (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that in this organ VEGFR2 mainly controls EC migration and survival, not proliferation.

Together, our data suggest that ECs lacking VEGF signalling during active angiogenesis suffer an acute VEGFR2 withdrawal effect, followed by a period of adaptation to the loss, after which they can form new vessels. ECs that are more distant from the VEGF source, and therefore have less VEGF signalling, adapt better to the loss and can expand over time, particularly in veins and perivenous vessels.

To further confirm the insensitivity of more mature ECs to loss of VEGFR2 signalling, we deleted Vegfr2 in several adult quiescent vascular beds for 2 weeks. Only the quiescent sinusoidal liver endothelium showed a strong sensitivity and loss of Vegfr2KO ECs, whereas only the kidney endothelium showed significantly lower proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting that only fenestrated or discontinuous mature endothelial vessels present in these organs remain sensitive to VEGFR2 loss.

Given the observed differences in the biology of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of these cells and respective control Tomato+ cells to identify possible differences in their transcriptional profiles and potential mechanisms of adaptation to loss of VEGFR2 signalling in distinct organ vascular beds.

Although VEGFR2 is a central regulator of angiogenesis and widely regarded as essential for EC biology, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs showed only modest changes in their transcriptome (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6), even though VEGFR2 protein and downstream signalling were lost already within the first 24 h following 4-OHT administration (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). In general, the expression of genes related to sprouting or tip cell biology was decreased, whereas that of genes related to apoptosis and vascular permeability was increased in all organs analysed (Fig. 3a,b). However, considerable differences were observed among organs.

a,b, Heatmaps displaying the average logarithmic fold change (log2FC) of all (a) or top (b) DEGs in mutant ECs for the indicated filter conditions (see Extended Data Fig. 6a for the single-cell method). c,j, Violin plot and dot plots showing the expression levels of the last exon (exon 30) and the deleted floxed exon (exon 3), demonstrating Vegfr2 deletion efficiency, in brain (c) and heart (j). Negative numbers in red indicate the fold change between conditions. d,k, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) showing the identified EC clusters and histobar plots showing their proportions per condition in brain (d) and heart (k). e,l, Dot plots showing the top cluster marker genes in brain (e) and heart (l). f,m, UMAP spatial distributions of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in brain (f) and heart (m). Bar plots show log2 ratios of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 over control cells per EC cluster. g,n, Volcano plots depicting the top DEGs and other selected and biologically significant genes when comparing control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in brain (g) and heart (n). h,o, Top significantly upregulated and downregulated hallmark pathways in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs compared with control ECs in brain (h) and heart (o). Highlighted hallmarks match the colour code used in g and n. i,p, Heatmaps showing the average log2FC of apoptosis- and tip cell-related genes in Vegfr2IECKO-P4-P7 ECs compared with control ECs in brain (i) and heart (p). For volcano plots and heatmaps (a,b,g,i,n,p), statistical analyses used Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For hallmark pathways (h,o), statistical analyses used the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea) and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

In the brain, clusters of proliferating (S–G2–M) ECs expressing venous capillaries markers were increased after Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days (Fig. 3c–f). This was consistent with higher clonal expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs from P1 to P20 in this organ (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Clusters comprising capillary and activated or angiogenic ECs (with high expression of Apln, Adm, Mcam, Lamb1 and Angpt2) were decreased (Fig. 3d–f). In total, only 569 genes were significantly deregulated (Fig. 3g). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an increase in the expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as G2M, DNA repair and mitotic spindle genes, confirming the increase in EC proliferation (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a). The expression of most tip cell marker genes was decreased in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6a–f).

In contrast to those in the brain, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 capillary ECs in the heart were significantly less proliferative (Fig. 3j–m and Extended Data Fig. 7b), matching the 54% decrease in Ki-67 percentage observed in sections (Fig. 2f). The proportion of mutant ECs found in bigger vessels (arteries and veins) was increased 2- to 4-fold (Fig. 3k–m), suggesting a proportional fast depletion of Vegfr2KO capillary ECs in only 3 days. Unlike in the brain, GSEA of Vegfr2KO heart ECs showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as decreases in expression of G2M, mitotic spindle and tip cell genes (Fig. 3n–p), in accordance with the decrease in proliferation and sprouting of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 heart ECs. Vegfr2KO heart ECs also showed upregulation of genes related to apoptosis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Fig. 3n–p), as has been shown previously for ECs losing ERK signalling28.

In contrast to the results for brain and heart, we found no significant difference in the proportions of proliferating cells among control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in lung (Extended Data Fig. 6g–j), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 and clonal analysis (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). The proportion of the vein cluster was only slightly increased, and the capillary cluster was slightly decreased. Despite the lack of significant changes in cluster proportions, GSEA showed increased TNF signalling through NF-κB, hypoxia and reactive oxygen species signalling and a decrease in the interferon response (Extended Data Fig. 6k,l). In lung, there was only a small trend of decreased expression of tip cell marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 6m), and several genes related to apoptosis were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m).

In the kidney, similar to the heart, Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days led to an increase in the relative proportion of ECs of bigger vessels (arteries and veins), suggesting fast depletion of a fraction of capillary ECs in only 3 days (Extended Data Fig. 6n–q). Proliferation and clonal expansion of kidney capillary ECs were also reduced (Extended Data Figs. 6o,q and 7d), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 (Fig. 2f). GSEA showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F, G2M and mitotic spindle genes and an increase in the expression of genes related to p53, xenobiotic metabolism and apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), indicative of cellular stress in kidney ECs after short-term Vegfr2 deletion from P4 to P7. Similar to brain and heart ECs, the expression of tip cell marker genes was also decreased in kidney Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 6t).

Following our analysis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs of distinct organs to identify potential differences in gene expression related to long-term adaptation of cells to loss of VEGFR2 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In contrast to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs exhibited predominantly upregulation rather than downregulation of genes, including marked upregulation of several venous-enriched genes (compare Figs. 3a,b and 4a).
