After phase separation by centrifugation, the upper aqueous phase containing gDNA was transferred to a new tube. For Mtb-derived samples, a second 1:1 PCI extraction was performed in the presence of 500 mM NaCl, with gentle mixing followed by 30-min incubation at room temperature. The aqueous phase—either singly (Msm) or dually (Mtb) extracted—was treated with RNase A at 37 °C for 45 min to degrade RNA. A final 1:1 chloroform extraction was performed to remove residual phenol, after which gDNA was recovered by alcohol precipitation. To each sample, 1/10 volume of 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.2) and 1/300 volume of GlycoBlue (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM9516) were added, followed by either 1 volume of isopropanol (Mtb) or 2.5 volumes of ethanol (Msm). Samples were incubated overnight at –20 °C, then centrifuged to pellet the DNA. The pellet was washed twice with 70% ethanol and resuspended in either molecular-biology-grade water or elution buffer (QIAGEN, 19086). DNA concentration was measured with a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen) to ensure accurate input into library amplification reactions.

Genomic DNA was extracted using the Omega Bio-Tek Mag-Bind Universal Pathogen DNA Kit (M4029), along with a Geno/Grinder for cell lysis and a Hamilton Starlet for partial automation. The 3.3-ml cultures were transferred to 2.2-ml 96-well deep-well plates, with 2 ml of each culture allocated to one plate for extraction and the remaining volume to a second plate as a back-up. All plates were centrifuged (4,000 rpm, 10 min) to pellet the bacteria, and the supernatant was discarded. Back-up plates were covered with foil seals, bagged and stored at –80 °C. For the extraction plates, each pellet was resuspended in 520 μl SLX-Mlus buffer, and foil seals were applied. Plates were incubated at 80 °C for 1.5 h to achieve heat inactivation, allowing removal from the BSL-3 facility. After brief centrifugation (4,000 rpm, 1 min) to facilitate clean detachment of the foil seals, plate contents were transferred to an EZ-96 disruptor plate and resealed for mechanical lysis on a Geno/Grinder (2 × 1-min cycles at 1,750 rpm). After centrifugation (2,000g, 1 min) and unsealing, 53 μl DS buffer and 20 μl proteinase K were added to each well. Plates were resealed, vortexed and incubated at 70 °C for 15 min, with an additional vortexing step at the halfway point. Plates were again centrifuged (4,000 rpm, 10 min) and unsealed, and the remainder of the extraction process was done using a Hamilton Starlet liquid handling system. During this process, 300 µl was transferred from each well of the disruptor plate to the corresponding well of a 1.7-ml 96-well deep-well plate. To each well, 300 µl RBB buffer, 300 µl XP2 binding buffer and 20 µl Mag-Bind Particles RQ were added. Plates were vortexed at 1,000 rpm and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. Each plate was then placed on a magnetic separation device, and after 5 min the supernatant was aspirated and discarded. Plates were removed from the magnetic device, and 600 µl VHB buffer was added to each sample. Plates were vortexed, incubated at room temperature for 2 min and returned to the magnetic device. The supernatant was removed, and the VHB wash was repeated once. This procedure was then repeated using SPM buffer. After removal of the final supernatant, the magnetic beads were allowed to dry on the magnetic device at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, 50 µl of EB buffer was added to each well, plates were vortexed and samples were heated to 70 °C for 5 min on a heating station. Plates were then returned to the magnetic device, and 50 µl of gDNA from each well was transferred into the corresponding well of a clean 96-well PCR microplate. DNA concentration was measured with a Thermo Fisher Scientific NanoDrop ND-8000 spectrophotometer.

Illumina libraries were constructed as described previously10, with two key modifications—increased gDNA input and the use of custom amplification and sequencing primers—to accommodate the increased size and unique design of GI libraries. The barcode region was amplified from gDNA using NEBNext Ultra II Q5 Master Mix (NEB, M0544). The two barcodes are separated by only 6 bp, which minimizes template switching during amplification for deep sequencing. For the Msm screen, as well as for Mtb experiment 2, 4 µg of gDNA input was used, corresponding to around 5.6 × 108 genome copies and around 238× library coverage for Msm, and around 8.9 × 108 genome copies and around 398× library coverage for Mtb. For Mtb experiment 1, 2 µg of gDNA input was used, corresponding to around 199× library coverage. PCR cycling conditions were: 98 °C for 45 s; 12 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 64 °C for 30 s and 65 °C for 20 s; 65 °C for 5 min. Each PCR reaction included a common forward primer (0.5 μM final concentration) and a unique indexed reverse primer (0.5 μM). The forward primer contained a P5 flow cell attachment sequence. The reverse primer contained a P7 flow cell attachment sequence, a unique index for multiplexing and a standard Illumina read 2 sequencing primer binding site. After PCR amplification, each approximately 350-bp amplicon was purified using sparQ PureMag beads (Quantabio, 95196) using two-sided selection (0.75× and 0.12×). Eluted amplicons were quantified with a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer, and amplicon size and purity were quality-controlled by visualization on an Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies G2991AA, 5067-5585 and 5067-5584). To assess library quality and ensure equal read depth across samples, individual amplicons were at first pooled in equal volumes and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq according to the manufacturer’s instructions. To increase sequence diversity, a PhiX spike-in of 10% (PhiX Control v3; Illumina, FC-110-3001) was included. Sequencing was performed in single-read mode (1 × 50 bp) with an 8-bp i7 index read. A custom sequencing primer binding immediately adjacent to the barcode cassette was spiked into the standard Illumina read 1 primer mix to enable sequencing of both sample barcodes and PhiX DNA. After the MiSeq run, amplicons were repooled such that the volume of each sample was scaled according to its read count. The rebalanced pool was then sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeqX Plus sequencer according to the manufacturer’s instructions, using the same sequencing conditions as in the MiSeq run. Library amplification primers and the custom sequencing primer are listed in Supplementary Table 6.

Amplicon libraries from plasmid DNA were prepared using the same protocol as for gDNA, except that 10 ng DNA input and 11 PCR cycles were used. For validation of single-sgRNA libraries, sequencing was performed using the Illumina MiSeq Nano platform with 25-bp reads (sufficient because of the lower library complexity and single-barcode design).

Illumina libraries were constructed as described previously39.

Sequencing reads were aligned to a reference set of expected sequences using subread-align (v.1.6.0) with default parameters80. For GI libraries, the reference set included barcode pairs, and read counts were subsequently assigned to the corresponding sgRNA pairs. For RLC25, the reference set included the sgRNA sequences themselves. Differences in sequencing depth between samples were normalized using the trimmed total reads (TTR) method73.

Depletion of sgRNA pairs in GI screens was quantified by estimating the L2FC of the mean counts in the +ATc samples relative to the mean counts in the –ATc samples. The pairs containing two non-targeting control sgRNAs were used in a second normalization step that sets their median L2FC as equal to 0, controlling for the enrichment of non-targeting guides in the library10. Finally, L2FC data points were subjected to quality-control filters, including removal of points that flatlined10 or reached the limit of detection (fewer than five mean observed reads). sgRNA pairs with fewer than three data points passing quality control were excluded from further analysis.

Depletion of sgRNAs in chemical–genetic screens was quantified by MAGeCK81 (v.0.5.7), using the alphamedian method and normalizing counts relative to non-targeting controls (using the flags ‘--gene-lfc-method alphamedian --norm-method control’).

The depletion of sgRNA pairs in GI experiments was modelled using a previously established Bayesian piecewise linear regression model, referred to as a two-line model10. In brief, the parameters αl and βl represent the intercept and depletion of the initial phase of depletion, which then transitions at a point γ, to a second phase with a rate of depletion βe. With this model, a prediction of L2FC at a generation, G, can be obtained as follows:

Samples from the Bayesian two-line model were obtained for all sgRNA pairs using Stan (cmdstan v.2.35, cmdstanpy v.1.2.4)82. To quantify a GI score, we first defined the degree to which pairs of sgRNAs deviated from expectations using an additive model of L2FC (which is equivalent to a multiplicative model in linear space)83. Single-targeting pairs, in which a targeting sgRNA is paired with a non-targeting control, are used to determine the fitness effect of knocking down a particular gene. Expected effects of knocking down two genes are therefore taken as the sum of individual effects:

where \(\text{L2FC}(G|{g}_{1}=a,{g}_{2}=b)\) represents the L2FC predicted by the Bayesian two-line model at generation G for a given pair of guides, a and b, at sgRNA positions 1 and 2, respectively, and NT represents the non-targeting controls. Deviations from expectations are then defined as follows:

To summarize the deviations to a single value, we define ΔL2FC as the deviation from expectations at G = 25.

To address the possibility of a floor effect84 (cases in which the expected phenotype exceeds the maximal fitness cost that can be accurately detected in our experiment), a generalized additive model (GAM)85 was fitted using the bam function from the mgcv package (v.1.9-3) in R (v.4.3.1) to correct the observed deviations. Deviations were modelled as:

where \(\hat{s}\) is the penalized regression spline GAM (with k = 20, method = “ML”, scaled t-distribution family). By modelling deviations in this manner, the penalized smoothing encourages predictions to follow the observed trend in data-sparse regions (that is, a near-linear continuation of the observed versus expected relationship), effectively reducing abrupt changes in deviations when there is little data to support them. The final, corrected, deviations were thus calculated as:

Finally, the GI score for a pair of genes A and B was summarized as the median of the Δ′ for all of the guide pairs targeting those genes; that is,

A Bayesian mixture model was used to identify statistically significant interactions. The mixture consisted of two distributions: a normal distribution representing the null hypothesis of no interaction with a prior mean of 0, and a uniform distribution representing the alternative hypothesis. The posterior probability of a GI score belonging to the alternative hypothesis was calculated, and interactions were classified as likely interactions if the posterior probability was greater than 0.5, and as confident interactions if the posterior probability was greater than 0.95. We use a cut-off of 0.5 for likely interactions because this corresponds to the point at which GI scores are more likely to be explained by the uniform distribution than by the normal distribution.

To integrate the evidence from the two independent Mtb screens (experiment 1 and experiment 2) into a single, directly interpretable probability, a joint Bayesian mixture model was fitted to the paired GI scores. For each gene pair, the GI score in each experiment and its standard error (that is, mean GI score and the standard deviation of Δ′ from the Bayesian two-line model) were taken as the x,y coordinates and their measurement uncertainties.

The mixture consisted of five components defined over the range of GI scores: a null component and four interaction components, one for each quadrant. The null hypothesis of no interaction was represented by a bivariate normal distribution centred near the origin, with a correlation parameter, ρ, given a weakly informative prior centred at zero. Allowing ρ to be a free parameter allowed the model to learn any existing correlation observed in the null distribution, owing to each screen using the same library and protocols. Per-pair measurement error was incorporated into the null by adding each pair’s squared standard error to the variance on the corresponding axis and scaling ρ accordingly (see Stan model code for implementation details). This approach incorporates the uncertainty associated with each GI-score estimate, down-weighting imprecise measurements while integrating both the consistency and the precision of observed effects across the two screens.

The four interaction components corresponded to the concordant negative quadrant, the concordant positive quadrant and the two discordant quadrants in which the two experiments disagreed in sign (one positive and the other negative). Each quadrant was modelled as a product of per-axis uniform densities over the range of observed scores, which were winsorized at the 0.1st and 99.9th percentiles to reduce the influence of outliers. Because pairs near a quadrant edge could belong to a neighbouring quadrant owing to measurement uncertainty, the uniform densities were convolved with the per-pair measurement error at the origin. Thus, a pair lying near an axis is assigned partly to each quadrant, and the model identifies the most likely membership from the mixture. The mixture weights were given a Dirichlet(2, 2, 36) prior over the concordant, discordant and null components, placing an 18-fold higher weight on the null, reflecting the expectation that most gene pairs do not interact. Concordant and discordant weights were divided evenly between their two respective quadrants (two discordant quadrants and the concordant positive and concordant negative quadrants). The model was fitted using Stan (cmdstan v.2.35, cmdstanpy v.1.2.4). For each gene pair, the posterior probability of belonging to each component was computed and summarized as the probability of a negative, positive or discordant interaction, and of no interaction. As in the single-experiment analysis, a pair was classified as a likely interaction when the largest of its interaction-class probabilities exceeded 0.5 and as a confident interaction when it exceeded 0.95, and was labelled negative, positive or discordant according to the dominant class.

To explore patterns of similarity in GI profiles, the GI matrix was hierarchically clustered using average linkage with Pearson correlation as the similarity measure, as implemented in SciPy86. At each internal node of the clustering hierarchy, the descendant genes were tested for Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment using GOATOOLS87. GO annotations were obtained from UniProt and mapped to the go-basic ontology, with the full set of genes in the GI map used as the background. Enrichment P values were calculated using Fisher’s exact test and corrected for multiple-hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Nodes were designated as key nodes when they represented the most significant occurrence (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for at least one biological process term. Each key node was labelled with its most significant GO term, and a GO-DAG specificity constraint was enforced such that no parent node carried a more specific term than its descendants. To reduce redundancy, key nodes with highly overlapping parent gene sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.8) were removed. Distinct colours were assigned to the remaining key nodes and propagated through their descendant branches, producing functionally labelled dendrograms in which leaves inherited the most specific term in their lineage.

Pathways were defined using a combination of KEGG and PATRIC pathways together with manual curation (Supplementary Table 4). Genes were assigned to pathways on the basis of manual curation and AI-assisted literature review (Claude Sonnet 4.5). Gene pairs were categorized as having a significant GI (p > 0.5) or not, and Fisher’s exact test was used to assess the association between pathway pairs and significant GIs. Self-interactions, in which a gene is targeted twice (that is, A + A), were excluded from the analysis. The resulting P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The analysis was performed twice: once using all gene pairs and once excluding potential polar effects (defined as pairs in which the genes were five genes or fewer apart), to assess how significance changed.

Sequences for selected genes were co-folded with AlphaFold-Multimer28 (v.3) to predict protein complex structures and AlphaFold34 to predict PPIs. All model inputs for Mtb used amino acid sequences from the H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584). All model inputs for Msm used amino acid sequences translated using BioPython from strain mc2155 (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), with the following exceptions. MSMEG5414 in the reference genome was split into proteins MSMEG5414A and MSMEG5414B. Four genes are misannotated in the reference genome as pseudogenes, and their translations were manually included: MSMEG4629:folC and MSMEG1828 from another genome (GenBank: CP009494); MSMEG1843:ahcY from UniProt (accession A4ZHR8); and MSMEG1400:fusA1 from a previously reported sequence88,89. All sequence inputs for Msm can be found in the file msm_essential_proteome.fa in our linked GitHub repository (see ‘Code availability’). AlphaFold-Multimer inputs were formatted as pairs of monomers28. These complexes were predicted using LocalColabFold90 v.1.5.5 (https://github.com/YoshitakaMo/localcolabfold)90 on an NVIDIA L40S GPU and 16 24-GB CPUs. The model was run with three recycles and AMBER relaxation. AlphaFold3 inputs were prepared following a modified pooled AlphaFold3 approach27. Within the bin-packing strategy, smaller protein sequences were prioritized to maximize the number of monomers per pool. In both cases, five predicted structures were generated per input. Predicted TM scores (pTMs) and interface predicted TM scores (ipTMs) for any given gene or gene pair, respectively, were taken as a mean across all models. ipTMs were corrected for combined protein length as previously described27. In Supplementary Tables 2 and 3, columns from pooled inputs on the web server have the suffix or infix ‘_webserver’.

Structures and scores were also generated locally for Mtb using the same pooled inputs as the AlphaFold3 web server. Per-chain multiple sequence alignments were generated with ColabFold v.1.5.590 using MMseqs2 18.8cc5c91 against the UniRef30 (2023-02) and ColabFold environmental clusters (2021-08; comprising filtered BFD, MGnify, MetaEuk and SMAG sub-databases), with GPU-accelerated prefiltering (--gpu 1 --prefilter-mode 1). The output was written directly in AlphaFold3-compatible JSON form (--af3-json), yielding one unpaired multiple sequence alignment per chain. To avoid recomputing identical alignments across the many overlapping pools in this study, sequences were keyed by SHA-256 hash and computed only once; an indexed central cache of all previously generated alignments (about 3,800 unique sequences) was consulted on every job, with cache hits delivering byte-identical multiple sequence alignments and cache misses triggering a fresh ColabFold run that subsequently updated the cache. Co-folding was performed with AlphaFold3 v.3.0.14 executed inside an Apptainer/Singularity container on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs. For each pool, the per-chain multiple sequence alignments were combined into a single AlphaFold3 input JSON (dialect alphafold3, version 1), populating unpairedMsa from the ColabFold output; pairedMsa was left empty, deferring to AlphaFold3’s internal pairing logic. AlphaFold3 was invoked via run_alphafold.py with --flash_attention_implementation=triton and --resolve_msa_overlaps=false; all other parameters retained their AlphaFold3 defaults. A single random seed (modelSeeds = [1]) was used per input, producing five diffusion-sampled structures per pool from which downstream pTM and ipTM statistics were derived as described above. In Supplementary Table 3, the resulting columns have the suffix or infix ‘_local’.

For both the local and the web-server results, the total number of predicted PPIs for each single protein is listed with the prefix ‘degree’, following notation from graph theory. Each of these columns is suffixed with 1 or 2 to indicate the monomer to which it corresponds. These degrees are calculated cumulatively at three ipTM cut-offs (see Fig. 3f): for example, ‘degree_low_webserver1’ refers to all PPIs predicted for gene 1 with low or higher confidence using the web server.

All compounds were dissolved in DMSO (VWR, V0231) and dispensed using an HP D300e digital dispenser in a 384-well plate format using a twofold dilution series. DMSO did not exceed 1% of the final culture volume and was maintained at the same concentration across all samples. Cultures were synchronized in late logarithmic phase (OD600 nm = 0.2 to 1) and then back-diluted to a starting OD600 nm of 0.01 or 0.05. Fifty microlitres of cell suspension was plated in triplicate in wells containing the test compound. Plates were incubated standing at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The OD600 nm was evaluated using a Tecan Spark or Molecular Devices SpectraMax M2 microplate reader 7–14 days after plating, and the percentage growth was calculated relative to the DMSO vehicle control for each strain. MIC90 and MIC50 measurements were calculated in R using the drm function from the drc package92, with a four-parameter log-logistic model (LL.4). For all MIC curves, data are mean ± s.e.m. for triplicates.

Compounds were dispensed in a 384-well plate as described above for the MIC assays. For each pair of drugs, all combinations of the two-dilution series were plated, including dilution series in which each drug is present alone and a DMSO control in which neither drug is present. Each combination of concentrations was plated in triplicate. Cultures were grown and plated and the relative growth was measured as described for MIC assays, except that the cultures were seeded at OD600 nm = 0.025. Drug synergy was quantified using the synergyfinder v.3.14.0 R package93. For each checkerboard, mean percentage viability values were used to calculate the Bliss independence score94,95 at each combination of drug concentrations. The resulting scores were then scanned to find the most synergistic area (MSA) and most antagonistic area (MAA). These areas were defined as the 3 × 3 contiguous areas of the plate with the highest and lowest mean Bliss scores, respectively. The mean Bliss scores of the MSA and MAA are reported for each drug combination. Both metrics are reported to avoid bias in calling a drug pair synergistic or antagonistic. Following recommended guidelines96, drug pairs with an MSA mean Bliss score higher than 15 were considered synergistic, and drug pairs with an MAA mean Bliss score lower than –15 were considered antagonistic.

A wild-type H37Rv culture was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.05, and 500 μl of culture was added to each well of 24-well plates. Vertex-49 (6.25 μM or 12.5 μM) was added alone or in combination with either bedaquiline (0.45 μM or 0.89 μM) or ethambutol (3.61 μM or 7.21 μM) in triplicate for each concentration combination. Cultures were grown standing at 37 °C for 6 days and then plated in serial dilutions from 10−1 to 10−7 on 7H10 charcoal plates. Plates were grown for 21 days, and then colony-forming units (CFU) were counted. Because we did not have a full panel of concentration combinations, we opted to use the highest single agent (HSA) method of quantifying drug synergy97. In brief, the amount of killing (measured as the change in CFU per ml versus the no-drug control) with the combination of the two drugs is compared to the drug that shows the highest growth inhibition (the HSA) when used alone at the same concentration. The drug pair is considered synergistic if the combination of drugs results in more than 100-fold more killing than the HSA.

Cultures were grown for 5 days in 7H9-OADC with 100 ng ml−1 ATc to pre-deplete protein targets. The cultures were then washed twice in PBS containing 0.05% Tween-80 and adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.15 with fresh 7H9-OADC. After dilution, 4-ml screw-cap glass vials were filled with the cultures, and methylene blue dye was added at a final concentration of 0.001% (w/v). All vials were sealed tightly using a PTFE–rubber seal (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C4015-21), wrapped with parafilm and incubated shaking at 60 rpm at 37 °C in an anaerobic pouch (Becton Dickinson GasPak EZ container systems, BD 260683) for 3–4 days, after which photos were taken to determine whether the cultures turned clear (intact respiration) or remained blue (impaired respiration).

A 20-ml preculture of Msm in Middlebrook 7H9 medium (Sigma) supplemented with 0.5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin, 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80 was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm to saturation. Msm with pKM444 but no other genetic modification was grown without antibiotic in the preculture medium, whereas Msm modified with a 3×Flag tag encoded in its gDNA was grown with 50 µg ml−1 hygromycin in the preculture medium. Each preculture was used to inoculate 6 l of Middlebrook 7H9 supplemented with 0.08% (w/v) NaCl, 0.2% (w/v) d-glucose, 1% (w/v) tryptone and 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80, and was grown at 30 °C with shaking at 180 rpm for 48–72 h. The cells were collected by centrifugation at 6,500g for 20 min, and pellets were resuspended in 100 ml of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM benzamidine HCl, 5 mM aminocaproic acid and 1 mM PMSF. The cells were lysed with the Avestin EmulsiFlex-C3 homogenizer at 20–25 kpsi, and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 39,000g for 30 min, followed by isolation of the membranes by centrifugation at 200,000g for 1 h. The membranes were resuspended in TBS (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) and solubilized for 1 h with 1% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. Solubilized membranes were centrifuged at 200,000g for 1 h to remove insoluble material before binding to around 1 ml anti-Flag M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma) in a plastic column. The column was washed with ten column volumes of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside before eluting the bound protein with three column volumes of 150 µg ml−1 3×Flag peptide in TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside, followed by one column volume of TBS containing 0.05% (w/v) dodecyl maltoside. The eluted protein was concentrated with a centrifugal concentrator with 10-kDa molecular weight cut-off.

Protein (10 µg) was reduced with 20 mM dithiothreitol for 10 min at 95 °C and alkylated with 40 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min in the dark. Samples were diluted to a final concentration of 5% (w/v) SDS, and phosphoric acid was added to a final concentration of 1.2% (v/v). S-Trap protein binding buffer (165 µl) containing 90% (v/v) methanol and 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) was added to 27.5 µl acidified sample. The resulting mixture was passed through an S-trap micro column at 4,000g. The micro column was washed four times with the S-Trap protein binding buffer. Each sample was digested with 4 µg of trypsin in 20 µl of 50 mM TEAB for 1 h at 47 °C. Before elution, 4 µl of 50 mM TEAB pH 8 was added to the column. Peptides were eluted by centrifugation at 4,000g. Peptides were eluted from the column two more times with 40 µl of 0.2% (v/v) formic acid and 40 µl of 50% (v/v) acetonitrile with 0.2% (v/v) formic acid. Eluted peptides were dried and stored at –40 °C before mass-spectrometry analysis at the Network Biology Collaborative Centre at the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute using standard protocols for data-dependent acquisition.

The SAINTexpress98,99 software package was used to score protein interactions. In brief, peptide-level counts are summed for all detected proteins for both the tagged and the untagged samples (two replicates per condition). These were then used to obtain the protein-level L2FC of counts in the tagged samples relative to the untagged samples. The SAINTexpress package uses a Bayesian model to calculate the probability of an interaction for each protein and uses these probabilities to estimate the FDR.

IMV acidification assays were performed as previously described51. In brief, the membrane fraction from wild-type, ∆qcrB and ∆ms2764 Msm strains were isolated and resuspended in IMV resuspension buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgSO4, 5 mM 6-aminocaproic acid, 5 mM benzamidine hydrochloride and 20% [v/v] glycerol). IMV acidification experiments were performed in 96-well plates (BRANDplates pureGrade 96-well black microplates). NADH and succinate were prepared as electron donors as follows. NADH was prepared immediately before use by dissolving disodium NADH in water to a final concentration of 4 mM. Succinate was prepared by dissolving sodium succinate in water to a final concentration of 20 mM. A master solution containing ACMA assay buffer (10 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl and 5 mM MgCl2), 9-amino-6-chloro-2-methoxyacridine (ACMA) dye (3.125 µM), IMVs (5 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for succinate-driven acidification; 2 mg ml−1 total protein concentration for NADH-driven acidification) and 10 µM of Q203 (with a final concentration of 2% [v/v] DMSO) or an equivalent volume of compound-free DMSO vehicle was prepared and transferred into each well of the 96-well plate. The plate was incubated in the dark for approximately 15 min at room temperature before the start of the experiment. ACMA fluorescence was measured at 25 °C with a BioTek Synergy Neo2 Hybrid Multimode plate reader (Agilent Technologies), using an excitation wavelength of 410 nm and an emission wavelength of 480 nm. IMV acidification was initiated by the addition of NADH or succinate. Fluorescence was monitored for 20 min before the addition of nigericin in ethanol to a final concentration of 2 µM with 0.02% (v/v) ethanol. Fluorescence recovery was monitored for an additional 10 min. Fluorescence recovery was calculated as the absolute difference between the fluorescence immediately before and 10 min after nigericin addition. All IMV acidification experiments were performed with at least three replicates.

Sensor spot assays were performed as described previously100.

Cultures were grown and passaged twice to closely match optical densities. Final cultures were diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.17 (around 50,000 cells per μl), and tenfold serial dilutions were made. Multichannel pipettes were used to spot 2 μl of culture for each dilution onto 7H10 with or without ATc, with the appropriate selection of antibiotics. Images were taken after approximately 20 generations.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Raw sequencing data have ben deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under project numbers PRJNA1337647, PRJNA1338999 and PRJNA1346122. Pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding used the Mtb H37Rv reference proteome (UniProt: UP000001584) and translated sequences from the Msm mc2155 reference genome (RefSeq: NC_008596.1), unless noted otherwise in the Methods. Mass-spectrometry analysis used the Msm mc2155 reference proteome (UniProt: UP000000757). sgRNA sequences were designed using the Mtb H37Rv and Msm mc2155 reference genomes (RefSeq: NC_018143.2 and RefSeq: NC_008596.1, respectively).

a, Construction of dual-sgRNA libraries. Single-sgRNA constructs were cloned individually. To assemble the dual-sgRNA library, all single-sgRNA plasmids were pooled and subjected to two parallel digestions: (1) MfeI + XhoI to generate a backbone library, and (2) EcoRI + SalI to excise the sgRNA–barcode fragment and generate an insert library. Ligation of these two products places two sgRNA cassettes in tandem, followed by their corresponding unique barcodes. To quantify sgRNA abundance, the barcode region is amplified using flanking NGS primers. b, Overview of the pilot GI library design. Up to 24 sgRNAs were selected for each of 16 target genes. The resulting dual-sgRNA library was transformed into Msm and serially passaged +/–ATc, with samples collected every 2.5 to 5 generations. The relative abundance of each sgRNA pair was quantified by sequencing the barcode region. c, Density plot of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Vertical lines mark the expected L2FC window between –10 and –2. d, Heat map of GI scores for all dual-targeting constructs in the pilot library. Gene pairs highlighted in e–h are marked with dashed boxes. e–h, Scatter plots of ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC projected at generation 25 for all dual-sgRNA constructs targeting glgB and glgE (e), ponA1 and ponA2 (f), folA and folP1 (g) and rpoB and macE (h). Mtb experiment 1 and experiment 2 were derived from the same plasmid library. b,c,g,h,l,m, Heat maps of the Pearson correlation between sgRNA counts across all time points and replicates for the (b,c) Msm, (g,h) Mtb experiment 1 and (l,m) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. For each experiment, the (b,g,l) –ATc samples and (c,h,m) +ATc samples are shown on separate heat maps. d,i,n, Density plots of uncorrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (d) Msm, (i) Mtb experiment 1 and (n) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. e,j,o, Density plots of corrected ΔL2FC versus expected L2FC at 25 generations for all dual-targeting constructs in the (e) Msm, (j) Mtb experiment 1 and (o) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Corrected ΔL2FC values are calculated as the residual (observed – GAM-predicted L2FC) for each dual-targeting construct. For more information, see Methods: ‘Quantification of GIs’ and Figs. 1f and 2c and Extended Data Fig. 4c. f,k,p, Density plots of GI score versus combined gene vulnerability for all gene pairs in the (f) Msm, (k) Mtb experiment 1 and (p) Mtb experiment 2 libraries. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. g, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, Dendrogram of all genes (left), clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Representative clusters (right, from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, DNA replication, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis, and protein degradation). k, Scatter plot comparing GI scores in Mtb experiment 1 and Mtb experiment 2, coloured by joint model hit class. For each set, percent conservation was calculated as the number of conserved GIs divided by the number of Mtb GIs. The analysis was performed twice: once without additional filters (corresponding to the full bar height) and once excluding potential polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart; corresponding to the filled portion). g, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb, as in Fig. 3c. #1283. Fabregas: ‘Como must play our football, not scared of Champions League’

Cesc Fabregas insists Como ‘must always play the football that got us here’ in the Champions League against RC Lens. ‘You see some teams who look scared and scrape a point.’

It kicks off at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis in Lens Agglo at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and FC Porto vs. Napoli on the Liveblog.

This is only the second ever away fixture in Como’s Champions League history, and so the pressure is on to do the job even on unfamiliar territory.

So far in this historic campaign, they have beaten both RB Leipzig and Manchester United 4-1 at the Stadio Sinigaglia, but lost 3-2 away to Feyenoord.

“Every game is different and obviously we want to win, so I pick the players who are most suitable at this moment, there are four or five who can make the difference off the bench too, so fitness levels were influential,” Fabregas told Sky Sport Italia about his starting XI.

“It doesn’t matter if we are home or away, each match is important, but there is a lovely atmosphere here and it’s a good experience for us.”

The injuries remain substantive, missing Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao, Jesus Rodriguez and Jayden Addai, so Tasos Douvikas is the only available centre-forward, but Martin Baturina is rested.

“The lads seem fine, I spoke to them before leaving the hotel and it is a big opportunity for them. We’ve got to enjoy these moments. You see these teams who play so well domestically, then in the Champions League they look scared and scrape a point.

“We can win, we can lose, but we must always play the kind of football that got us here. That’s how we see it, because in our small world we must find the motivation to keep improving. We’ve been trying to create a clear identity for three years, whoever we play and wherever we play is not an alibi to forget out football.”

Como have won their last five competitive matches in a row, and have a huge fixture coming up this weekend in Serie A against Inter.

Como is the best football club in serie a that have graced the game so far.Entertaining football and good to watch.It looks like the Milan of late 80s and early 90s

#1282. NWSL Team of the Week: Croix Bethune breaks single-season assists record; Denver duo shines

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

No more second chances in the 2026 NWSL regular season. Decision Day is upon us, and before the chaos kicks off, players across the league are setting pitches ablaze with crucial performances. That means it's time to give out Attacking Third Team of the Week honors.

After weekly matches across the 2026 NWSL season, Attacking Third analysts will select players, a head coach, and an honorary captain based on weekend performances. Here you can find a mix of stats and data, analysis from our pundits, and highlights you may have missed over the weekend. If you're keeping track of who earned past honors, check out our previous team of the week.

It's been a wild year, and it feels like it's just getting started now that the postseason is rapidly approaching. That also means our team of the week honors will look slightly different following games moving forward. We'll hand out one more set of honors after Decision Day on November 1, but afterward, we'll be locked into playoffs and performances from the quarterfinals onward.

When it comes to the NWSL Shield, Gotham FC is taking the long road. If they manage to lift it, it'll be because they have a great goalkeeper to keep away any spoilers. Ann-Katrin Berger is back on the team of the week honors for keeping a newly eliminated and motivated Orlando Pride from deterring Gotham's quest for the title. She faced 19 shots, eight attempts on target, and made seven saves in a narrow but crucial victory.

Angel City's Evelyn Shores has become a bona fide two-way player this season and stands out on a backline that has Sarah Gorden and Savy King. She's back on the team of the week for another stellar performance, where she was instrumental in building up play and keeping the backline in shape. She led defenders on the team in duels (seven) and co-led in clearances (two) and interceptions (two).

Not that Tierna Davidson needed any more bullet points on her long resume for NWSL defender of the year, but scoring headers in the box was already on there. She did it again for Gotham FC and scored a decisive game-winner to keep the club ahead in the NWSL Shield race

Captain fantastic for @GothamFC second goal! 🎯Tierna Davidson doesn't miss in the box 💪Catch all the action on @CBSSportsNet 📺 pic.twitter.com/IJjecaVBDs

If you've ever heard of the iron woman concept in NWSL, then you're already familiar with Kaleigh Kurtz, but you might not be familiar with her dance moves. She showed them off after scoring her first goal with Denver Summit.

OUR IRON WOMAN GETS GER FIRST GOAL IN GREEN 🥲💚 pic.twitter.com/O1TTVwZMUV

Back on the team of the week is Janine Sonis after a two-assist performance for Denver Summit in a must-win game. Denver's playoff destiny is tricky, but possible, and Sonis is making sure she's leaving with something, her seventh and eighth assists of the year.

TASH FLINT, THAT'S YOURS. 💥 pic.twitter.com/J8fsKMFqz3

When the going gets tough this season, the tough runs away in fear of Jessie Fleming. The defensive midfielder has stepped up the club in a massive way between roster injuries and a red card suspension for Sophia Wilson. The Canadian international co-led the team in touches (66), led the team in recoveries (eight), and was a frequent outlet in building up play in a massive win over North Carolina.

Boston Legacy midfielder Alba Caño helped keep the team's spoiler reputation alive with an equalizer against San Diego. No NWSL Shield claimed on Boston's watch.

CAÑO HITS THE TOP CORNER 😤 pic.twitter.com/X3Ghk2G002

In 2024, Croix Bethune matched a single-season assist record (10) as a rookie. Now, it solely belongs to her. She delivered the record-setting assist to Vanessa DiBernardo for the game-winner.

Signature @haleyyhopkins pressure.Poise from @CroixBethune.Blast by @vdibernardo10.2-1 #KCBABY!!!! pic.twitter.com/xeOpsgNE8p

Seems like three points are easy to nab when Natasha Flint scores a break. The three points and goal differential could prove big in the playoff push.

Two minutes later, Denver goes again!!!Tash Flint makes it five. pic.twitter.com/LTrUb1snZf

Flexing her versatility over the weekend was Gisele Thompson for Angel City. Took her time on the ball and nailed the clinical finish.

Gisele Thompson gets it DONE 😤Her fifth of the season puts Angel City in front! pic.twitter.com/UO6ADFUL6m

Portland Thorns are a club with a lot of history, and Marie Muller etched her name into the chapter of big moments. A lethal blast on goal clinched a playoff spot for the team.

A LASER 🎯 BY MARIE MÜLLER pic.twitter.com/ucAyKUcwTu

The head-coaching rumor mill has gone pretty silent after Angel City's impressive second-half run under interim manager Leif Smerud. Another three points at home and the club is back in the playoffs for the first time since 2023. The performance is going to make it difficult for the front office to move on from the interim magician.

It wasn't just Portland Thorns thanking Marie Muller for her game-winning goal, but several others. Not quite decision day, but it was a defining goal for several clubs. The game-winner clinched playoff spots for Portland, Kansas City Current, Utah Royals, and Angel City FC.

#1281. Barcelona headline Women's Champions League Matchday 3 as league phase hits midway point

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League will reach the midway point of the league phase as Matchday 3 action kicks off Wednesday. The league phase table hardly looks like a final verdict, with only one team on maximum points, while some clubs are comfortable with split results and others are desperate to keep their campaigns alive. Matchday 3 offers an opportunity to either shake up the table or for clubs to separate themselves, with just four rounds of play left before February's knockout playoffs. Fans can watch all the action across CBS Sports platforms. Paramount+ will livestream matches all season, while select fixtures will also air on CBS Sports Golazo Network and CBS Sports Network. With Matchday 3 split across Wednesday and Thursday, here are four things we're keeping an eye on:

The reigning title holders return to the Champions League with even more hardware than before. The club and several players racked up plenty of honors at the Ballon d'Or ceremony on Monday. The club took home best club, manager Pere Romeu nabbed women's coach of the year, Vicky Lopez won best young talent and Cata Coll was named best goalkeeper.

Alexia Putellas, now with London City Lionesses, was awarded the women's Ballon d'Or, largely for her accomplishments during her final season with FC Barcelona, since the voting period ran from August 2025 to July 2026.

After defeating Paris FC 5-2 on Matchday 1, Barcelona followed up with a 6-0 blowout of Roma on Matchday 2. They're cruising during the league phase, especially with an attack powered by several standouts, including Lopez, Claudia Pina, Kerolin and Ewa Pajor.

Pajor, the Polish international, is now the all-time leading scorer in the Champions League's group and league phases, with 18 goals.

A new UWCL record for Ewa Pajor 👏Her 18th goal makes her the highest scorer in UWCL group/league phase history 👑Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/2LaFr3y5cj

They'll visit HB Koge on Thursday, and the Danish side is steadily growing into the competition after picking up its first win by beating Servette 5-1. The league phase leaders will be favorites to win, but Koge might not make it comfortable, as they play with nothing-to-lose energy.

OL Lyonnes made one of the biggest statements of the league phase so far with an opening-day 8-0 demolition of Servette, in which Melchie Dumornay scored a brace and Marie-Antoinette Katoto scored a hat trick. They're a Champions League mainstay and perennial contenders, but they were shut out by Chelsea on Matchday 2, with Blues goalkeeper Hannah Hampton putting her stamp on the tournament.

HANNAH HAMPTON STANDING ON HER HEAD 🤯Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/gd2mxcGJIF

OL Lyonnes will now face another club unbeaten in the league phase, Inter, on Wednesday. Inter have a win and a draw and have shown they are a plucky side to deal with, but if OL want to be lethal contenders, they have to make a statement against the tournament debutants. Dumornay's creativity and Katoto's clinical finishing, with U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes anchoring the midfield and a stacked roster around them, will be a tough challenge for any team, especially those newer to the league phase. Chelsea, meanwhile, have to contend with Roma, an Italian squad that's well on its way to another Champions League crashout, showing little improvement in year two of the new league phase format with just one draw over two games. If the Blues could keep OL off the scoreboard, they should be confident they can do the same against Roma, and if they don't, it'll bring more questions about the club's ability to manage Champions League expectations. German side Bayern Munich welcome Real Madrid in a showdown that could tip the league phase table. Bayern had a chance to make an opening-day statement but instead gave up a two-goal lead and settled for a draw against Manchester City, before picking up a crucial win away against Benfica in Portugal. Matches in this competition have often been won or lost late, and veteran Pernille Harder had her say for Bayern at Benfica, scoring her 50th UWCL goal in the 3-0 victory.

50 UWCL GOALS FOR PERNILLE HARDER 🌟She becomes just the fourth player in competition history to reach the milestone 👏Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/wG9RWk22sl

Real Madrid's two consecutive draws in the competition leave everyone wanting more. Colombia international Linda Caicedo is elite and has consistently shown her quality over the two matches, and if she and Felicia Schroder continue to build chemistry in attack, they'll be a dangerous combo to deal with.

The meeting between the German and Spanish clubs on Wednesday will be a key fixture to watch, as a win for either could put it in a more favorable position in the league phase table at the halfway point.

There were plenty of doubts around Paris Saint-Germain heading into the tournament, given their steep fall from Champions League grace. After a miserable campaign last season, the Parisians got off to another worrisome start with a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, in which they trailed for over 70 minutes before equalizing from the penalty spot. They quickly followed that up with a five-goal win over OH Leuven on Matchday 2, and now find themselves in a far better position than they were last year. Next up is Manchester City, a side that is still on the hunt for its first win of the tournament. Two sides carefully rebuilding their UWCL pedigree could produce either a cagey matchup or a momentum-shifting performance. Arsenal continue to baffle on the pitch. After a smash-and-grab for all three points on opening day against underdogs HB Koge, the Gunners were challenged by Paris FC in a 2-2 draw the following matchday. Winning ugly doesn't hide the fact that this is a team that has struggled to break opponents down, despite a talented roster, and it raises fair questions about manager Renee Slegers and her tactical approach. Goals from Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway help, but there is more that's expected from the group that won the UWCL title in 2025, even with Mariona Caldentey managing an injury at the moment. If they struggle against Benfica on Wednesday, it'll cast more doubt on the club's direction this season.

The bottom of the league phase table is already somewhat crowded, even with some unexpected clubs at the moment, but that's what makes the midway point of the tournament so exciting. Manchester City and Real Madrid might steal eyeballs, as neither team can keep drawing for much longer, but former dark horse BK Hacken and last year's dancing debutants OH Leuven have struggled to find the net. Hacken join Servette with zero points through two matchdays and will face Paris FC on Thursday. Paris FC are eager to take the next step in the UWCL, from unpredictable underdogs to bona fide contenders. Whoever drops points in the head-to-head could be out of the race for the top 12 in the league phase.

#1280. Champions League RECAP: Man City edge thriller against RB Leipzig and Arsenal hold on for win at Slavia Prague

By HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER and LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER

Relive Daily Mail Sport's coverage of Wednesday's Champions League fixtures, with Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City all in action.

The Champions League always manages to deliver.

We started the night with a shock upset as Fenerbahce managed to come from behind twice to defeat Liverpool in Istanbul - and the Reds' fans are not happy about it; there is a meltdown on X.

Then we were treated to a further 39 goals, including Como's record-equalling 9-1 crushing of Lens. I still can't get over that one.

Manchester City and Arsenal both played their parts in the goal-fest, bagging victories for themselves.

Now, we need to shoot off, but thank you once again for joining us on another entertaining night of footie.

We will see you all very soon. Goodnight.

You can watch the full highlights from Arsenal's win by clicking below.

It wasn't classic Arsenal, but they got the job done. And they were good in the first-half, with some good goals from players that needed them.

The Gunners are sitting pretty in third in the table, with three wins and that draw against Bayern Munich.

They will be pretty confident of reaching the last-16 again. Here's what they have left in the league:

Joleon Lescott, former Man City defender, TNT Sports:

I feel like his Man City career has been a bit of an odd one. He was never meant to be No 1, until he became available, and they jumped.

City ended up again selling one of the best young goalkeepers in Europe in James Trafford to accommodate him, and he's not really repaid them. Quite a few errors lately.

#1279. Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe apologizes after Mao meme comments amid growing backlash in China

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe issued an apology Tuesday after comments he made about former Chinese leader Mao Zedong led several sponsors to drop him and drew a backlash from Chinese state television. The day after the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony, which saw Mbappe leave the London Palladium empty-handed, began with an international drama involving China, Mbappe and LaLiga. It all started when Mbappe told French talk show "The Bridge" that the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." The clip also showed Mbappe's face on an image resembling Mao. To put that into context, a recurring joke, repeated in multiple memes, associates Mbappe with the word "dictator" for his influence in the sport and for how he interacts with teammates and players. During the 2026 World Cup, 2025 Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele called him "Mbappe Mobut," referring to Mobutu, the dictator who ran the Democratic Republic of Congo for more than 30 years. In September, Mbappe addressed the memes in an interview with France Football, saying that while he understood the jokes, they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people. There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history. Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life." Two Chinese brands that have deals with the French striker issued statements condemning the player's statements. Mengniu, the country's largest dairy producer, wrote that it, "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." Later on Tuesday, drinks giant Dongpeng issued a statement as well. "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments." According to the state-owned Global Times newspaper, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV's apps won't feature news related to the player, and the broadcaster will also stop streaming LaLiga matches.

Mao is obviously one of the most famous figures in modern China's history. He founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led the Communist Party until his death in 1976. Much has changed in China since his death, but the Chinese Communist Party still governs the country and sees jokes and memes about Mao as an insult to the party and the nation. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said, "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

The French striker issued a statement about the matter: "During a recent interview with me, I commented on an image of myself, but my comment was not appropriate, and I now realise that it hurt the feelings of many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone whom my words upset, as that was never my intention at all. I hold deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I express my sincere regret."

LaLiga also issued a statement, defending the agreement they still have in place with Chinese state television. "LALIGA deeply regrets the offence caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé's recent comments. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. Within the scope of our institutional responsibility, we apologise on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs. Spanish football stands for respect, coexistence and unity among people from all cultures. We extend our respect to China, its institutions and its people, and deeply value the support of the millions of fans who follow us every week. We reaffirm our commitment to a relationship built over many years. We are working with our partners and institutional counterparts in China to address this situation. Furthermore, in collaboration with clubs and players, we will introduce an awareness and communication protocol aimed at promoting respect for different cultures and helping to prevent similar situations in the future."

LaLiga president Javier Tebas, who recently also had multiple public disagreements with Real Madrid, wrote on X he "cannot allow the actions of an individual to tarnish this relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs competing in our professional leagues and the millions of Chinese fans. We are taking all measures within our power and working directly with our partners and counterparts in China to resolve this situation."

"Real Madrid C. F. wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort that may have been caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappé. Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people. Real Madrid reaffirms its commitment to the values of respect, coexistence, and understanding among cultures, and expresses its desire to continue strengthening the bonds of friendship and affection that unite it with China and its citizens."

#1278. Allegri: ‘Spoke to De Bruyne, difficulty but not alibi for Napoli’

Max Allegri makes surprising changes as Napoli visit FC Porto in the Champions League, but is tight-lipped on Kevin De Bruyne’s role. ‘There are objective difficulties, but they mustn’t be alibis.’

It kicks off at the Estadio do Dragao in Porto at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and RC Lens vs. Como on the Champions League Liveblog.

The Partenopei had a rough start to the Champions League this season with defeats to Arsenal and Villarreal, but finally got off the mark by beating Bodo/Glimt 4-3 in a chaotic encounter at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

This is a tricky trip to Porto, where Francesco Farioli’s side have a perfect domestic record, yet lost all three European fixtures to Manchester City, Real Betis and PSV Eindhoven.

“Unfortunately, it’s a risk to start Noa Lang because he had strong cramp on Sunday, he played four games in a row, so I preferred to rest him today,” Allegri told Amazon Prime Video Italia.

“De Bruyne told me his ankle is fine, I spoke to him, so I put him in the starting XI.”

Where the Belgium international is playing is confusing, as it could be in support of lone striker Rasmus Hojlund, or in the deep playmaker role with Scott McTominay more advanced instead.

“We must be aware that in football there are periods where things don’t go well, we need to be calm, aware that we’ve got to do more, but it is up to us to turn things around,” noted Allegri.

“We have two more games to play before the break for international duty, hopefully we’ll recover a few players after that. I believe in football when you hold back by just a centimetre, something you might take for granted, it makes a difference and you are punished for that.

“The results prove it, especially in the Champions League, where we alternated results and performances, so it is a step up we need to make. An example is Bodo/Glimt, when we conceded too easily at the end, because goal difference is crucial in the Champions League with this format.

“It’s a matter of responsibility and understanding the moments of the match, which we also saw on Sunday against Juventus.”

The 2-0 defeat at Juventus over the weekend only added to the injury crisis, as Giovanni Di Lorenzo and Mathias Olivera were the latest absentees.

They join Stanislav Lobotka, Leonardo Spinazzola, Alisson Santos, Benoit Badiashile, Costantino Favasuli, David Neres and Alessandro Buongiorno on the treatment table, while Luca Marianucci is ineligible for this tournament.

“We have many players who were and are out for a long time, so we’ve got to try to make the results co-exist with the fitness levels of the players. There are some objective difficulties, but they mustn’t become alibis,” insisted Allegri.

“We cannot concede goals the way we did against Bodo/Glimt and Juve. We absolutely must do better. When you are not afraid of conceding a goal is when it becomes easier to let them in.”

#1277. Are Brighton a Premier League contender? Manchester City EFL Cup match will be biggest test yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Is this the year Brighton and Hove Albion make the leap? In their 10th season in the Premier League, the Seagulls have long since moved on from being a side well run enough to keep its distance from the relegation race. Now they might reasonably aspire to another step forward, away from the mass of sides just outside the premium European places and into real contention for Champions League qualification. Indeed, if you are a more exuberant Brighton fan, the question you might be asking yourself is not whether your side has made the leap but whether it has bounded up two tiers over the course of one summer. After all, they sit third in the Premier League table with the division's best attack and its third-best defense; combine those and you have a plus-16 goal difference. Their nearest rival by that metric, Manchester City, is at plus-11. Beat City in the second of this week's doubleheader with Enzo Maresca's side and they will be two points off the league leaders, though Arsenal might well open up a gap. Then again, what do Brighton have to fear from the champions? They've already smashed them 3-0 this season. Even their 2-0 defeat to Liverpool did little to quell Brighton's momentum. Not for the first time in his managerial career, Fabian Hurzeler couldn't resist a snipe at the manager of a big-six opponent in defeat, but he did have a point when he argued that "there was one team who really tried to create and try to win this game." The Seagulls went down swinging at Anfield, drawing seven shot blocks from Andoni Iraola's side. It really was not an exaggeration to say that if Yasin Ayari or Charalampos Kostoulas had scored early on, this might have been another famous win for the boys from the south coast.

Does this all sound too good to be true? Well, then it probably is. Admittedly, Hurzeler's side had looked primed to push on at the end of last season, an impressive run of results in March and April securing an eighth-placed finish and Conference League football. Then, in customary Brighton fashion, their best players left. Danny Welbeck had been their leading scorer, Jan Paul van Hecke the leader in league minutes and a crucial ball progressor, and while Carlos Baleba had endured a down year in which he had battled injuries, he still looked the most likely to ascend to a Moises Caicedo/Alexis Mac Allister level in Brighton's long line of breakout talent in midfield. Brighton could be trusted to replace the players they sold well. Swapping out Van Hecke for Luka Vuskovic already looks like the greatest of swindles on Tottenham, who are happy enough with what they have, even if they might have let the next great center back slip away. It is arguably easier, though, to deal with players you have lost for a fee than with those snared from you by injury. Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh were the star wingers in last season's side, the former top 10 in the league for expected possession value added, the latter top 10 for take-ons. These wingers were critical for getting the ball into the box and creating threat when they got there. Injuries mean they have yet to take the field this season. You should not be able to cope with the loss of this much talent for so long. Some of Hurzeler's fixes have been ingenious. Maxim De Cuyper carried plenty of attacking thrust from left back, and after dalliances with a more advanced role last season, he has been converted to it permanently. The careful, steady integration of Kostoulas and Diego Gomez has paid dividends too. Meanwhile, at 35, Pascal Gross is as effective as he has ever been, with four assists and three goals already in this season's Premier League. Gross' pressing has also been critical to Brighton's success. According to data provided to CBS Sports by Gradient, the German international has made eight pressures leading to dangerous situations, placing him in the 99th percentile among Premier League players this season. Kostoulas and De Cuyper are similarly willing runners off the ball, adding up to a team that is even more energetic without the ball this season than it was last. In 2025-26, Brighton led the Premier League in passes per defensive action with 9.3, according to Wyscout. This season they also lead the division in this pressing metric, allowing opponents an average of 7.6 passes per defensive action. It is for that reason that only Wednesday's opponents, Manchester City, allow the other team fewer active minutes in possession than Brighton's 21.5.

Brighton's pressing intensity also means it is not that much of a surprise that they lead the league in counterattacking goals. As they do in goals from corners. As they do in higher-value chances where the shot is worth 0.1 expected goals or higher. As they do too in shots from outside the box. It all looks great, but then the sample size is still only eight games. That might be enough to form the outline of a conclusion in normal circumstances, but Brighton are one of only two teams in the league to have had a man advantage in two games so far this season. It should be said that both Aston Villa and Coventry looked like beaten teams when their player saw red, but we have to take the data set with a pinch of salt when over 10% of it involves Brighton having one more player. (There was also an impressive 33 minutes with 10 men against Sunderland, in which they held on to and ultimately added to a 1-0 lead.) So we should take some of their headline numbers under advisement. Drill deeper and there might be more factors to consider. Brighton lead the league in scoring and are second in xG, but there is a big gap between their 16.2 xG and 23 goals. This is a year in which Brighton's goal-of-the-season contest might be a reasonable proxy for the Premier League's as a whole (Lewis Dunk leads the way for me, Clive). Their shooting form was typified by that 3-0 win over Arsenal. They at least matched the champions in the first half, but they led 2-0 because both Gross and Kostoulas walloped shots in from range. You're not building a title challenge on that. Nor are you necessarily doing the same when you look porous at the other end. It isn't just that Brighton have allowed 11.4 xG to their opponents and are riding a run of shot-stopping that seems unlikely to continue even for a goalkeeper of Bart Verbruggen's quality. Hurzeler's side are also allowing the third-highest xG per shot of any team in the division. Much of that is a function of a worrying set-piece defense, but they are not much better from open play either, allowing 0.117 xG per shot, 10% above the Premier League average. When a team breaks their press like Chelsea did early in the season, that's when they end up in trouble. You don't compete for titles when you are giving up what Brighton are giving up defensively, but then that is a ludicrous conceit in the first place. What is clearly no longer ludicrous is the idea that this team might regularly beat Man City in a one-off match, whether that be the rotated outfit Enzo Maresca is due to field in the EFL Cup on Wednesday or the full-strength outfit that will presumably welcome them back to the Etihad on Saturday afternoon. Indeed, in the reasonably likely event that a sanction obliterates City's standing in this season's Premier League, Brighton could comfortably find themselves among the four or five Champions League qualifiers. The likes of Bournemouth, Nottingham Forest and Brentford are at best performing around Brighton's level so far this season in xG terms but have not picked up anywhere near as many points. Maybe the quality of Liverpool shows down the stretch. Perhaps Xabi Alonso simplifies things at Chelsea. Even then, that probably leaves a fifth spot for an English team to advance to the top tier. There is no question now that Brighton look better placed than anyone else to claim it, propelling themselves into a new class of club. If the experience of the last 10 seasons is anything to go on, this club tends to establish itself quite firmly when it moves up in the world.
