#1269. From last place to the playoffs: How the Philadelphia Union pulled off MLS's most stunning turnaround

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. -- At the end of the World Cup, the Philadelphia Union were at the bottom of the Eastern Conference and all of Major League Soccer with only seven points, moving on from Supporters' Shield-winning head coach Bradley Carnell and turning to 36-year-old Ryan Richter to save the season. Given Richter's path as someone who oversaw the Union's MLS Next Pro side before becoming an assistant under Jim Curtin with the first team, it seemed like a moment where the Union would be in the process of preparing for next season and seeing what they did next.

But with the return of a familiar face in Kai Wagner, a meeting at Two Persons Coffee in South Philadelphia between captain Alejandro Bedoya and Richter, and one of the most impressive runs that we've seen of youth talent in league history, the Union were able to clinch a place in the MLS Cup playoffs, and they did it in impressive fashion, too, by playing Nashville SC to a scoreless draw away from home without 17-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan being available for the match. It caps off a turnaround that has seen the Union pick up 40 points since the World Cup, winning 12 matches, drawing four, and only losing one. Those 40 points outpace the second-best team in the time range, which is Nashville SC, by five.

Sullivan has been one of the spark plugs of this improvement with seven goals and 11 assists, with most of that coming after the World Cup break, but with 38 of the Union's 59 league goals absent for that game as Bruno Damiani and Milan Iloski missed out on the match, it truly showed the mentality that the squad has.

Plenty preach about "next-man-up" mentality, but matches like this one show why no one should want to face the Union in the playoffs. If the season ended today, they'd face Inter Miami in a three-game series, which would be sure to bring fireworks after the scuffle that their last meeting created, but there's still more work to do with two games remaining, as the Union could slide down to the eight-versus-nine play-in game if they lose their final two games of the regular season.

Under Carnell, the Union were a traditional high-press team that tried to force their opponents into mistakes. While it worked with only MLS games to play, adding in the Concacaf Champions Cup saw the team unable to keep up that intensity, especially without Wagner at left back and with Neil Pierre on loan in Denmark instead of being with the squad. While Richter did benefit from both of these players being in the mix, he has also dialed things back to more of a zonal press, allowing the midfield to have time to rest in between plays so that they can keep the same intensity at minute 90 as they have entering the game.

Pierre and Nathan Harriel on the back line have assisted greatly with that, being mobile centerbacks in their own right. Richter knows the impact of having a 6-foot-7 defender like Pierre, who is also comfortable when being on an island, and it's clear how he helps the attack function.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Richter said. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Putting that in front of three-time MLS Goalkeeper of the Year Andre Blake, it's easy to see why the Union's defense has improved from the first half of the season, but the attack is where major strides have been made.

You'd have to be living under a rock to have not heard the name Cavan Sullivan by now, and for good reason, as the 17-year-old has been taking MLS by storm and helping push the Union attack forward with his creativity. Since the World Cup break, Sullivan is second only to Evander in assists with nine and has pitched in goals alongside that. He may not be the biggest or fastest player on the pitch, but the quick bursts that he has into space have been tormenting defenses.

Alongside Pierre and Frankie Westfield, he was able to earn his first national team cap under Mauricio Pochettino and also didn't look out of place there either, but when speaking to him and people around the team, the shift in mentality is clear. Sullivan asked to do extra training during the World Cup break instead of taking the time off, and has come back a more complete player. Already set to join Manchester City when he turns 18 next year, the path for future development is clear (assuming City are in the Premier League), but this is one of the best American soccer prospects ever developed. Being able to play alongside his older brother Quinn also helps with this transition, but Cavan has grown into a player of his own, and while this season has been a coming-out party for him in many ways, the playoffs are going to be a moment that can thrust him into the stratosphere as he looks to lead his hometown club to the first MLS Cup title in their history.

Which American has the most goals in Major League Soccer? Usually, the answer to that question is Brian White, but this season, it also resides in Philadelphia in Milan Iloski, a longtime journeyman, he has found a home in Philadelphia and has scored 19 goals with seven assists, which is third in the league. After moving Tai Baribo to D.C. United, there were valid questions of where the Union's goals would come from, and Iloski has delivered and shown that there isn't a finish that he doesn't have in his locker, and he's not overperforming, either, with an xG of 18.77.

Alongside him, Bruno Damiani has stepped up with 12 goals, and the Uruguayan could be key to any serious playoff run that the team has. If teams crowd Sullivan and Iloski, other people on the team need to be able to make them pay, and Damiani is chief among them. The hope was that new signing Ezekiel Alladoh would be able to take on that mantle, but with one goal and one assist in 26 appearances, he may find minutes hard to come by in the playoffs unless there's an injury. While it's unlikely that they'd upset the likes of Nashville and Miami to win the MLS Cup, the mantra of "Why not us" has always carried Philadelphia and looking at these numbers, you can't say that they don't have a chance. Given that, it is also only a matter of time until the interim tag is removed from Richter's coaching title, but that's an offseason issue to deal with; right now, there are more soccer games to win.

#1267. Inter and AC Milan unveil plans for new 71,500-seat Generali Stadium to replace iconic San Siro

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was an historic day in Milan as Inter and AC Milan have finally unveiled the project for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, the current arena that hosts the home games of both teams. The new San Siro will be named "Generali Stadium" after the Italian insurance company Generali acquired the naming rights of the stadium in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years, according to multiple reports. The Generali Stadium will be ready by the 2031-2032 season, according to the two clubs, just in time for the UEFA 2032 Euro that will be co-hosted by Italy and Turkiye, with construction starting in 2028. The current San Siro will be demolished only after the new stadium is ready to be used by the teams, giving more time for fans to attend a match in the iconic Italian stadium that was built in 1926.

Let's now go into the details of the new arena: According to the joint news release from both clubs, it will be a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience". A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. A "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, AC Milan and Inter ownerships, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football".

Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the iconic Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a striking structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

Engineered to capture and intensify crowd energy, the stadium's acoustic design ensures supporters remain at the heart of the spectacle, helping create an environment designed to be among the most atmospheric in world football. Enhanced accessibility, modern hospitality concepts and a broad range of seating options, from world-class premium experiences to popular seating areas, will ensure the venue welcomes every generation of fan, while offering new ways to experience the game.

The two teams will continue to share their home stadium, a unique tradition that started in the late '40's of the 20th century, when Inter moved to San Siro as well. Unlike most of the teams around the world of soccer, Inter and AC Milan decided to continue sharing their home stadium after leaving the current arena. After years of failed projects and attempts, the new stadium is now a concrete reality. In 2025, the Milan City Council approved the sale of the city's San Siro stadium to the two clubs Inter and AC Milan. Now, the two Italian teams have decided to move into a new direction and era.

As Italian soccer is facing a crisis also regarding their infrastructures, the Generali Stadium can drastically increase the match revenues of both Inter and AC Milan, putting them at the level of the European rivals. At the same time, seeing the teams leave the legendary San Siro will be hard.

San Siro has been the home of AC Milan and Inter, but its history extends far beyond soccer. The iconic stadium has hosted some of the most memorable sporting and cultural events, including the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympic Games and legendary concerts by some of the biggest names in music. From Bob Marley's historic performance in 1980, the first-ever concert at San Siro, to unforgettable shows by the Rolling Stones, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Madonna, Taylor Swift, U2 or Bruce Springsteen, who has famously described San Siro as his second home, the stadium has become a landmark far beyond the world of sport. Now, a new era is about to start but the "old" San Siro won't be forgotten.

Un nuovo simbolo per Milano.Una nuova casa per le future generazioni di tifosi Interisti.​Generali Stadium 🏟️ ‌ pic.twitter.com/9wmNGfrVI9

#1266. Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies1, but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale2,3,4,5,6. This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction4,5,6. Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.

Hydrogen (H) and hydrogen-containing compounds such as ammonia offer promising routes for low-carbon energy storage and utilization, supporting global decarbonization efforts1. Developing hydrogen energy technologies requires a fundamental understanding of how hydrogen interacts with materials. Hydrogen embrittles high-strength alloys in transport and storage systems2,7,8; its behaviour in metals determines the capacity and reversibility of solid-state storage9; hydride formation in zirconium-alloy cladding threatens fission reactor integrity10; and isotope retention is critical to fusion viability11. Across all of these applications, knowing where hydrogen resides in materials is essential.

Hydrogen in crystalline materials exists in three principal states: dissolved as an interstitial solute in solid solution8, bonded to hydrogen-affinitive elements as thermodynamically stable hydrides (for example, titanium hydride)12,13 or trapped at crystal defects, including vacancies14,15, dislocations3,16 and grain boundaries3,17. Experimentally, these states can be analysed by APT2,4, which uses time-of-flight mass spectrometry to identify hydrogen with nanoscale spatial resolution. In practice, deuterium (2H or D) is often introduced instead of protium to distinguish genuine hydrogen signals from background hydrogen in the instrument, which is predominantly 1H (refs. 4,5).

Among the three states, hydrides and defect-trapped hydrogen have been investigated more extensively by APT. Hydrides are identifiable through their characteristic stoichiometries12,13 and defect-trapped hydrogen can often be co-localized with solute-decorated defects (for example, Cottrell atmospheres such as that of carbon)3,16. When defects are not decorated with identifiable elements, associating hydrogen with defect traps becomes challenging because such defects are ‘invisible’ in APT, unless correlative techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are used16,18.

By contrast, characterizing hydrogen in solid solutions is particularly challenging for several reasons. First, the solubility of hydrogen is generally low in many alloys; for example, body-centred cubic (BCC) iron typically contains only a few tens of atomic parts per million (at. ppm) of hydrogen2,7,8, which approaches the APT detection limit6,19. Second, unlike hydrogen in stable hydrides, interstitial hydrogen is highly mobile and can diffuse to the surface and desorb before analysis20,21; cryogenic sample transfer (cryo-transfer) for APT mitigates, but does not eliminate, such signal loss4,20,22.

A further complication arises from the methods used to introduce hydrogen into the needle-shaped APT specimens. Electrochemical charging is commonly used2,4, but it can impose extremely high hydrogen fugacity on the specimen and generate large numbers of vacancies—so-called ‘superabundant vacancies’14,23. Further artefacts can be introduced during specimen preparation: electron-beam or ion-beam irradiation in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or focused ion beam (FIB) can also create vacancies that subsequently trap hydrogen15. Careful interpretation of APT hydrogen maps is therefore required whenever SEM-FIB processing has been used.

In this study, we use a series of FCC alloys as model systems to address this challenge. Compared with BCC alloys, FCC lattices offer higher hydrogen solubility and lower diffusivity7,24, improving signal-to-noise ratio and reducing diffusion-related losses. Our results provide experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in FCC metallic solid solutions and establish a methodological basis for robust, artefact-aware APT characterization of hydrogen in materials.

Throughout this study, APT tip specimens were electrolytically charged with deuterium, which saturates specimens more efficiently than gaseous charging, while reducing corrosion concerns3,4. Voltage pulsing rather than laser pulsing was used for all APT analyses to minimize ambiguity in deuterium signal identification against instrumental background hydrogen4,6. Full experimental details are provided in Methods.

As shown in Fig. 1, we first present results from an equiatomic CoCrNiFeMn MPEA, first developed by Cantor et al.25. This alloy is known to have a locally distorted lattice, which can more effectively hinder hydrogen diffusion and thus reduce signal loss26. Immediately after D charging, we spent approximately 3 s to remove the D-charging electrolyte and then quenched the charged tips in liquid nitrogen (LN2) to ‘freeze’ the deuterium in the MPEA. Once LN2 evaporation stopped—indicating thermal equilibration between the tips and LN2—the specimens were transferred into the APT system using the cryo-transfer procedure described previously3. As shown in Fig. 1a, the APT mass spectrum of the D-charged CoCrNiFeMn specimen exhibits a clear D peak in red at mass-to-charge ratio of 2 Dalton (Da), distinct from the peak of ambient hydrogen (predominantly protium, 1H) at 1 Da, together with the peaks from the principal alloying elements. The overall D concentration reaches 1.3 atomic percent (at.%), equivalent to 473 parts per million by weight (wt. ppm). Figure 1b presents the three-dimensional reconstruction of the APT dataset and 30-nm-thick two-dimensional slices showing the spatial distributions of the major elements, together with H in light blue and D in red. The H map shows a hydrogen-rich cap at the specimen apex, which arises from the field-induced migration and evaporation of ambient hydrogen adsorbed on the tip surface during APT analysis4. By contrast, the D map shows a relatively homogeneous and random distribution, consistent with what is expected for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution. To confirm reproducibility, we repeated this experiment on a second tip and obtained a comparable result, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 1.

a, Mass spectrum, showing a notable deuterium peak at 2 Da with respect to the peak of background hydrogen at 1 Da. b, Three-dimensional reconstruction of all elements (left) and the 30-nm slice views of the principal elements, hydrogen (H, representing background) and deuterium (D, representing signal). c, The statistics of the atomic distance of solute D with the first nearest D neighbour as well as the randomized counterpart with the same number of D atoms in the same volume. d, The repeated analysis of c except using fifth nearest D neighbour. Scale bar, 50 nm.

Because deuterium can segregate to defects that are not visible in APT (ref. 16), we carefully evaluated whether the observed deuterium distribution is truly random. We performed nearest-neighbour analyses of deuterium atoms, as shown in Fig. 1c,d, for the first and fifth nearest deuterium neighbours, respectively. This approach detects clustering by comparing interatomic distances between deuterium atoms in the experimental dataset with those in a randomized dataset of equivalent size19,27. A marked shift towards shorter distances indicates clustering, whereas agreement with the random distribution is consistent with deuterium occupying a large population of equivalent interstitial sites27.

Figure 1c shows the distribution of deuterium–deuterium pair distances for the first nearest neighbour. The most probable pair distance in the experimental data is close to that in the randomized dataset (both approximately 0.8 nm), indicating that the deuterium atoms are randomly distributed. We repeated the analysis for the fifth nearest deuterium neighbour (Fig. 1d) and obtained a consistent result, with a larger most probable distance of about 1.2 nm, as expected when a more distant neighbour is considered. These results are consistent with interstitial deuterium (as a proxy of hydrogen) in solid solution. Notably, hydrogen solution in the CoCrNiFeMn matrix is not highly thermodynamically favourable according to our first-principles calculations, for neither octahedral nor tetrahedral interstitial sites (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Figure 1 therefore suggests the effectiveness of cryo-APT for preserving the charged D atoms and enabling observation of their distribution in solid solution. Random D distributions were also consistently observed in solution-treated CoNiV and (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 alloys (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1), supporting the generality of this observation among FCC MPEAs.

As a similar randomness of D distribution could also arise if a large number of superabundant vacancies was introduced during electrolytic charging and act as traps14,28, we used a dual-phase FCC (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MPEA containing L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) intermetallic precipitates with highly coherent interfaces with the matrix, which provides a heterogeneous microstructure less favoured to form superabundant vacancies. The specimens were first solution-treated at 1,000 °C for 1 h to obtain a precipitate-free state and then aged at 800 °C for 5 h to induce precipitation. Structural and compositional characterization of the aged (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 FCC MPEA is shown in Fig. 2. Figure 2a presents an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) inverse pole figure map; a comparison of EBSD maps before and after ageing is provided in Supplementary Fig. 2, indicating that ageing to form precipitates does not substantially change the grain morphology.

a, EBSD inverse pole figure map. b, STEM image, showing a high density of L12 precipitates (green arrows) with an average diameter of 18.5 ± 3.5 nm. c, HRTEM image of the coherent interface between the matrix and L12 precipitates along the [011] zone axis. d, SAED pattern showing the characteristic diffraction spots of the FCC L12 precipitates (green), which are distinct from the FCC matrix (white). e, High-resolution HAADF-STEM image of the coherent interface between the FCC matrix and L12 phase along the [001] zone axis, showing the analysed regions for f, g and h. f,g, FFT data of the FCC matrix and the L12 precipitate from regions in e, respectively. h, EDS mapping results from the region in e, with the matrix elements (Co, Cr and Ni) and the L12 precipitate elements (Ni, Al and Ti). i, Voltage-pulsing APT mass spectrum, showing the 1-Da peak (blue arrow) associated with background hydrogen. j, Three-dimensional data reconstruction (left) and the 10-nm slices of the matrix elements (Co, Cr and Ni) and L12 precipitate (Ni, Al and Ti). k, Proxigram from the isoconcentration surfaces (isosurfaces) of 60 at.% Ni, showing the stoichiometry of Ni3(Al, Ti). Scale bars, 100 μm (a); 20 nm (b,j); 1 nm (c,e,h); 5 nm−1 (d,g).

Figure 2b shows a dark-field STEM image, revealing a high number density of L12 precipitates with an average diameter of 18.5 ± 3.5 nm in the matrix. Figure 2c is a high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image of the L12–matrix interface showing a highly coherent interface. The diffraction pattern in Fig. 2d confirms the presence of L12 phase within the FCC matrix. Figure 2e is another HRTEM image marking the regions analysed in Fig. 2f–h. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern from the FCC matrix region (Fig. 2f) is distinct from that of the L12-containing region (Fig. 2g), further confirming the presence of L12 precipitates. Figure 2h shows the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) maps with the enrichment of Ni, Al and Ti in the L12-containing region.

The APT mass spectrum of a deuterium-free specimen in Fig. 2i shows peaks from the major elements and a H peak at 1 Da, but no D peak at 2 Da. Figure 2j shows the three-dimensional APT reconstruction and 10-nm slices of the main elements, clearly revealing precipitates enriched in Ni, Al and Ti. Figure 2k presents a proximity histogram (proxigram) across an isoconcentration surface (isosurface) defined at 60 at.% Ni, showing the agreement between the theoretical stoichiometry and the composition of the L12 precipitates measured by APT. APT reconstructions from a precipitate-free (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimen are provided in Supplementary Fig. 3, which show homogeneous elemental distributions and a mass spectrum similar to that in Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 3, respectively, confirming the precipitation owing to heat treatment in good agreement with literature29.

Such high-strength, ordered FCC L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitates embedded in a high-entropy CoCrNi matrix can be more resistant to damage arising from high-fugacity electrolytic charging30,31. Also, this dual-phase material provides an opportunity to study interstitial hydrogen behaviour in two different FCC lattices. Because L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) has a strong affinity for hydrogen12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 2b), we anticipated that such precipitates should bind hydrogen more strongly and therefore retain a higher deuterium concentration than the surrounding CoCrNi matrix.

To compliment APT analyses, we used thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) to compare hydrogen retention in the precipitate-free and precipitated (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimens on the macroscopic scale. As indicated by the arrow in Supplementary Fig. 4, the precipitated specimen shows an increased amount of hydrogen desorbed at higher temperatures, indicating the presence of microstructural features that hold hydrogen more strongly than the FCC matrix; these features are most likely the L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitates. Although the experimental approaches are different, these TDS results are consistent with the trends predicted by our first-principles calculations using density functional theory (DFT) for evaluating the solution energies of hydrogen in all relevant interstitial sites (that is, both octahedral and tetrahedral), as shown in Extended Data Fig. 2b, considering in the CoCrNi matrix, at the L12–matrix interface and within the L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) lattice. Owing to the chemical disorder, the solution energy values for hydrogen in the MPEAs are broadly distributed compared with those in pure metals. We find that hydrogen exhibits the lowest solution energy (approximately −0.28 eV) at the specific octahedral sites of the L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) phase.

For the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimen containing Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitates, we repeated most of the procedures used for the CoCrNiFeMn specimen. The only modification was an extended holding time for 10 s before LN2 quenching and cryo-transfer, with an intention to promote preferential deuterium desorption from the matrix, thereby enhancing the deuterium concentration contrast between phases with low (matrix) and high (precipitate) hydrogen-binding energies in the APT dataset. This controlled holding after deuterium saturation allows the charged deuterium atoms to remain mobile briefly before quenching, leading to more pronounced deuterium loss from the low-binding-energy phase than from the high-binding-energy phase. The measured deuterium distribution can reflect both thermodynamic and kinetic effects during this brief redistribution, as demonstrated in our previous work16.

The APT results are shown in Fig. 3. The mass spectrum in Fig. 3a shows a clear D peak in red at 2 Da, together with the peaks of the major elements. Because of the controlled holding at room temperature, the D peak is less intense than that observed for the CoCrNiFeMn specimen in Fig. 1a. Figure 3b shows the three-dimensional reconstruction with the principal elements and D atoms (red), with green outlines added to enhance the visibility of the L12 precipitate. A distinctly higher D concentration is observed inside the L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitate. In Fig. 3c, we plot the one-dimensional concentration profiles of D, H and the major alloying elements along a cylindrical region of interest indicated in the Al map in Fig. 3b. The D profile (red) is clearly different from the H background (blue), indicating that the D signal is not associated with the artefact related to background hydrogen. Figure 3d shows another view of the reconstruction, together with the D atoms, the Ti isosurface and the positions of the 10-nm two-dimensional slices used to generate Fig. 3e–g. We repeated the experiment on another specimen and the corresponding results (Extended Data Fig. 4) show the same D enrichment in the L12 precipitates, confirming reproducibility. Taken together, these observations show that the Ni3(Al, Ti) L12 precipitates contain a higher hydrogen (represented by deuterium) concentration than the surrounding CoCrNi FCC matrix. We interpret deuterium enrichment in the L12 FCC precipitates as being predominantly associated with interstitial hydrogen in the FCC lattice, for the reasons discussed below.

a, Mass spectrum, showing a notable deuterium peak at 2 Da (red arrow) with respect to the peak of background hydrogen at 1 Da. b, 10-nm slice views of the principal elements in the matrix (Co, Cr and Ni) and L12 precipitate elements (Ni, Al and Ti), as well as deuterium (D, representing signal) with green outlines, delineating the incorporated L12 precipitate. c, One-dimensional profile from the region of interest noted in the Al map in b, across the matrix–L12 precipitate interface, showing the element concentration variations corresponding to the L12 precipitate as well as the D concentration (red) in the L12 precipitate, distinct from the concentration variation of the background H (blue). d, Three-dimensional view of D atoms (red) and 6 at.% Ti isosurface (pink), as well as the locations of the slices for e, f and g. e–g, 10-nm slice views of D atoms (red) and 6 at.% Ti isosurface (pink). Scale bars, 10 nm.

First, our previous work has shown that APT can resolve D concentrated within a second phase while showing little or no D at an adjacent interface with a low elastic strain field18. It demonstrated that APT detected D in cementite rather than at the pearlite interface, consistent with DFT predictions for the relative hydrogen affinities of cementite, ferrite and their interface, ruling out artefacts related to ion-trajectory effects in APT (ref. 19). The present study has a related microstructural configuration—a hydrogen-affinitive FCC L12 second phase, an FCC matrix and a coherent interface with weak local elastic strain—so a similar enrichment of D in the L12 phase, rather than at the interface, is expected.

Second, to validate the low populations of vacancy traps in our specimens, we performed positron annihilation measurements on both the precipitate-free and precipitated (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimens, their 2%-strained counterparts (which should contain more vacancies) and pure nickel reference specimens. The results, summarized in Supplementary Table 1, show that, although the nickel references give measurable positron signals (rows 1 and 2), all (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimens (rows 3–6) are below the detection limit of the instrument. This indicates that the vacancy concentrations in these alloys are indeed low. Our DFT calculations also show that the vacancy formation energies in CoCrNi and L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) are greater than 1.5 eV (Supplementary Fig. 5), indicating that the formation of a substantial equilibrium vacancy population is unlikely.

We further examined whether the electrochemical D-charging process could introduce crystalline defects that might act as trapping sites for deuterium, as suggested in previous studies31,32,33,34. Quasi in situ TEM observations were performed on the same L12 precipitates before and after D charging, and no stacking faults, dislocations or other newly introduced crystalline defects were detected (Extended Data Fig. 5). Also, as shown in Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7, positron annihilation spectroscopy, which is commonly used to characterize vacancy defects and hydrogen–vacancy complexes35,36, showed no notable increase in vacancy concentration after D charging. This contrasts with the irradiated specimen, which contains more defects (primarily vacancies) and thus exhibited higher positron annihilation signals.

The combination of DFT calculations, quasi in situ TEM observations during D charging and positron annihilation measurements suggests that the vacancy concentrations are low, so detected D is predominantly associated with interstitial lattice sites in the L12 phase, although a minor contribution from non-detectable vacancies or vacancy–Hn/Dn complexes, or even elastic fields or the intrinsic APT detection limitations, cannot be completely excluded14,28,37,38.

With the establishment that APT can resolve hydrogen in different phases, we extended our study to a more complex alloy system containing several types of precipitate, which is an Inconel 718 nickel-based superalloy (54Ni–19Fe–21Cr–2.6Nb–1.6Mo–0.97Ti–0.58Al–0.24C at.%), by 3D printing and tailored it to contain two types of coherent precipitate—Ni3Nb body-centred tetragonal (BCT) D022 and Ni3(Al, Ti) L12 FCC—embedded in an FCC matrix. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 8, we conducted TEM analyses to confirm the presence of a high number density of precipitates in the Ni matrix, Ni–Al–Ti enrichment in the L12 phase, Ni–Nb enrichment in the D022 phase and the high coherency of L12–D022 and matrix–D022 interfaces. This co-precipitation strategy enabled both phases of interest to appear within the small APT field of view, allowing a comparison under identical experimental conditions.

We performed identical treatment for the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimen. The results are presented in Fig. 4. Figure 4a,b shows the spatially connected dual-precipitate region in three-dimensional reconstruction and a 10-nm slice, respectively. The Al-rich L12 precipitates are identified in turquoise using 4 at.% Al isosurfaces, whereas the Nb-rich D022 precipitates are identified in green using 10 at.% Nb isosurfaces. In Fig. 4c–i, we show a single L12–D022 composite particle from two viewing directions, highlighting the Al and Nb isosurfaces (Fig. 4c,d), the Al and D atoms (Fig. 4f,g) or the Nb and D atoms (Fig. 4h,i). The corresponding mass spectrum is shown in Supplementary Fig. 6.

a, Three-dimensional reconstruction with 4 at.% Al (turquoise) and 10 at.% Nb (green) isosurfaces, as well as the location of the slice for b. b, 10-nm slice view of the Al and Nb isosurfaces, D atoms (not all shown owing to blockage of the isosurfaces) and the region of interest for c. c,d, Two viewing aspects of a dual precipitate of L12 (turquoise) and D022 (green) in three dimensions. e, One-dimensional concentration profile from the region of interest noted in c, showing the presence of D concentration primarily in the L12 region, not the D022 region, in contrast to the distribution of background hydrogen (blue). f,g, The Al (turquoise) and D atom maps, corresponding to c and d, respectively. h,i, The Nb (green) and D atom maps, corresponding to c and d, respectively. j, Cumulative proxigram from the Al isosurfaces shown in a, showing the D concentration in L12 precipitates. k, Cumulative proxigram from the Nb isosurfaces shown in a, showing the lack of D in D022 precipitates. Scale bars, 10 nm (a,b); 2 nm (c,d).

As a result, D atoms were found predominantly within the L12 precipitates, as confirmed by the one-dimensional concentration profile in Fig. 4e, which was obtained from the cylindrical region of interest indicated in Fig. 4c. To quantify this further, we acquired proxigrams using either the turquoise Al isosurfaces (representing L12) or the green Nb isosurfaces (representing D022), as shown in Fig. 4j,k, respectively. These profiles clearly show an increased D concentration in the L12 precipitates (Fig. 4j) and only a low D concentration in the D022 precipitates (Fig. 4k). We repeated the experiment on another Inconel APT tip and the data in Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Fig. 7 show the same trend, confirming reproducibility. We also conducted DFT analysis to determine the hydrogen solution energies in a pure Ni reference (Extended Data Fig. 2c), the Ni2FeCr Inconel FCC matrix (Extended Data Fig. 2d) and the Ni3Nb D022 BCT precipitate (Extended Data Fig. 2e), finding that none of the sites in D022 can hold hydrogen better than those in the L12 precipitates, which is consistent with the APT results in Figs. 3 and 4.

In summary, we investigated interstitial hydrogen/deuterium in solid solutions of FCC MPEAs, in both bulk matrix and precipitate forms, by APT, with results consistent with DFT predictions of hydrogen solution energies. The deuterium partitioning reflects interstitial occupancy, although minor contributions from vacancies, vacancy–hydrogen/deuterium complexes or elastic fields cannot be fully excluded. Chemical affinity and crystal structure are shown to govern local hydrogen distribution. These findings establish an experimental protocol for connecting atomistic predictions with direct observation, enabling new opportunities for understanding hydrogen thermodynamics and kinetics in materials and providing guidance for designing alloys with improved performance for hydrogen-related applications.

The ingot of CoCrNiFeMn high-entropy alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting a mixture of pure elements with purity greater than 99.95 wt.% under an argon atmosphere after a vacuum of 3.3 Pa has been reached. The ingot was melted at least four times to ensure compositional homogeneity, followed by homogenization at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold rolling to a 90% thickness reduction (from 10 mm to 1 mm) and annealing at 950 °C for 4 h.

The sample with a nominal chemical composition of (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 (at.%) was synthesized through vacuum arc melting high-purity metals (purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under an argon atmosphere. To ensure compositional homogeneity and prevent element segregation, the sample was melted five times before being poured into a round ingot with a diameter of 50 mm. The as-cast sample was homogenized at 1,200 °C for 3 h and then cold-rolled along with its thickness to reduce the thickness by 50%. Two different microstructures were achieved by applying distinct heat treatments to the as-rolled samples: heating at 1,000 °C for 1 h, yielding the precipitate-free state (solution-treated), followed by 800 °C for 5 h, yielding the precipitated sample. All heat-treated samples were water-quenched.

The ingot of CoNiV alloy was synthesized by vacuum arc melting under an argon atmosphere (99.99% purity) after a pressure of 3.3 Pa. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots were remelted five times. The ingots were then hot-forged at 1,200 °C into rectangular slabs with a thickness of 5 mm and a width of 20 mm, followed by homogenization at 1,200 °C for 3 h. Subsequently, the homogenized alloys were cold-rolled to a total thickness reduction of 50%. Finally, the cold-rolled sheets were subjected to solution annealing at 1,000 °C for 1 h (solution-treated).

The Inconel 718 nickel-based superalloy had a chemical composition of 54.72Ni–18.60Fe–18.70Cr–4.24Nb–2.62Mo–0.80Ti–0.27Al–0.05C wt.% (53.93Ni–19.26Fe–20.80Cr–2.64Nb–1.58Mo–0.97Ti–0.58Al–0.24C at.%). This alloy (diameter 15 mm, length 70 mm) was fabricated using a commercial selective laser melting system (EOS M 400) with an average powder size of 30 ± 11 µm, a scanning strategy of 67° rotation, a laser power of 340 W, scanning speed of 1,100 mm s−1 and layer thickness of approximately 50 µm. The printed samples were initially homogenized at 1,100 °C for 1 h and then water-quenched to room temperature. Subsequently, the samples were subjected to a two-step ageing treatment: first at 720 °C for 1 h, followed by furnace cooling to 620 °C, at which they were held for 8 h before final air cooling to room temperature. The sequential D022 (γ″-type) and L12 (γ′-type) precipitates are introduced during the 720 °C and 620 °C ageing treatments, respectively.

Samples for the EBSD analysis were initially polished using 5000-grit SiC sandpaper, subsequently polished with diamond paste for 3 min and finally electrolytically polished in a 1:9 solution of HClO4 and C2H5OH at 243 K for 20 s under a DC voltage of 25 V. The pre-thinned TEM foils, with a thickness of 50–60 μm, were polished using double-jet electropolishing at 243 K in 10 volume percent of HClO4 in methanol to prepare the TEM sample.

EBSD mapping used a Symmetry S2 detector (Oxford Instruments) and TEM imaging was conducted on a JEM-2100F (JEOL). High-resolution STEM imaging was performed using the FEI Themis Z microscope equipped with an EDS detector. Atomic-resolution chemical characterization with compositional mapping was performed using four in-column Super-X silicon drift detectors.

The sample preparation began with matchstick bars with dimensions 1 × 1 × 13 mm3. The samples were initially polished using 800-grit sandpaper. Coarse electropolishing was then performed using a 25% perchloric acid solution in glacial acetic acid at voltages ranging from 15 to 30 V to polish the samples into needle-like specimens. Fine electropolishing was subsequently performed using a 2% perchloric acid solution in ethylene glycol butyl ether at voltages ranging from 10 to 25 V. This fine electropolishing procedure used a platinum wire ring cathode and was monitored under a 40× optical microscope. A key step involved forming a neck until the top portion detached, creating a sharp tip.

Before deuterium charging, FIB tip sharpening was performed on the electropolished tips to ensure that the samples satisfied APT requirements in tip sharpness. APT was then performed using a LEAP 4000X instrument (CAMECA), operating in voltage-pulsing mode with a 0.2% detection rate, 200-kHz pulse frequency, 20% pulse fraction and sample temperature of 50 K. Data processing was performed using AP Suite software (version 6.1, CAMECA). The image compression factors and k factors used for reconstruction were 1.3 and 3.3 for the CoCrNiFeMn alloy and the Inconel 718 nickel-based superalloy and 1.5 and 3.3 for the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 alloy, respectively. These reconstruction parameters were selected following standard APT reconstruction procedures and, for the precipitate-containing datasets, refined by comparison with precipitate morphologies independently observed by TEM. Peak ranging was performed by considering the full isotopic distributions of the major alloying elements and possible molecular ions; the bulk composition analysis is shown in Supplementary Tables 2–4. A peak-free region around 2.5 Da was defined as noise and used to estimate the local low-mass background adjacent to the 2-Da signal. Three representative mass spectra are shown in Supplementary Fig. 8 and the results for all eight successful cryo-APT datasets out of 68 trials are summarized in Supplementary Table 5. Because D+ and H2+ overlap at 2 Da and cannot be resolved directly, this overlap was treated separately as a systematic uncertainty and assessed using uncharged reference specimens analysed under identical voltage-pulsing conditions. APT reconstruction sensitivity was further evaluated by reconstructing the dataset shown in Fig. 3 using an alternative image compression factor value of 1.3, which did not alter the observed preferential deuterium enrichment within the L12 precipitate (Supplementary Fig. 9).

A charging solution of 0.1 M NaOH in D2O (Sigma-Aldrich) was used to create a deuterium-rich environment around the samples at the cathode in an electrolytic circuit, with a gold counter-electrode. This was carried out in a custom-designed cryo-transfer glovebox (M. BRAUN Inertgas-Systeme). Four sharp specimens were pre-mounted in a four-needle atom probe sample puck with polyether ether ketone insulation. The four tips protruded from the puck to the same height and were immersed into the charging solution at a depth that was barely visible and could only be identified by means of the capillary of the liquid solution. Deuterium charging was conducted at 1.6 V for 90 s powered by Keysight 2901A, followed by immediately immersing the whole puck in a LN2 bath.

After deuterium charging and LN2 quenching, the specimens for Figs. 3 and 4 were transferred from the glovebox to a Hydra plasma focused ion beam (PFIB; Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a cryo-stage using a cryogenic sample carrier (Ferrovac). The sharpening process was completed on a cryo-stage at approximately −190 °C. Two ion-beam conditions were used—30 kV–0.1 nA and 30 kV–30 pA—to remove ice and further refine and smooth the tips during the annular milling process. A final polishing step at 5 kV–50 pA was applied for 10 s to remove the possible ion-damaged layer. The APT specimens were then transferred using the cryogenic transfer suitcase from the PFIB system to the APT system for APT measurements.

For the TDS tests, samples measuring 1 × 8 × 10 mm3 were polished using 5000-grit SiC sandpaper. The samples were then charged for 72 h at a constant current density of 20 mA cm−2 in a solution containing 0.5 M H2SO4 and 2 g l−1 CH4N2S. TDS measurements were subsequently performed using a mass spectrometer (JTF-20A), with heating rates of 100 °C h−1, 200 °C h−1 and 300 °C h−1.

All DFT calculations were performed using the projector augmented wave39 method, as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)40. The exchange-correlation effects were selected as the generalized gradient approximation determined by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof functional41. To simulate chemical disorder, the special quasirandom structure (SQS) approach42 was applied using the Alloy Theoretic Automated Toolkit (ATAT)43,44. A plane-wave cut-off of 450 eV was used and the Brillouin zones were sampled with a gamma-centred Monkhorst–Pack grid45. Next, the Methfessel–Paxton method46 was used with a smearing width of 0.1 eV. The supercell size and atomic positions were allowed to relax until the Hellmann–Feynman forces were less than 0.01 eV Å−1 and convergence criteria for energies and forces were set to 1.0 × 10−5 eV per atom and 0.02 eV Å−1, respectively.

CoCrNiFeMn MPEA, CoCrNi MPEA and L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) precipitates, pure Ni, Ni2FeCr (matrix of Inconel 718 superalloy) and D022 Ni3Nb precipitates were studied in this work. The CoCrNiFeMn, CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti), Ni and Ni2FeCr are all FCC structures and D022 Ni3Nb has a tetragonal structure (I4/mmm, space group 139), the Ni atoms occupy the 4d (0, 1/2, 1/4) and 2b (0, 0, 1/2) positions and the Nb atoms occupy the 2a (0, 0, 0) positions. The SQS method was used to model the disordered phases including CoCrNiFeMn, CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and Ni2FeCr. The CoCrNi, Ni2FeCr, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and Ni phases were modelled using 108 atoms with 3 × 3 × 3 supercells according to their compositions, with all of the Ni atoms occupying the face-centred sites in L12 Ni3(Al, Ti). CoCrNiFeMn and D022 Ni3Nb were constructed by a 5 × 3 × 2 supercell containing 120 atoms and a 2 × 2 × 1 supercell containing 36 atoms, respectively. The CoCrNi (\(1\bar{1}\bar{1}\))/L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) (\(1\bar{1}\bar{1}\)) interface was constructed on the basis of experimental data and more than three SQS configurations for each bulk and interface structure were evaluated for comparison.

The DFT analysis mainly considered both octahedral interstitial and tetrahedral interstitial sites. The solution energy (Es) of a hydrogen atom at a trapping site was calculated using equation (1):

in which Etrap+H and Etrap denote the total energies of the system with and without an interstitial hydrogen atom, respectively, and \(1/2{E}_{{{\rm{H}}}_{2}}\) denotes the half energy of a H2 molecule. Given the heterogeneous chemical environment surrounding the interstitial sites in MPEAs, more than 20 randomly selected interstitial sites were sampled in each bulk phase structure, along with ten randomly selected interstitial sites at each interface structure, including both octahedral interstitial sites and tetrahedral interstitial sites.

We performed further calculations about the formation of vacancy. We selected three representative phases (CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb) to conduct the relevant investigations, which can reflect the general energetic characteristics. Vacancies were introduced by removing atoms from the perfect supercell, the vacancy formation energy \({E}_{{\rm{V}}}^{{\rm{f}}}\) was computed as follows:

in which EV and Ebulk are the energies of defective and defect-free supercells, respectively, and μi is the chemical potential of the removed atom from the supercell. The chemical potential of the vacancy atom i was calculated according to the Widom-type substitution technique47. We calculated 40 substituted structures to determine the μi of each element i. The calculated chemical potentials of different elements in CoCrNi were used to calculate the formation energies of vacancies in CoCrNi. For L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb, μi denotes the total energy of the X atom at its ground state.

According to quantum mechanics, particles maintain a residual non-zero energy even at 0 K, which is defined as zero-point energy (ZPE)48. Here we used the ZPE and entropy corrections on H solution energies for three of the investigated alloys (CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb). The Gibbs free energy of hydrogen dissolution, ΔGs is defined as follows:

in which Es is the calculated solution energy, ΔEZPE is the difference in ZPE of hydrogen in the dissolved state and the gas phase and ΔS is the entropy difference between the dissolved state and the gas phase of hydrogen at standard conditions (atmospheric pressure, 298 K). The calculated ZPE of a diatomic H2 gas is 0.269 eV, which is in good agreement with previous studies48,49,50. Supplementary Fig. 10 illustrates the comparison of energy results with and without ZPE and entropy corrections. The energy slightly increases after ZPE correction is applied and the increase of tet sites is marginally larger than the oct sites for CoCrNi and Ni3(Al, Ti). The energy increases further with more entropy corrections for all three alloys. It can be seen that the ZPE and entropy corrections exert no notable influence on the energy comparison.

Isotopic effect was also considered for these alloys (CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb). H atom was substituted by D atom and the calculated results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 11. Replacing H with D exerts a negligible influence on the solution energies for all three phases. The energy slightly increases with the ZPE correction, which is similar to the case for H. However, the general trend of energy comparison is insensitive to isotopic effects. The diffusion of H/D atoms within the three phases (CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb) was investigated using the climbing-image nudged elastic band method. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 10, the diffusion barriers of H and D in the three phases are similar to each other. After applying the corrections, the saddle points of the diffusion curves of all three phases (CoCrNi, L12 Ni3(Al, Ti) and D022 Ni3Nb) shift upward slightly, with minor differences observed between H and D. The general energetic trend remains the same after the corrections.

Electropolished TEM foils of the aged (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 alloy were used for quasi in situ D-charging experiments. Before charging, specific regions containing L12 precipitates were identified and characterized using bright-field TEM, high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM), selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) and HRTEM. The specimen was then electrochemically charged in 0.1 M NaOH prepared in D2O using a gold anode. A charging time of 1.5 min and the charging conditions used are the same as cryogenic APT experiments.

After charging, the specimen was removed from the electrolyte, dried and re-examined by TEM. The same regions and individual precipitates were relocated and compared with their former states. SAED and HRTEM analyses were performed after charging to assess whether D-charging introduced crystalline defects, including stacking faults, dislocations or other lattice defects.

Ion irradiation was performed using a NEC 2 × 1.7 MV tandem accelerator at Peking University. The (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 specimen (10 × 10 × 0.9 mm3) was irradiated with 3 MeV Ni2+ ions to a fluence of 1.5 × 1016 ions cm−2 at 500 °C, corresponding to a peak damage level of approximately 16 dpa, as calculated by SRIM-2013 using the quick Kinchin–Pease model. The displacement threshold energies used in the SRIM calculations were 40 eV for Co, Cr, Ni and Ti and 25 eV for Al. To minimize oxidation and other possible surface contamination during high-temperature irradiation, the target chamber was evacuated to a pressure below 1 × 10−4 Pa before heating and irradiation were initiated. After irradiation, the specimen was kept under vacuum during cooling and removed from the chamber only after the temperature had decreased to less than 50 °C.

Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy was performed using a 22Na positron source to complement the Doppler-broadening measurements and assess vacancy-type defects in the investigated alloys, corresponding to Supplementary Table 1. Vacancy-type defects introduced by hydrogen charging, performed under the same conditions as those used for the cryogenic APT experiments, and by ion irradiation were characterized by Doppler-broadening positron annihilation spectroscopy using a slow positron beam51,52 at the Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. A 22Na radioactive source was used to produce the positron beam, with a beam diameter of approximately 0.55 cm. To minimize specimen-to-specimen variability, Doppler-broadening positron annihilation spectroscopy measurements were performed sequentially on the same specimen in the pristine state, after electrochemical hydrogen charging and after subsequent Ni-ion irradiation. The incident positron energy varied from 0.5 to 25.0 keV. The corresponding mean positron implantation depth ranged from approximately 1.5 to 804.0 nm (corresponding to the irradiated region spanning approximately 5.8–15.3 dpa), as estimated using the empirical relation:

in which Z is the mean positron implantation depth in nm, ρ is the mass density of the target material in g cm−3 and E is the incident positron energy in keV. A density of 8.58 g cm−3 was used for the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 alloy. Positron annihilation γ-ray spectra were recorded using a high-purity Ge detector. For each spectrum, more than 4.5 × 105 counts were accumulated within the 499.5–522.5 keV annihilation peak. The Doppler-broadening spectra were analysed using the S and W parameters, which represent positron annihilation with low-momentum valence electrons and high-momentum core electrons, respectively. The annihilation peak was integrated over the energy range 499.5–522.5 keV. The S parameter was defined as the ratio of the counts in the central energy window of 510.2–511.8 keV to the total counts in the 499.5–522.5 keV annihilation peak. The W parameter was defined as the ratio of the counts in the high-momentum wing regions of 505.1–508.4 keV and 513.6–516.9 keV to the total counts in the 499.5–522.5 keV annihilation peak. An increase in S accompanied by a decrease in W indicates enhanced positron trapping at vacancy-type open-volume defects.

a, Mass spectrum with the presence of D peak (red). b, Three-dimensional reconstructions of the principal elements (Co, Cr and Ni) and the L12 precipitate elements (Ni, Al and Ti) and a 32.5 at.% Ni isosurface (green), as well as deuterium (D, red). c, Cumulative proxigram from the Ni isosurfaces, showing D concentration in the L12 regions.

a,b, Experimental set-up used for quasi in situ D-charging of TEM specimens in 0.1 M NaOH prepared in D2O. c1,c2, Low-magnification TEM images showing the same specimen region before charging and after D-charging for 1.5 min. The arrow marks the same feature used for relocation. d1,d2, Corresponding higher-magnification HAADF-STEM images of the same area containing L12 precipitates. The same precipitates were tracked throughout the charging process. No obvious microstructural changes were observed after D-charging. e1,e2, HAADF-STEM images showing the same L12 precipitates before charging and after D-charging for 1.5 min. The precipitates labelled 1 and 2 were selected for repeated characterization. f1,f2, SAED patterns acquired along the [011] zone axis. Superlattice reflections associated with the ordered L12 structure remain visible throughout the charging process. g1,g2,h1,h2, HRTEM images of precipitates 1 and 2. No stacking faults, dislocations or other newly introduced crystalline defects were detected after D-charging, as confirmed by the corresponding FFT patterns (data not shown).

a,b, S parameter (a) and W parameter (b) as functions of the mean positron implantation depth. The H-charged specimen shows values close to those of the pristine specimen, indicating no detectable increase in vacancy-type open-volume defects after 1.5 min of H-charging process. By contrast, the specimen irradiated to 16 dpa exhibits a pronounced increase in S together with a decrease in W, indicating enhanced positron trapping at irradiation-induced vacancy-type defects.

a1, Cross-sectional two-beam bright-field (BF) TEM image of the Ni-ion-irradiated specimen acquired under g = 200, Z = [011] conditions, showing a high-density irradiation-damaged layer extending from the surface to a depth of approximately 1 μm. a2, Corresponding weak-beam dark-field (WBDF) TEM image obtained under g/3g conditions, further revealing the dense distribution of irradiation-induced defects within the damaged region. b,c, STEM-BF images and corresponding EDS elemental maps collected from the irradiation-damaged region and the underlying pristine region, respectively. The comparable elemental partitioning between these two regions indicates that the precipitates retain their original morphology and spatial distribution after irradiation. d, Higher-magnification TEM-BF image of the near-surface damaged region, in which numerous faulted loops are observed. e, HRTEM image of a representative faulted loop. f1,f2, FFT patterns taken from the dark yellow and pale yellow-green boxed regions in panel e, respectively. The streaking features along the <111> direction confirm that the dominant irradiation-induced defects are Frank-type faulted loops with Burgers vectors of b = a/3<111>. No TEM-visible vacancy clusters or voids are detected in the high-magnification images.

a, Representative TEM image showing the microstructure of Inconel 718 nickel-based superalloy. b, SAED pattern of a, showing the characteristic diffraction spots of the L12 precipitates (turquoise) and D022 precipitates (green), which are distinct from the FCC matrix (white). c, Dark-field TEM (DF-TEM) image of L12 phase, showing a high density of L12 precipitates. d, DF-TEM image of D022 phase, showing a high density of D022 precipitates. e, High-resolution HAADF-STEM image and the corresponding EDS mapping, with the matrix elements (Ni, Cr and Fe), the L12 precipitate elements (Ni, Al and Ti) and the D022 precipitate elements (Ni and Nb). The L12 and the D022 precipitates are spatially connected dual precipitates. f, HRTEM image of the sequential precipitation of L12 (turquoise) and D022 (green) precipitates. g, FFT images of the FCC matrix, the L12 and two variants of D022 precipitates. h, HRTEM image of a single L12–D022 composite particle, showing the L12–D022 and matrix–D022 coherent interfaces. i, FFT images of the coherent L12 and D022 precipitates.

#1265. Champions League Liveblog: FC Porto vs. Napoli, RC Lens vs. Como

Join us for all the build-up and action as it happens from the Champions League, as Napoli visit Francesco Farioli’s FC Porto and Como are away to RC Lens.

They both kick off at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

The Partenopei finally got their first European points with a 4-3 victory over Bodo/Glimt, but are coming off the weekend’s 2-0 Serie A loss to Juventus.

Cesc Fabregas and Como won both home games in the Champions League, but lost away to Feyenoord, so the pressure is on against Florian Thauvin’s Lens.

Max Allegri admits Napoli have ‘limitations’ after a 4-1 defeat to FC Porto, as their Champions League campaign hangs by a thread. ‘These are the mistakes that cost you matches.’

Cesc Fabregas admits the 9-1 win in Lens was ‘a wonderful night for Como, but we need to keep our feet on the ground’ as Champions League ambition starts to genuinely build.

Como made history with an astonishing 9-1 victory away to RC Lens in the Champions League, including a Tasos Douvikas hat-trick and 18-year-old Matteo Papaccioli scoring on his debut.

He scores on his debut! It’s not offside! The 18-year-old runs onto the pass from Liberali, then goes to hug Fabregas!

Napoli had got back on track with Scott McTominay, but crumbled in a 4-1 defeat to Francesco Farioli’s Porto with some terrible defending on set plays and late Rafa Marin red card.

Sends Meret the wrong way, and Napoli’s goal difference takes another hit.

Remember, this Porto side is top of the domestic league, but lost all three previous Champions League games.

Samu on the counter-attack, brought down with zero attempt to play the ball from Rafa Marin.

Nearly 1-9… Cross for Yan Couto at the back post, he can’t keep his volley down!

📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/g6eg4MXtQ8

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) November 4, 2026

Gilmour has a pop from distance, but that’s not going to trouble Porto.

Napoli refusing to learn any lessons and allowing another completely free header on a corner, this time the former Spezia and Arsenal defender.

Giovane and Lang on, Anguissa and Vergara off.

Inbeom Hwang and Fofana on, Gabriel Veiga and Pepe off.

Porto let Napoli off the hook with a similar counter-attack, Samu gets greedy and goes for goal himself, but it’s too weak to beat Meret!

Angled drive into the far bottom corner after dribbling into the box.

Napoli have not made a change yet, and they look tired.

Porto take advantage, as Gabriel Veiga runs onto the Santiago Gimenez pass, is one on one with Meret and deposits into the net.

It’s turning into a siege here, Gabriel Veiga strike from the edge of the box hits the bar!

Santiago Gimenez into a promising situation, but scuffs the finish into the arms of Meret.

Pepe scuffs the half-volley from a promising position and sends it wide.

Santiago Gimenez and Zaidu Sanusi on, Borja Sainz and Martim Fernandes off.

Corner routine finds Aguilar unmarked to hit a fine volley into the far bottom corner from 12 yards.

Mad scramble on a set play, Rafa Marin makes the crucial block from five yards with his chest on Alberto Costa!

Liberali sprints down the right and beats the goalkeeper with an angled drive.

Douvikas off, debut for Matteo Papaccioli.
