#1213. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Liverpool's attack in need of jump start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Champions League reaches its midpoint Wednesday night and if the last few rounds of fixtures are anything to go off, it will do so amid a hailstorm of goals. Wouldn't that be good news for Liverpool, even though their Champions League scoring record is already more impressive than in the Premier League? Meanwhile, there are plenty of high-stakes matchups at each end of the table. Real Betis are one of only four teams still standing with a 100% record but that could well be tested on the road against Borussia Dortmund.

At the other end of the table, Porto have a lot of work to do. Marooned in 35th, only the Portuguese league leaders and Slovan Bratislava are yet to get among the points. Surely if they do not do something tonight against Napoli, their competition will be done, right?

All that, plus Real Madrid, Arsenal and Manchester City in action tonight. It's sure to be a busy day.

If all you had to assess a team on from the season so far was the league phase table, you would believe that Liverpool are as advertised. That half a billion or so they have spent on their attack since the start of last season seems to be well spent, 12 goals from their first three Champions League games as Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Dominik Szoboszlai share in the scoring. Andoni Iraola's side may look a little vulnerable at the other end, but if you look at the talent in the Reds' roster, you score three, we'll score four-ball seems a pretty shrewd use of talent.

And yet the free-scoring Liverpool of the Champions League have been hard to spot in their domestic games. With the caveat that most teams' numbers take a dink after they run into Arsenal, at the nine-game mark in the Premier League season Liverpool have just 11 goals to their name. Only some of that can be accounted for through poor finishing -- Szoboszlai, Wirtz, Barcola and Cody Gakpo have two Premier League goals off 5.24 xG -- and the bigger issue is that this team ranks 11th in the league for expected goals.

As the graphic above indicates, there are quite widespread issues with the quality of shots Liverpool are settling for. Across Europe's top five leagues, the xG value of the average shot this season is 0.111. In no context do Iraola's team get particularly close to that mark. Instead, they take a lot of shots from outside the box, just under 40%, and they lead Europe's top five leagues for the proportion of their shots that are blocked, 37.9%.

Curiously low-quality shots were not exactly an issue that bedevilled Iraola's previous team. Last season Bournemouth ranked quite highly in terms of xG per shot both from open play and dead balls. A sign of a team that was humming as a unit and had grasped how the coach wanted to turn the chaos they engendered into quality scoring chances? Iraola will hope so. That augurs better for Liverpool than the possibility that the talents in which so much has been invested just don't quite gel.

That Liverpool's numbers are different in the Champions League might be telling us little more than the fact that their last two games in particular -- away to LASK, at home to Villarreal -- have been fairly favorable to run up the goals. The 12 they have scored have come off 7.23 worth of xG and a quarter of their shots are being blocked. You would not, then, want to get carried away with the idea that this is a team who will just be able to flick a switch when the Champions League music starts playing in Istanbul on Wednesday night.

Defeat at home to Napoli would not actually be critical to Porto's hopes of advancing to the knockout round of the Champions League. De facto, however? Yeah, probably. If projection models and past seasons are anything to go on, nine points is a decent guide to where the cut line will land after eight games. You do not want to have to accrue all of them after the turn. After all, Porto don't really have three gimmes left after the international break. You'd fancy Francesco Farioli's side to beat Slavia Prague away and LASK at home but their other games are on the road. Feyenoord could be tough, Liverpool would be.

Porto might reasonably feel they could have got more from these games. The first half against Manchester City was played even and there were half openings before Erling Haaland's late goal. Real Betis also did for them late on, two goals in the final 16 minutes earning the La Liga side a win in Seville while PSV beat them with perhaps the game's only clear opening last time out. That last line speaks to the issue that will have to be resolved over the next five games. Porto just do not take enough shots.

Thirty of them worth a combined 2.7 xG just is not going to cut it for a team who are averaging not far off that number per game in domestic competition. Strikers Samu Aghehowa and Andre Silva have just four shots between them. Domestically, this is a team that does supplement their output from center forward with more attempts from deeper but Gabri Veiga has just five shots to his name. Borja Sainz averages nearly three and a half in the Primeira Liga. He is yet to take a shot in the Champions League. This looks like the familiar story of a Portuguese team dominating 15 dramatically inferior opponents at home and struggling when the difficulty level ramps up in Europe.

"The Champions League is a different competition," said Farioli. "The demands and the details make all the difference. Being effective at every moment is important, as we've seen in the first three matches.

"I hope experience helps us be more effective than we have been. In terms of performances, we're doing well, but we can do more, because this isn't enough. We're working to raise our level, and tomorrow is the moment to do that and claim the points we want so much."

Fail to do so and that might effectively be it for Porto and this season's Champions League.

One might discount a player who has scored 40 goals in his last 71 league games for Borussia Dortmund with the two most devastating words in the footballing lexicon: Bundesliga tax. And you know what, sometimes those words cut through because there is truth to them. I fear that may be the case for a certain F. Wirtz.

Serhou Guirassy, though? Well, right now he is finding ways to score in every competition. A poacher's finish from his only shot helped earn Dortmund a backs-to-the-wall 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich, setting him up nicely for his return to a competition where he has excelled for a number of years. In 31 Champions League games, four for Rennes and the rest in Dortmund colors, the 30-year-old has 23 goals. Admittedly, seven of those are penalties but a goal every other game at the highest level of club football is not to be sniffed at. Nor are 0.63 non-penalty expected goals per 90 minutes.

Notably, Guirassy has enjoyed some of his greatest success against Spanish opposition, scoring in each encounter, a hat trick against Barcelona in 2025, perhaps his best moment. It might be that the Guinean striker is just an archetype that the best of La Liga do not face that often. At 6ft 2in, Guirassy is big, strong and impressively mobile, at least when his opponents aren't the big, hulking center backs of Chelsea and Manchester City. Could he have baited the same penalty off them that he got against Villarreal back in September? Certainly you wouldn't fancy him to have quite the same bully ball joy off set pieces that he did against Villarreal, Athletic Club and Barcelona.

As for Wednesday's opponent, it might be tricky for Real Betis. It's worth saying that in their three Champions League games so far they have allowed just over 2.5 xG against good opposition: Lille, Porto and Feyenoord. In La Liga, however, they rank 18th for set piece xG allowed and set piece goals conceded. They're not particularly great at limiting touches and xG in the box either. This could be another banner day for Guirassy.

#1212. Mauricio Pochettino mixes veterans, youth on USMNT roster for Nations League matches

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After a September/October international break where some United States men's national team regulars were able to get a rest while Mauricio Pochettino got to look at a younger group of players, now it's time to return to competitive play with two matches against Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals. The USMNT will look to book their place in the last four with games on Nov. 14 and Nov. 17. While many regulars such as Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie, and Folarin Balogun have returned to this squad, many of the young players who got their first taste of USMNT camp, such as Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall, will be called on yet again for the full Concacaf experience of competing in Nations League play.

While some players such as Miles Robinson, Johnny Cardoso, and Ricardo Pepi have been dealing with injuries as of late, it could be a door closing for others like Tim Weah and Yunus Musah as young players have been called in at their positions. Pochettino did confirm that both Pepi and Balogun aren't 100% fit, so it only made sense to call in one while also giving opportunities to Justin Ellis and Hall to earn opportunities to play against Haiti.

Yet again, Pochettino has called in uncapped players, as Reed Baker-Whiting seeks his first USMNT cap, and Paderborn midfielder Santiago Castaneda, who is also eligible to represent Colombia, has been rewarded for his stellar play in the German Bundesliga.

With many members of the USMNT, such as Pulisic, Sebastian Berhalter, and Gio Reyna in good form, it will be an attack-heavy lineup. However, there are plenty of questions as to how Pochettino will set up his defense. After the core that made the World Cup, anything could happen, but there's a clear goal of bringing along the next generation of U.S. Soccer now, as we'll get to see what the younger players can do in competitive matches.

Speaking about the roster, Pochettino stressed balance, and he may have alluded to some interesting lineup mechanics as he integrates that youth with established players such as Pulisic. A U-23 camp may be going on at the same time as this one, and while many players in the current squad are eligible, if a player is good enough for the senior team and fits Pochettino's vision, then they'll be with the senior squad.

"I think it's important to always try to add new ideas, new ways to try to perform, and to create different patterns on the field with the ball. Always our priority is with the ball, but also when we don't have the ball is to create a good organization to recover the ball as soon as possible and to get the ball back," Pochettino said. "But I think that roster provides a very good opportunity to try different things. The most important thing is the combination, to try to see the chemistry between because I think for Christian and Matias [Albert] is the first time that they are going to be together. I think the combination, also, we need to see during the camp. From Monday, we are going to start to see the chemistry off the field, but also on the field that is really important too, and try to see how that works."

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

GOALKEEPERS (3): Matt Freese (New York City FC; 20/0), Diego Kochen (Lyngby Boldklub/DEN; 2/0), Brian Schwake (Nashville SC; 2/0)

DEFENDERS (9): Reed Baker-Whiting (Nashville SC; 0/0), George Campbell (West Bromwich Albion FC/ENG; 3/0), Sergiño Dest (PSV Eindhoven/NED; 46/3), Alex Freeman (Villarreal/ESP; 26/3), Neil Pierre (Philadelphia Union; 3/0), Bryan Reynolds (Stade Rennais/FRA; 7/1), Chris Richards (Crystal Palace/ENG; 43/4), Antonee Robinson (Fulham/ENG; 62/5), Auston Trusty (Celtic/SCO; 14/1)

MIDFIELDERS (8): Tyler Adams (AFC Bournemouth/ENG; 62/2), Mathis Albert (Borussia Dortmund/GER; 4/1), Sebastian Berhalter (Middlesbrough/ENG; 22/4), Santiago Castañeda (SC Paderborn/GER; 0/0), Weston McKennie (Juventus/ITA; 71/12), Adri Mehmeti (Red Bull New York; 3/0), Gio Reyna (RC Strasbourg Alsace/FRA; 47/10), Malik Tillman (Bayer Leverkusen/GER; 39/7)

FORWARDS (5): Folarin Balogun (Monaco/FRA; 31/12), Justin Ellis (Orlando City SC; 3/2), Julian Hall (Red Bull New York; 4/3), Christian Pulisic (AC Milan/ITA; 90/33), Cavan Sullivan (Philadelphia Union; 3/1)

While Pulisic has come on as of late, signing a new contract with Milan and scoring twice in his last three appearances for the club, the forward who has been putting the ball in the back of the net for club and country as of late lies in Major League Soccer. Balogun has found it tough to get starting minutes during a strange time at Monaco since not departing during the summer transfer window, but with the rise of Hall with Red Bull New York, there will be goals against Haiti. Hall has scored 13 goals in MLS play while already adding three for the national team, and given Balogun's fitness, he'll earn minutes in this camp too. Since coming back to New York from national team camp, Hall has scored three more goals in six appearances and seems to have leveled up since spending time with the national team.

Pochettino is happy with his forwards, and why shouldn't he be?

"Balogun is a great opportunity to keep helping him to evolve after a tough summer after the World Cup. That is why I think the balance is there, because Justin and Julian are fully fit," Pochettino said. "That is why we didn't bring even though he played a few minutes last week, Ricardo. In our way to see and assess the players, we decided it was much better to keep him training and establish himself being more solid in his fitness and be more confident to attack the future. That is why we didn't want to bring both, because I think both are not 100%, but I think the combination of Balogun, Ellis, and Hall I think is perfect."

Haiti will be a true test of who can withstand Concacaf play, so this is a camp that will go a long way to determining who is set for time with the U-23s versus who will stick with the senior team long term.

While these games are competitive, we're still in experimental mode with the USMNT, and that stands for almost every position. It was a tough first camp for Neil Pierre and George Campbell, but they've been called in again to show their growth. Campbell was withdrawn at half of West Brom's last match due to an injury, so there will be a late fitness test there to see if he can actually join the camp, but behind Chris Richards and Auston Trusty, other members of the USMNT will need to be ready as their time could come at any moment.

Albert still hasn't played much for Dortmund, but Pochettino described him as a player who can bring something different, and that's what's going to be fascinating to watch with this squad. During his time as a club manager, Pochettino was excellent at taking players under his wing and improving the standing of young players, and as the Argentine has committed to another cycle, his excitement about being able to bring the next generation of Americans along is also showing. In his press conference, Pochettino pondered seeing Cavan Sullivan and Weston McKennie together, and it's hard not to imagine the duo as dual 10s that make something happen. Even listening to Pochettino ponder Albert, this is more than just the USMNT manager speaking; this is someone invested in American soccer.

"I think he is a player with a quality that is not easy to find in in another in another player. For me, Matias is one of the most talented players in the USA," Pochettino said. "And I think even if he's not playing too much or Borussia Dortmund is not giving him too much game time, I think he's fully fit and is he is capable of, you know, bringing something different to the national team. That is why I think we consider it, and I think the combination with the players that we have in front of us, he can perform, and we really trust, and we are very convinced that also giving the opportunity to be with us, I think we will help him to recover his confidence and also help in the future in his club, to have the possibility to play more."

It's an exciting time for the national team, and it's one where Pochettino has the ability to truly make his mark. They're well positioned to dominate the region, and with more than 100 players being tracked by the national team, there's no room to get complacent because Pochettino has shown that if someone doesn't live up to his standard, he's willing to make the call to get a new body in.

#1211. Matthias Jaissle throwing his players under the bus is a dangerous game. Newcastle have no identity, no direction and no patterns - and that's on the manager, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 05:50 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 04:25 EDT, 4 November 2026

There often comes a point in a manager’s reign when the blame for defeat shifts from the dugout to the dressing room, and it is invariably the point of no return. Rarely does it arrive after just nine matches.

So when Matthias Jaissle took aim at his players in the wake of Newcastle’s 1-0 defeat by Everton on Monday, it was arguably a more concerning display than the 90 minutes which had preceded it, as alarming as those had been.

Jaissle’s post-match reflections were not inaccurate. This was not a manager talking nonsense. He fronted up and gave what felt like honest answers.

The 38-year-old is bright and articulate and, with each defeat, has shown an increasing humility that was less visible during the optimism of his introductory days.

To show the players the underside of the bus so soon, however, is as baffling a tactic as the strategy enacted on the pitch, even if Jaissle insists that performance had no resemblance to what he had asked of his team.

Rather, says the German, he had wanted his players to keep the ball on the floor and get the wingers in one-on-one situations high up the pitch. What he saw was a collection of long balls and a heading-practice session for Everton’s centre backs. The wingers, meanwhile, were spectators.

When a manager blames the players for defeat - as Matthias Jaissle did after Newcastle lost to Everton on Monday night - it is often the beginning of the end for the man in the dugout

Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes struggled to get on the ball during the defeat by Everton

‘The plan was not to shoot the long balls,’ he said.

Nor was the plan to shoot at all, it seemed. It took until the 85th minute for Newcastle to trouble Jordan Pickford, and even then the goalkeeper wasn’t overly concerned.

Short ball? Long ball? Whatever pass Newcastle pick, it is invariably the wrong ball. They are a team without identity – no patterns, no partnerships and, certainly, no sign of progress. So while there is some sympathy with Jaissle if players are failing to follow his instructions, it always comes back on any manager to make sure they do.

I once wrote of Everton boss David Moyes, when in charge of Sunderland, that he had inherited a sinking ship, only to drill another hole. Moyes, for the record, is a very good manager, he just wasn’t at Sunderland.

And that is the danger with Jaissle. He, too, walked into a difficult situation post Eddie Howe and the loss of several star players. Their replacements have been bench-warners or cold starters.

But Jaissle has to be the solution, not another problem. At present, the fear is that a young manager with no major-league experience is held hostage by his ideals and refuses to bend to what his players want and need.

His continued use of a 4-2-3-1 system, with two midfielders who cannot really run and a revolving cast of No 10s who are not No 10s, feels with each passing week and each passing defeat like a blueprint for relegation.

Maybe the team ignoring their manager’s wishes on Monday night was a cry for change. A protest, even? Do they not believe in his methods or do they not understand them?

Newcastle's Yoane Wissa rues a missed chance against Everton in what was Newcastle's third loss in their last five Premier League games

Jaissle tries to get his message across to Joelinton and Harvey Barnes at St James' Park

Either way, Newcastle must try something different. The Everton loss, and the nature of a performance absent of direction or conviction, was not a surprise. This run of form – four defeats in five in all competitions – has been coming since the early weeks of the season, when results flattered performances and the underlying numbers told a more troubling story.

It is not the time to change manager, and nor do the club’s hierarchy think so. The change has to come from within – approach, attitude, execution. That is on Jaissle and the players, not one or the other.

That is why before the head coach addresses what happened on the pitch, he must clarify to his players what he said off it. To lose matches is one thing, but to risk losing your dressing room is quite another.

That would leave Jaissle facing the one situation from which his ‘vertical football’ could offer no way forward.

#1209. Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, said.

“We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”

Saints win the pen and hoof it downfield.. but now it’s their turn to make a hash of the lineout as Chessum, back from his HIA, gets his paws to the ball.

Tigers take it wide and win a penalty and begin advancing into Saints’ 22.. they shift it wide to Radwan but the winger is brusqely shuffled into touch.. and theres some fiesty afters, in true derby fashion, ensues.

Tempers begin flaring as players from both sides get involved. Mitchell appears to say something to Chessum and then carnage ensues. In the melee, Kemeny and Wainwright are at each other. Chessum and Pollock exchange a few words and the drama continues as both teams head down the tunnel. Pollock stops halfway up the steps and appears to mimic doing up his boot laces, inviting a shove on from Chessum.

Tigers have a line-out and this time Langdon’s arrow is good and the home side looks to pounce. Van Poorvliet looks to scamper his way through a few white shirts before Carnduff makes a fine carry but the wet conditions derail Blamire, who spills it. Another opportunity wasted for the hosts, but they’ll have another opportunity.

Searle boots it into the corner.. this time it’s short but still Tigers manage to mess it up and knock on. Kemeny is being such a nuisance in there.

Mitchell gets scragged by Hamer-Webb and in the rain misses a kick attempt, as Tigers edge their way closer into Saints’ 22. The hosts are averaging only 50 per cent at the moment - Kemeny is making a real nuisance of himself and getting into Blamire’s head - and they lose another in a promising position.

Saints are knocking on Tigers’ door and Fin Smith makes some good post-contact metres as he eats up grass and edges towards Tigers’ try line. Some staunch defence from the hosts, who survive after Prowse is penalised for not rolling away.

Eeek, after his 50m hoof Steward is the first to blink in a brief kick tennis exchange and spills the ball in Tigers’ territory. Tigers collapse the scrum - they’re pushing a bit too hard before the engagement - and Saints look to work up a head of steam.

Smith asks questions with another chip over the defence but Tigers deal with it well enough and van Poortvliet fires it clear.

But Saints aren’t done, they come again and Smith looks cross field and picks out Rory Hutchinson, who is met by Hamer-Webb.

There’s a bit of spice between the pair before referee Craig Maxwell-Keys intervenes and declares it was a good contest.

Tigers have already crafted some decent opportunities in these opening exchanges but their execution has been poor, as the hosts come again - this time through Kata - but it’s Chessum who spills once more. Saints win a scrum penalty after van der Flier engages too early. Saints look to work their way down field but we’ll come back for a Tigers’ penalty after Pollock was offside from Smith’s kick.

Steward lines up a kick from 50 metres and he splits the uprights. Tigers are on the board.

He's struck that beautifully! 😍 Freddie Steward nails a penalty from halfway to get @LeicesterTigers on the board 🐯👏 📺 Stream TNT Sports on HBO Max https://t.co/ISqfkeU3vl https://t.co/opyNyxbART

Fin Smith is hobbling a little which might cause some alarm in Northampton and beyond. Hopefully nothing serious for the England stand-off. He is still able to take re-starts so that is a good sign…

Craig Maxwell-Keys, the referee, won’t be short on advice this afternoon. Two penalties to Northampton and the home crowd are already growing restless.

He is going to need eyes in the back of his head this afternoon. It took all of two minutes for the first coming-together after a thumping double hit on Fin Smith from Archie van der Flier and Olly Cracknell.

There’s something heartening primal about an East Midlands derby and this one feels like it is right on the edge. It’s a sell-out and it is intense.

Tigers respond positively by flooding Saints’ half and win a lineout deep in the red zone. It’s a huge defensive set from Saints, who manage to force their rivals back and Leicester can’t seem to make the pressure count.

Searle pokes through a cross-field grubber but there’s top much on it for Seale, but Tigers will come back for the free kick after Saints are penalised for collapsing a driving maul.

They come again but the Tigers lose it through Chessum five-metres out - it’s a very wet ball out there so we can expect to see a lot of that - and Pollock leads the celebrations among the forwards. You can bet he’ll be in their faces all afternoon.

Saints strike first! They make a mess of their first line out but Chessum manages to knock on and the visitors have a scrum in Tigers’ 22. The hosts are too eager to engage and Mitchell takes the free kick quickly. Saints edge forward with some patient phase play - they get the offside advantage and Smith chips the Tigers’ defence.

Billy Searle is tracking the ball but he’s scampering back awkwardly and completely misses the catch. Instead James Pater gathers the loose ball and watches it into his hands.. and grounds it. Saints strike first! Conversion is good.

Striking first on derby day 💥 James Pater capitalises on a Leicester error to open the scoring for @SaintsRugby 😇 📺 Stream TNT Sports on HBO Max https://t.co/ISqfkeU3vl https://t.co/kpjaHgHERp

Billy Searle gets proceedings underway and its Saints who gain some fine field position early on after the hosts are penalised for not rolling away. Fin Smith is smothered by a double-tackle and the England fly-half spills the ball. Saints don’t like it and there’s a few afters but things calm down pretty quickly. Tension already!

.. and enter what looks like a horrendously wet Welford Road. Rain is pouring - expect dropped balls and greasy conditions!

Our rugby reporter Charles Richardson relieves the time Manu Tuilagi gave one - or a few - to Chris Ashton back in 2011.

In a fiery – when is this fixture not? – first half, both were sin-binned for their involvement in what might be described as a disagreement.

Tuilagi took Ashton out, slightly high, off the ball as the wing attempted to support scrum-half Lee Dickson’s quickly taken penalty. Ashton then gave the 19-year-old, uncapped Tuilagi a little shove on the floor, before the red mist descended on the future England centre. Catch the full read here.

Henry Pollock’s cornrow phase is over. He’s sporting a mousy mop for today’s East Midlands derby.

The Northampton No 8 - currently warming up in a snood - will be pantomime-villain-in-chief for the Saints in these parts but he has a big afternoon ahead.

This is exactly the sort of occasion and arm wrestle which he needs to excel in to prove to Steve Borthwick he is worth more than a bench role for England next month.

Wrapped up against the storm ⛈️ It's wet and windy ahead of the East Midlands derby - just ask Henry Pollock! 😅 📺 Stream TNT Sports on HBO Max https://t.co/ISqfkeU3vl https://t.co/1pirJ1Nm2D

Leicester were buoyed in the week by re-signing Jack van Poortfliet, who extended his contract with his boyhood club.

I grew up supporting Leicester, it’s always been my club,” said the England scrum half. This place feels like home in my rugby life. The club is in a really good position, I think we have a great group of lads and great coaches.

I love playing rugby here, I have my best mates here and I believe that we’ve got a group of lads that we can do great things with. I want to be in a place that I love playing for and I believe can win trophies.”

Squally conditions this afternoon at Mattioli Welford Road - in fact make that horrible. An interesting test then for Northampton as lovers of the beautiful game.

You would imagine that the rain and wind would suit a Leicester side whose DNA is set piece power better.

Expect the catch and drive to get plenty of game time and Jack van Poortvliet and Billy Searle to go to the air regularly. It could be a stern examination for teenage Saints full-back James Pater.

It’s a big day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Northampton Saints: J Pater; T Freeman, R Hutchinson, F Dingwall, G Hendy; F Smith, A Mitchell, E Iyogun, C Langdon, C Kundiona, A Coles, E Prowse, J Kemeny, T Pearson, H Pollock.

Replacements: R Smith, D Fischetti, I Neculai, JJ Van Der Mescht, T Lockett, C Chick, A McParland, O Sleightholme.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

#1208. Inside Mason Greenwood's new life in Turkey ahead of Liverpool clash: How former Man United star has stayed under the radar, why Fenerbahce fans have welcomed him - and his new luxurious gated community

Published: 05:18 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 06:46 EDT, 4 November 2026

If you're choosing a club to keep a low profile – the claustrophobic fervour of Fenerbahce seems a strange option.

But Mason Greenwood – since being mobbed by fans at Istanbul Airport with his partner Harriet Robson and two young daughters in the summer – has tried to fly under the radar.

From Man United prodigy to club-hopping pariah on a European exile, the 25-year-old hasn't found a comfortable home in three years since leaving his homeland.

A reminder of the why... Early in 2022, Greenwood was arrested and later charged with attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour and assault causing actual bodily harm.

Those charges were subsequently dropped but after a six-month internal Man United investigation into his conduct, the club agreed he could not continue to ply his trade at Old Trafford.

Greenwood's attempt at career resurrection took him on loan to Getafe and later a turbulent two years in Marseille before Fenerbahce broke their transfer record to snap him up for £33million.

Former Man United star Mason Greenwood joined Fenerbahce from Marseille in the summer

Greenwood has largely tried to fly under the radar alongside his partner and two daughters

Greenwood has found a home in Istanbul's luxury gated district of Sariyer (pictured above with the all-female team of estate agents who helped him with the purchase)

While there was noisy resistance to Greenwood joining Marseille, he found no such opposition in Turkey, where one prominent journalist claimed 95 per cent of the population would not know or care about his past.

He didn't face any questions about the dropped charges or his public image in his first press conference and outside of brief post-match comments, has not conducted any interviews of note.

Greenwood has been hiding from the limelight a record signing would usually bask in, especially in the football-crazed city of Istanbul.

He found a home in a district called Sarıyer, a favourite among footballers, who largely live in gated communities.

Sarıyer is located on the eastern side of the city towards luxurious Black Sea beaches and quieter historic towns.

Greenwood is said to count team-mates N'Golo Kante and Marco Asensio as neighbours and was seen in a rare online post after securing his new home, posing with the all-female team of estate agents who helped him with the purchase.

Since the big-money move, Greenwood has only posted four times on his Instagram profile, all of which were generic action shots after matches.

In his latest offering, accompanied by snaps from his different clubs, he wrote: 'From my first professional goal to number 100. Different clubs, different countries, so many memories along the way. A special milestone for me.'

His partner, Harriet, is also selective with how much she shares from their new life.

She only has four posts in total, with around 20 photos in each 'round-up', offering a glimpse into the high-life, though Greenwood himself only appears twice.

One of the images is of him looking exhausted in hospital at the birth of their second daughter in 2023 and another shows him holding hands with their eldest, Summer, who is three.

Sariyer is located on the eastern side of Istanbul towards the Black Sea beaches and quieter historic towns - and away from the mayhem of the city's centre

Greenwood and his partner Harriet are cautious in what they share but one image (pictured above) shows him looking exhausted in hospital at the birth of their second daughter in 2023

The forward will be hoping to make an impact when Fenerbahce take on Liverpool this evening

Greenwood's engagement through new media and traditional remains deliberately cautious.

He's slipped into a quiet life in the suburbs, punctuated by the intense matchday experience at Sukru Saracoglu Stadium.

So far, Greenwood has made 11 goal contributions in 18 matches for his new side, an impressive return, particularly with the club enduring a turbulent start to the season.

He missed Fenerbahce's defeat at the weekend after suffering with a virus but ex-Liverpool cult hero Dirk Kuyt – who is interim manager – is expecting him to be available for the most high-profile match of the season so far.

Turkey has provided an unchallenging and comfortable new home for Greenwood. For many watching him on Wednesday night, the overriding feeling may still be one of unease.

#1206. A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Inspired by macroscopic weaving techniques1,2,3,4, molecular weaving, which interlaces molecular strands into ordered networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy for designing functional materials with emergent properties5,6. However, so far, molecular weaving has relied mainly on linear building blocks and biaxial structures. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Here we report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative B–N polymerization. The resulting material not only exhibits unique topological chirality and robust mechanical properties but it also serves as a porous material that permits the separation of representative aromatic/aliphatic compounds. This functional utility highlights how higher-order triaxial woven topologies can provide unique advantages in terms of regulating material properties and introduces an extra topological dimension for the construction of functional materials.

#1205. Sensational Spurs storm Stamford Bridge as Palmer loses his head

So much for Xabi Alonso’s call for cool heads from his Chelsea players. Cole Palmer lost his and was sent off, while goalkeeper Mike Penders punched the ball into his own net to give Tottenham Hotspur a helping hand on their way to a second win at Stamford Bridge in 42 attempts.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Christopher Kavanagh, the referee, let him off with a yellow card, but 10 minutes later Palmer inexplicably gave Kavanagh no choice but to book him again and send him off, following a late challenge on substitute Conor Gallagher.

"It's PETULANT from Cole Palmer...you have to take it on the chin" Jamie Redknapp and Daniel Sturridge react to Cole Palmer's pair of yellow cards 🟥 https://t.co/Voxoo3Ea7V

Palmer was just about the only Chelsea player not to have been sent off last season, but it seems that Alonso has not yet managed to deal with the club’s disciplinary problem.

Jordan Henderson had given Palmer a talking to at the end of the win at Everton in which the forward was booked. But he evidently did not heed the advice or the words of his manager.

Alonso had said he was confident his players could keep calm ahead of the game, but he got that wrong – along with his team selection and substitutions.

In between Palmer’s two bookings, Penders suffered his own moment of madness with a bizarre own goal on his league debut for Chelsea. The Belgian was standing in for Emi Martinez, who watched in disbelief from the home dug-out after undergoing surgery on his jaw.

Fernandes sent in a corner that Jan Paul van Hecke challenged for. Penders looked like the easy winner in that contest, but he got his punch horribly wrong and the ball spun backwards and over the goalline.

Spurs have taken the lead after Mateus Fernandes' corner ends up in Chelsea's goal ⚽️ https://t.co/X65gyO9yPX

A man and a goal down, Chelsea then saw hundreds of their own fans walk out when Mathys Tel scored a brilliant second for Spurs with three minutes remaining. The visiting fans, who had seen one win at the Bridge since 1990 prior to Saturday, could hardly believe what they had seen.

"Just look what it means!" A glorious solo run and finish from Mathys Tel! 🤩 https://t.co/Qg7WMFNlwQ

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi celebrated wildly with his staff. The two benches had clashed and De Zerbi had been booked after Palmer’s first yellow card that the Italian felt should have been a red. But De Zerbi will not care about that now, with Tottenham’s season finally up and running thanks to successive league wins against Coventry City and Chelsea.

"They were brilliant Spurs, they really were" Gary Neville's immediate reaction to Chelsea 0-2 Tottenham 🗣️ https://t.co/QWhi7Blmfz

Tottenham should really have been ahead in the first half. De Zerbi revealed before the game that Dominic Solanke had dropped down to the substitutes’ bench because the striker “felt fatigue” after the victory over Coventry.

With Solanke resting up on the bench until the 65th minute, De Zerbi moved Omar Marmoush, who had scored his first Spurs goal against Coventry, into the middle and brought in Tel on the left.

Tel was involved in the 29th-minute move that should have resulted in the opening goal for Marmoush. The Frenchman played a one-two with Andy Robertson and the Scotsman picked out Marmoush with a low cross. But, six yards out and with time to pick his spot, the former Manchester City man allowed Penders to make a save.

The missed Marmoush chance was the first time Penders had been called into action. At the other end, Tottenham goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky made unnecessary work for himself.

Kinsky played a bad pass straight to Pedro Neto. The ball was worked to Henderson, but Kinsky recovered to make a save and then stopped the follow-up from Neto. The offside flag then went up, but it was unclear whether it would have spared Kinsky on both occasions had Chelsea scored.

It was not the first time Kinsky had handed possession back to Chelsea in a dangerous area, although the 23-year-old had also made a good save to palm away a curling effort from Palmer. That came after Fernandes had the ball pinched from him far too easily.

Neto was Chelsea’s most dangerous player, but it was the wrong call by Alonso to leave Danny Welbeck on the bench, with João Pedro out injured, and he was too slow to change things. Leaving it until the 88th minute, when the game had already been killed by Tel, to send on the striker was a clear error.

Storm Boelo created wet-and-wild conditions on the Stamford Bridge pitch, while there were still remnants of Storm Austen, or should that be Storm Austin, on the home bench.

Chelsea set-piece coach Austin MacPhee let out an incredibly loud “for f---’s sake” when one corner routine went wrong. Nobody could hear what he was shouting over the Tottenham celebrations when Penders scored his own goal, but it would almost certainly have started with “f” again.

James Maddison had been a doubt before the game after missing training during the week and it only took four minutes of the second half for him to signal to De Zerbi that he needed to come off.

Maddison had scored a brilliant goal on his first league start in 18 months against Coventry, but he had to be replaced by former Chelsea midfielder Gallagher at Stamford Bridge.

James Maddison is forced off with an injury and is replaced by Conor Gallagher, who receives a mixed reception from his former fans 🔃 https://t.co/GSeXQQ3eoa

The Chelsea fans predictably booed Gallagher, a graduate of the club’s academy who at times even stood in as captain. The foul on Gallagher that earned Palmer his marching orders silenced the jeers and the Chelsea fans’ boos only returned at the final whistle for their own players.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has told Cole Palmer he must learn from his red card that contributed to his team’s London derby defeat by Tottenham Hotspur.

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi insisted Palmer should have seen red for shoving his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes. But, having got off with a yellow card, the Chelsea midfielder then fouled substitute Conor Gallagher.

“I haven’t seen them [the yellow cards] on TV, but as far as I have been told, he [the referee] probably got it right,” Alonso said. “So, for sure for Cole, but for everyone. We think [up until] now we haven’t received any red cards [this season] and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, there was still 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be calm. I need to check the action to talk with Cole, but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Asked if he thought Palmer should have been sent off for the first yellow card, De Zerbi, who was booked for his protests, replied: “Yep.”

Jordan Henderson had spoken to Palmer at the end of the previous week’s victory over Everton in which the forward could also have been booked for a second time and sent off.

But Alonso claimed he does not have any wider concerns about Palmer’s character. He said: “Today, for sure, yes, but it is not a [wider] concern. I think that Cole when he is focused on the game, when he is enjoying and today after the 1-0, it is a moment to keep calm, a moment to keep mature and for everyone.”

De Zerbi hailed his side’s character and claimed that Tottenham have “suffered enough” after two 17th-placed finishes and a slow start to the season until successive victories over Coventry City and Chelsea.

“We want to improve, improve and improve, to be better game by game, week by week. I think we have suffered enough,” De Zerbi said. “Changing the spirit of the group, changing the performance of the players, especially the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We played very well. Great individual performances, great collective performance because we played very well. And then we put something different than Tottenham, I think, in the last period. Different attitude, different relationships with the players, different group.”

Chelsea were without João Pedro because of an injury and Alonso is waiting to find out how long the striker will be out.

“We don’t know yet because he has a lot of fluid,” Alonso said. “So he felt it yesterday [Friday] and we need to wait probably until tomorrow [Sunday] to do the test and to know the whole situation and the whole seriousness of the injury. We will know soon enough.”

A long-awaited Stamford Bridge victory for @SpursOfficial 👏 https://t.co/Qqwgbuj3Y3

“When we have dinner together and spend time together in the dressing room, I see a different group, different relationships and a different atmosphere among the players.

“The character was great today, but we have many, many new players. The players who stayed here from last season and two or three seasons ago suffered from the results, including two 17th-place finishes.

“We are working to change the last part of the club’s history. We are lucky because we have many great people in the dressing room and many great players. I think if we work hard, we can do something important.

“The week in Marbella, speaking face to face, opening ourselves up and removing the mask, was important for the spirit and belief.

“The atmosphere inside the dressing room is maybe more important than the tactics.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Tottenham boss said: “It was a big moment for the fans, the club and the players. They deserved this win and prepared very well.

“We are improving a lot in our mentality, as a group and in our relationships with the players. We are also improving on the pitch.

“Against Aston Villa and Everton, for 30 minutes we were playing very well. Maybe we didn’t score because our finishing wasn’t good enough, and perhaps in the first difficult moment we changed our mentality.

“Now we are a complete team. The players are playing better and we have improved our style.

“I have to believe in this group. I never lost confidence in my players.

“We have to keep working hard and improving. We have many great players, and I believe we can do something important if we continue in this way.”

"I thought our midfield was outstanding" 👏 Andy Robertson credits his Tottenham teammates after a rare win at Stamford Bridge. https://t.co/G7HpoJBZBg

"We are here to change the mentality of the club" 😤 Mateus Fernandes reacts to Spurs' win at Chelsea. https://t.co/KIGNRqDCFD

"They were brilliant Spurs, they really were" Gary Neville's immediate reaction to Chelsea 0-2 Tottenham 🗣️ https://t.co/QWhi7Blmfz

Tottenham have a rare and fully deserved victory over 10-man Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. An own goal from Penders and Tel’s brilliant solo strike sealed the three points for De Zerbi’s side. Chelsea produced a dreadful performance with Palmer sent off in the second half to compound a miserable evening for the hosts.

Three GLORIOUS points at Stamford Bridge 🤩 https://t.co/czWx6bUB78

Chelsea supporters have emptied Stamford Bridge. Tottenham fans are making all the noise. The visitors have been better in every department on the pitch today.

Rogers is booked for an ugly challenge on Gallagher. Amid the chaos, Welbeck finally enters the action, replacing Pedro Neto, while Kulusevski and Davies come on for Tel and Kudus. There’s seven minutes of added time.

Spurs are on their way to a historic win at Stamford Bridge. Tel starts a dribble from inside his own half, escapes Acheampong and glides past Lacroix, before arrowing a clinical effort into the bottom corner, sending De Zerbi and the away support absolutely wild. Incredible scenes. Chelsea have been miles off the pace today.

"Just look what it means!" A glorious solo run and finish from Mathys Tel! 🤩 https://t.co/Qg7WMFNlwQ

Kudus wins the ball off Palestra and tees up Gallagher, who shoots from a tight angle, but his low drive is parried away by Penders.

It goes from bad to worse for Chelsea. Palmer catches Gallagher with a late tackle and stamps on his ankle. It’s a definite second yellow card, and despite the Chelsea protests, Palmer can have no complaints. Chelsea have a mountain to climb now with a numerical disadvantage.

Cole Palmer is SENT OFF! 🟥 https://t.co/qArrUhFrf0

Penders comes out to claim a corner and mistimes his punch, directing the ball into the Chelsea net for an own goal, despite Lacroix’s best efforts to keep it from crossing the line. It’s a calamitous error from Penders on his first Premier League start. Tottenham have a priceless goal at Stamford Bridge and they deserve it.

Spurs have taken the lead after Mateus Fernandes' corner ends up in Chelsea's goal ⚽️ https://t.co/X65gyO9yPX

Estevao is on for Chelsea and replaces Quenda. The Brazilian is involved straight away as he strides into the penalty area and shoots into the side netting.

There’s a scuffle between both sets of players. Van de Ven lunges in with a late challenge on Caicedo, before Mateus Fernandes slips over and handles the ball as Palmer attempts to dribble forward. The Englishman reacts angrily, barging into Fernandes to spark a mini scuffle. Palmer is booked for that flashpoint. It was a foolish and risky challenge from the Chelsea man.

Things are heating up at the Bridge as Cole Palmer and Mateus Fernandes both receive a yellow! 🟨 https://t.co/hYXFl6xlZi

Here comes a Chelsea change, but it’s not an attacking one. It arrives at full back, with Palestra replacing Hato.

De Zerbi then makes a double substitution as Solanke and Porro come on for Marmoush and Robertson.

Can any of these alterations inject some more life into this encounter?

Neto forces a save from Kinsky. Chelsea pounce on Mateus Fernandes’ wayward pass, allowing Palmer and Neto to combine. The latter fizzes a venomous effort straight at Kinsky, which he bats away. That’s Chelsea’s best chance for some time.

How long will Alonso wait before introducing some substitutes for Chelsea? The hosts’ attacking threat is notably lacking. Welbeck and Estevao must be itching to enter the action.

This game is still being played at a relatively slow pace and is lacking some serious bite. Will Maddison’s injury take the wind out of Spurs’ sails or inspire them to victory?

Confirmation of that change as Gallagher replaces the injured Maddison, who heads straight down the tunnel. There’s some boos for Gallagher on his return to his former employers.

James Maddison is forced off with an injury and is replaced by Conor Gallagher, who receives a mixed reception from his former fans 🔃 https://t.co/GSeXQQ3eoa

There’s a break in play as Maddison goes down without anyone around him and glumly sits on the floor. He just can’t stay fit. Former Chelsea captain Gallagher is getting ready to come on.

Palmer surges forward before tumbling to the floor, believing he was clipped by Mateus Fernandes. There’s half-hearted appeals from some Chelsea players for a free kick on the edge of Spurs’ penalty area, but the referee isn’t interested.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break. Will we be treated to a more exiting second half? Let’s hope so.

It’s half-time at Stamford Bridge in a game lacking chances and attacking threat. Tottenham came closest to scoring just before the half-hour mark, when Marmoush forced Penders into terrific save on his first Premier League start. At the other end, Palmers tested Kinsky with a whipped effort, which the Spurs goalkeeper parried away. There’s much to ponder for Chelsea boss Alonso, whose plan to start to without a recognised striker has underwhelmed, while De Zerbi will feel more encouraged by his side’s display.

Hato takes a quick, clever free kick and finds Pedro Neto, whose made a great run. The winger flashes a low, driven shot off the wet surface from a tight angle, but Kinsky is there to gather it.

Spurs come forward on the counter through Tel, Marmoush and Kudus. However, the attack seems to lack conviction and it ends with Mateus Fernandes’ arrowed cross harmlessly drifting out of play.

We’re still waiting for this game to explode into life. It’s lacked the normal drama and controversy that this fixture normally provides.

Chelsea come alive as Kinsky miscues his pass, giving the ball to Pedro Neto. Palmer and Rogers get involved in the attack and it ends with a placed Henderson shot, which Kinsky does well to parry away. Chelsea look most dangerous when Kinsky has the ball at his feet and gives it away. The Tottenham goalkeeper needs to be careful.

Spurs burst forward on the counter and threads a pass through to Tel. Penders rushes out to smother the winger’s one-on-one effort. The offside flag was up, but Penders still did well to make the intervention.

Massive chance for Tottenham. Robertson slides a low, pinpoint cross into Marmoush, who shoots first-time from close range. Penders is up to the challenge and makes a pivotal stop to parry it away.

Penders comes out of his box and unconvincingly intercepts a through ball over the top of Chelsea’s defence. His pass has no power, but luckily for the young goalkeeper, it lands at Lacroix’s feet.

Spurs aren’t playing with their usual inferiority complex at Stamford Bridge. They looking confident. Chelsea are yet to strike a rhythm. Tel darts into Chelsea’s box, but Pedro Neto tracks back and makes an important tackle.

Chelsea’s substitutes have just been handed fluffy white towels to keep themselves dry and warm. I want one.

Tel’s deep cross finds Kudus at the back stick. The Ghanaian bends a curling strike around the covering defender. However, the shot evades the far post. Tottenham can certainly be encouraged by their start to this game.

Lacroix denies Maddison with a brilliant sliding challenge to win a goal kick for Chelsea. Maddison was convinced it was a corner.

We just heard a rather loud “For f***s sake” from Chelsea set-piece coach Austin MacPhee. Given we’ve just had Storm Austen, it feels appropriate that the Scotsman is giving the players a battering.

Pedro Neto does excellently to dispossess Mateus Fernandes, allowing Rogers to tee up Palmer. The playmaker whips a fierce effort aimed for the far top corner, but Kinsky is there to make a eye-catching diving save.

Tottenham have had more of the early possession, but both teams are still sounding each other out as we await the game’s first big chance. Palmers, Rogers and Henderson attempt a cheeky free kick routine, but Kinsky is alert to the danger.

Kinsky comes out of his box and Chelsea pounce on his poor pass to launch an attack. Palmer fizzes a delightful cross into the box, but no one is there to get on the end of it. Where’s Joao Pedro when you need him?

Rogers is playing highest for Chelsea as a false striker. He did it a few times for Villa, so it shouldn’t be anything new to him.

An early spell of Tottenham sees Chelsea defend a couple of free-kicks and clear a corner.

There will be no out-and-out strikers on the pitch today. Joao Pedro is out for Chelsea with an, as yet unspecified injury, while De Zerbi has said that Dominic Solanke “felt fatigue” against Coventry City so he has dropped to the bench. Antonio Conte, a former manager of both of these teams, wouldn’t be having a player missing a London derby for “feeling fatigue”.

Chelsea get us under way. The rain is hammering down on the pitch.

Can Spurs get their second win at Stamford Bridge, or will Chelsea's dominance continue? 👀📊 https://t.co/dNYgN2SKYA

These two bitter rivals meet again. The noise inside Stamford Bridge is deafening.

Cesar Azpilicueta is back at Stamford Bridge today. The club’s former captain relished a London derby and, more often than not, finished on the winning side against Spurs. Predictably he was given a big cheer by the home fans and loudly booed by the away end.

It’s a good job Oscar isn’t still playing for Chelsea, as, according to the club’s former manager Jose Mourinho, the Brazilian could not play in wet and wild conditions like we’ve got today. It was in 2014 that Mourinho said: “He’s not a natural physically strong man, suffers with the accumulation of matches, suffers with the difficult weather we had.”

Since joining Chelsea in the summer on an eight-year contract for £40m, Geovany Quenda has played just 28 Premier League minutes for his new club this season. Now, with Joao Pedro absent, Xabi Alonso has chosen Quenda to start in Chelsea’s attack alongside Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers instead of either Estevao and Danny Welbeck. It’s a bold decision. Will it pay off?

Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has been ruled for a “few weeks” after he collided with Jarrad Branthwaite and undergoing surgery on his jaw.

Speaking on the issue, Xabi Alonso said: “Emi is doing better. He had the surgery and day by day he is feeling better, but we still need to wait. A few weeks. Hopefully, less than more, but we need to wait.

#1203. Gianluigi Donnarumma was signed to be world's best shot-stopper, but at Manchester City, he's merely fine

Hard as it may be to believe or justify after events in Leipzig, there was a logic to Manchester City jettisoning their decade-long policy for goalkeeper recruitment last summer and signing Gianluigi Donnarumma. When your greatest defensive attribute is how your possession constricts your opponents from your third of the pitch then what you want from your No.1 is someone who can keep and progress the ball. Ederson is the dream. Even an aged Claudio Bravo is tolerable.

That all changed when Rodri's anterior cruciate ligament went in September 2024. Suddenly Manchester City were unable to shut down the opposition, to block off the counter and keep the other team to hitting and hoping. Having allowed somewhere around seven and a half shots in each of the previous four seasons, City allowed 9.34 in 2024-25, 9.71 in 2025-26. Now that Enzo Maresca has taken the helm and concluded that Elliot Anderson is enough of a midfield, we are at 10.56 in the Premier League. In the Champions League, where so many of City's opponents know best how to play on the front foot, it is 11 shots allowed per game (that average isn't as warped by playing PSG as you think).

If you're going to allow that much extra pressure on your goal, you want someone who can keep the ball out. In principle, Gianluigi Donnarumma is that guy, certainly if he is the player who carried Paris Saint-Germain through so many crucial moments and to their first Champions League title. But, of course, he isn't.

In Leipzig tonight, the outfield players managed to cover for their increasingly error-prone goalkeeper, Erling Haaland scoring a 13th goal in nine meetings with the Bundesliga side and earning a 3-2 win for City. Covering for Donnarumma was not something this team were able to do when he let Nicolas Jackson's shot through his gloves at Villa Park, nor when he got done by Desire Doue and Vitinha in PSG's heavy win at the Etihad.

Those errors betrayed a 6ft 5in frame with the manoeuvrability and burst of an 18-wheeler. Donnarumma might still be just 27 years old but his movement in recent months betrays every one of his 12 years as a first-team player, 553 games on the clock and a lot of rubber burned off those tyres.

You could potentially add Antonio Nusa's goal, Leipzig's second equaliser, into the category of shots Donnarumma might have got down to quicker. It's a 0.2 xG shooting position, one that the Norwegian hit fiercely enough that its post-shot value was 0.65. In other words, Donnarumma would have been doing very well if he saved it. This is, however, Manchester City's goalkeeper, one recruited for his shot-stopping above all else. You're entitled to expect him to do very well.

Especially when he was so cataclysmically clumsy for the first equaliser. Any goalkeeper's primary job is to protect his goal. In drifting three yards off his line when Riedle Baku was in a crossing position, Donnarumma was trying to take the easy way out. Again, a shot-stopper who is quicker to get down to the ball might have dealt with it. Certainly the Italian couldn't argue much that he had been unlucky; replays would suggest Baku saw the gap and hit it precisely.

Ridle Baku sneaks one in at the near post past Donnarumma 😤Stream the #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/tgP6KwASuh

Of course Donnarumma had had his moments earlier, a smart diving save denying Christoph Baumgartner's long-range strike. The same is true of this season and his City career as a whole. At his best, he has recovered that aura of his final months at PSG and across 56 games in the Premier League and Champions League, he has conceded six fewer goals than the post-shot xG value of the shots he has faced. In last season's Premier League he was one of the better pure shot-stoppers in the league; this time he is there or thereabouts.

As a whole, Donnarumma has been fine. It's just that he was not bought to be fine. If you're tolerating a goalkeeper who can't give you much at all in possession, it is because you want the best in the world at keeping the ball out. It seems like a long, long time since Donnarumma could lay claim to that moniker.

#1198. Emerging economies are embracing solar power and skipping fossil fuels much faster than Europe or the US

Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. While the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the world's poorest countries are banking on solar, wind and water instead.

As emerging economies and global living standards rise, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels as the West did; they're investing in electricity powered by renewables.

When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th centuries, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion-engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting fuels.

Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.

Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables, but centuries of legacy infrastructure hold them back.

Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.

That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources.

In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.

At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.

While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.

All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.

"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."

In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power.

Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.

And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam, respectively. The global average was five percent.

This boom has meant middle- and lower-income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electricity than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.

But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, especially across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia and Namibia are rapidly expanding their energy infrastructure to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids.

Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable."

Until a few years ago, he says, people defaulted to diesel generators to meet their energy needs. That came at a cost because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.

These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no-brainer."

"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”

And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.

"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.

Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.

In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.

Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.

Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.

"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”

Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.

"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”

Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.

"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.

"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage."

All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository.

#1194. Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur

After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.

The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.

That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.

That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.

Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.

Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.

"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.

That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.

Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."

James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.

For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.

"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.

But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.

"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.

Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.

Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.

This article was originally written in German.
