#1189. Most expensive goal in Liverpool history gives Iraola era lift-off

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

“I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two big chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an important moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite quickly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

Everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

Alexander Isak scores to double Liverpool's lead at Anfield! 💥 https://t.co/oYs2jnHZEb

“The performance was really good,” said Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”

Brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Liverpool and Brighton & Hove Albion at Anfield.

Liverpool are on a three-game winning run in all competitions, and came from two goals behind in their previous outing in the Champions League on Tuesday, earning an enthralling 4-3 victory over Villarreal. Last weekend, Andoni Iraola’s men also initially fell behind against Brentford in the Premier League, but netted two second-half goals through Daniel Munoz and Alexander Isak to win 2-1 as their opponents finished with nine men.

In his programme notes, Liverpool boss Iraola was excited about the prospect of a second game in a week at home. “As someone who believes every single opportunity we have to play a game at this stadium and in front of our supporters is a privilege, I also feel very passionately that this is a period that we should continue to embrace,” he said.

“It is also a spell in which we will carry on being tested because the quality of the opposition dictates that there is no chance of anything else. Villarreal pushed us all the way in midweek and everything about the way Brighton have played so far this season tells us that it would be foolish to expect anything but the same today.”

Brighton have emerged as one of the surprise packages of the Premier League season thanks to their blistering start. Fabian Hurzeler’s side sit third in the table, having scored a whopping 23 goals in their opening seven games, while conceding just five. Nevertheless, they’re unbeaten since their 4-3 league loss to Chelsea back on August 30.

#1188. Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals

Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?

It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

"I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.

It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.

Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.

#1185. Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease

After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

#1179. Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

#1176. Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amanda Heidt is a freelance journalist in southeast Utah.

Imaging can be used to measure the degree of variation and complexity across brain regions that correspond to conscious states.Credit: AJ Photo/Hop Americain/SPL

At first glance, human consciousness seems like the one thing we should never have to doubt. We know we are conscious because we experience the world in vivid detail: the small luxury of a piece of chocolate; a song imbued with sadness; or a childhood memory that takes us back to another place and time.

But for such a fundamental aspect of reality, what underlies consciousness — the experience of being aware of one’s own existence — has proved deceptively hard to pin down. Researchers and philosophers have spent centuries debating how and why physical processes in the brain result in the subjective, first-person experiences we all seem to have. This issue, known as the ‘hard problem’ of consciousness, continues to drive research today.

Scientists are still far from explaining how brain activity begets an entire inner world, but the field is making progress. The advances that researchers have made include the ability to reliably measure brain activity and connectedness and probe for signs of hidden awareness.

The emerging picture — based on insights from not just neuroscience, but also far-flung disciplines such as plant science, artificial intelligence and astrobiology — is not of consciousness as a single light that can be switched on, but as a coordinated condition that is potentially more widespread than previously thought. The rapid rise of AI, for example, has fuelled discussions over whether only humans can be conscious — and of whether a brain is even required for consciousness.

“People are often troubled by the fact that our understanding remains somewhat vague,” says Matthias Michel, a philosopher of cognitive science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “However, it’s very important to note that definitions in the history of science come at the end of the scientific process, not at the beginning. I’d argue we’re now in the thick of it, which is an exciting place to be.”

There is no direct test for evaluating human consciousness, but researchers have made advances in establishing what are known as neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs). These criteria, which can be a single metric or a combination of events, identify the minimum neuronal mechanism required to kickstart a conscious experience. Specific neurons might need to fire, for example, and particular brain activity patterns could signify an internal experience. Below these thresholds, a person might move through life not fully conscious of their behaviour — zoning out while driving, for instance, only to snap back to attention moments later.

Some NCCs have been determined by studying people in states we don’t typically associate with consciousness, such as those who are asleep, anaesthetized or in a coma. According to Melanie Boly, a neurologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, this type of research is crucial to help separate true NCCs from activities that merely signify being awake and responsive to our surroundings.

“That’s been a big breakthrough, isolating the true features of consciousness, rather than simply measuring something that is associated with or a consequence of the conscious experience,” Boly says.

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Through that work, scientists know that about one-quarter of individuals who present as medically unconscious are, in fact, experiencing a type of covert consciousness in which they continue to perceive the world around them. In a landmark 2024 study, a subset of 241 people who had been left seemingly unresponsive by brain injuries were asked to imagine themselves engaging in activities such as playing tennis or opening and closing their hand. Dozens of patients’ brains became active on imaging scans during these challenges — calling into question whether consciousness persists in otherwise-inert states1.

In recognition of this finding, researchers have moved away from thinking of consciousness as a binary experience towards an understanding that consciousness is a dynamic process that exists on a continuum. From these principles, it has been possible to develop metrics that test the underlying scientific assumptions about consciousness. One of the most promising of these is called the perturbational complexity index (PCI)2.

PCI evaluates a person’s level of consciousness by assessing how their brain responds to a brief magnetic pulse, as measured by electroencephalography (EEG), which traces the brain’s electrical activity using electrodes. In a conscious brain, the neural response usually spreads while remaining complex and distinct from one brain region to another — features referred to as integration and differentiation, respectively. During sleep or under anaesthesia, the response becomes simpler and more repetitive.

“PCI is considered to be a very accurate correlate of consciousness that can be useful in many research settings,” says Johan Frederik Storm, a neurophysiologist at the University of Oslo. Widespread clinical adoption has unfortunately been hampered by the fact that it’s a laborious metric to gather, he adds, “but even still, it is gaining traction”.

This growing understanding has led to the development of hypotheses that move beyond simply measuring aspects of consciousness towards a more foundational understanding of what it is. At present, there are more than 450 such theories, many of which share overlapping features even as they distinguish themselves by scale or focus. The two most popular are the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) and the integrated information theory (IIT).

The GNWT posits that most brain activity is restricted to specialized areas — visual regions process shapes and colours, for example, and language areas process words. Consciousness emerges when information becomes important enough to be broadcast across regions. A face whose representation remains inside the visual system might trigger a simple, unconscious reaction, but a face that triggers regions across the brain, collectively known as the global workspace, can be used by many systems to build a conscious experience.

The IIT tries to answer a different question: what is experience like? When we view the world or recall a memory, we experience a cohesive scene, not separate elements of colour, sound and touch. The IIT argues that consciousness depends on how strongly the parts of a system affect one another while still remaining distinct — there must be both integration and differentiation to give rise to diverse states and experiences. A conscious system must be more than a collection of independent parts, and it must form a whole that has a state that cannot be fully explained by looking at each part separately.

A major issue with proving such hypotheses is that researchers have often tested them in ways that lack true neutrality and rigour. A 2022 analysis of hundreds of experiments found that research into consciousness has often been done in ways that pre-emptively bias the results in support of a particular theory3. This has made it a challenge to directly compare studies of consciousness, according to Christof Koch, a consciousness researcher at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who has studied the topic for decades.

“People become very attached to their theories, and that confirmation bias can sometimes get in the way of an honest, collaborative effort,” he says.

Lucia Melloni, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, recently led a first-of-its-kind effort to force a direct comparison of the two schools of thought. She brought together proponents of both theories, as well as neutral participants, and asked them to agree in advance to a set of experiments and predictions. The group probed foundational assumptions of both theories4 using three measurement techniques — EEG; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks brain activity by detecting tiny changes in blood flow; and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures magnetic fields produced by the brain’s electrical currents.

Plants lack brains, but are capable of decision-making and problem-solving.Credit: Jason Milligan/Courtesy of Understory

One of the main differences between the two ideas is which part of the brain is considered most essential to the act of being. The GNWT predicts a sudden ‘ignition’ of widespread brain activity when a stimulus prompts a conscious experience, and so the prefrontal cortex is expected to play an important part because it uses information to form complex behaviours. ITT focuses instead on a ‘hot zone’ located towards the back of the brain that includes parts of the systems responsible for vision, hearing and touch, because it follows that this is where the relevant stimuli converge to generate a full experience.

The team found conscious information represented in both regions. However, the results also challenged important predictions of both theories. The long-lasting activity predicted by the IIT to occur in the back of the cortex was not clearly represented, and the ignition expected by the GNWT was limited. As such, the study did not settle the debate, instead suggesting that both theories might offer parts of an answer.

Melloni doesn’t see this as a failure, and considers such results the most exciting outcome. “I’m happy with what we found because neither theory was left untouched,” she says. “Having your predictions confirmed doesn’t leave you anywhere to grow, whereas having your thinking challenged makes you do better science.”

One way that scientists are attempting to expand their thinking is through interdisciplinary collaborations, drawing evidence from fields as distant as plant and non-human animal biology, robotics and even the search for extraterrestrial life to flesh out the conditions under which consciousness can arise. It’s not certain, for instance, that brains — or even neurons — are required. Astrobiologists have long been searching for sentient life, yet given the expanse of the known Universe, they cannot reasonably assume it will look anything like us.

#1174. As I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, the raw emotion and magic of Old Trafford was all around me. It was a stark reminder that the fans and the place they flock to really are Man United's greatest gift, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 07:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 10:54 EDT, 4 November 2026

The sound came rolling down in waves, crashing down around us as I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, in the moments after Manchester United had conceded a most dreadful first goal. It was low and sonorous and quite extraordinary, really.

When a club go nine games without winning and fall behind again, you expect an air of sullen resignation – not that ‘UNITED’ which took hold and grew in a collective, magical act of defiance.

Much more would follow in a significant escalation of protest against the Glazers and their minority partner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. But in that moment – and once more when Roma’s second goal threatened to turn this into a catastrophe – it was just about the terraces and their team. A fanbase refusing to go gently into a night of quiet desperation.

Much has been made of the supposed need to let go of a history which has weighed heavy on this club since Sir Alex stepped away. In turn, United try to release it and then cleave to it again, blindly staggering around in their wilderness.

But on Tuesday night, in the stand bearing the great manager’s name, you looked around and were reminded of how the folk memory of Law, Best, Charlton, Cantona and Rooney is such a powerful weapon. It binds the fans back to what was once great. It is fuel.

What those fans brought into the stadium was not a naive and nostalgic sentimentality. They still demanded the best of the players. There is a clear acceptance among many that Bruno Fernandes is trying to repair things, but when he went down theatrically and protested about a challenge, he was told, ‘stop whinging’.

Michael Carrick celebrates Manchester United's victory over Roma on an incredible Old Trafford Champions League night

Matheus Cunha reacts after scoring United's third goal in their comeback win

This is a discerning, intelligent football public. ‘Standards’ is the word on that banner that’s been flying on the Stretford End.

But the collective view before kick-off was that if the players gave fully, then the fans were with them. ‘I just need to know they’re trying,’ said my friend Jocelyn, as we threaded our way through the crowds to the stadium.

Harry Maguire, who has lived this period of United struggle in the raw and was terribly exposed in a wretched first half, still wore that perpetual look of defiance on his face. When United were fatefully awarded the retaken penalty kick, some were saying that Maguire should be handed the ball. ‘At least he’ll put his foot through it.’

There was a frustration with the way that moments of promise broke down, as passes from Kobbie Mainoo and Carlos Baleba went astray. And with the time it takes Senne Lammens to decide how to distribute the ball, which slows United dreadfully. Yet a recognition of the fight shown by individuals who were patently playing for and engaging with the struggles of Carrick, while contending with a scorching scrutiny.

The shadow on the wall was the owners, of course. It was significant that the chants of derision for them struck up on the Stretford End each time United scored. As if to say that the green and gold campaign won’t fade with the slightest prospect of hope this time. There were tennis balls, balloons and a sense that something is building.

Even now, after 21 years, do the Glazers, hiding in their Florida redoubt, really know that they are playing with fire? This now feels as visceral as Liverpool fans’ hate for Tom Hicks and George Gillett Jnr, 20 years ago.

That club’s fans found ways of getting them out. They email-bombed every outfit that seemed ready to offer to help them, from Royal Bank of Scotland to US equity firm Blackstone. The audible boos when the tennis balls rained down after 20 minutes and five seconds – 20.05 represents the year the Glazers staged their leveraged buy-out – suggests protests affecting play are unwelcome for some and perhaps many. Yet the fury is unbridled. The centre may not hold this time.

The night, however, was about the power of this place to do extraordinary things. Even when Bryan Mbeumo crashed a golden chance to equalise against the post in the early stages of the comeback, you sensed something was afoot.

You’re so close to the pitch in the lower tiers of the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand that you feel you can almost reach out and touch the players. As the stadium gave, so they received. Fernandes marshalled. Youri Tielemans made a difference. Matheus Cunha seized the game by the throat.

Cunha and Shea Lacey race towards the jubilant crowd after United's third goal

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again. At the end Diego Dalot was flat out on his back before us. Mason Mount, who’d been on the field barely five minutes, was in delirium and the post-match acknowledgement of fans by Carrick with his players felt like a victory lap. It meant that much.

The Carrick anthem was still being sung on the concourses as we flooded out under the clear night sky, and you knew for sure in that moment why no one wants the distinctly average names like Eddie Howe, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann being touted for this job.

‘I don’t want us to start all over again,’ Jocelyn told me, still trying to compute what we’d just seen, after we'd joined the departing throng. ‘I want Carrick to do it. I want more nights like this.’

We learned in the aftermath that Carrick’s career-saving half-time speech had involved him telling his players how Old Trafford could do this. ‘I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there,’ he said. ‘This place does magical things. It's done it before and it'll do it over and over again.’

Yes, that really did encapsulate the essence of a night on which we discovered, once more, that the fans and the place they flock to really are Manchester United's greatest gift.

#1172. '90s art scene in the UK: An international, edgy trendsetter

The 1990s are remembered for Brit-pop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of nostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.

Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.

Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.

But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017. Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"

Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation. While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as Tate curator Helen Little argues, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has undergone significant cultural reexamination since then: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Dior, while Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc. McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past." In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

#1169. Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson

Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."

Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regarded translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did reveal in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.

The winner of the Nobel Prize in literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.

On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1164. Shea Lacey has showed the fearlessness Man United need to lift themselves out of the mire. It's time for misfiring Amad Diallo to be dropped for the teenager - and it could be the making of both players, writes NATHAN SALT

Published: 07:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 10:59 EDT, 4 November 2026

Ruben Amorim, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Michael Carrick can’t all be wrong when it comes to Amad Diallo’s unrelenting desire to fulfil his potential.

‘Amad is such a dream to work with,’ Carrick said last season. ‘His attitude is so positive. He wants to learn, he wants to keep pushing.

‘He asks for more – “what can I do more?” or “how can I improve?” He is desperate to do well and has been a huge part of the team.’

Amorim and Van Nistelrooy spoke similarly of Amad’s thirst for extra work and personal development. Nobody inside Carrington denies how much Amad wants to be great.

But there comes a point where an attacking player simply must score goals. And Amad doesn’t do that. It’s the elephant in the room that people seem uncomfortable talking about.

It is now 324 days and counting since Amad scored a goal of any kind for United, dating back to December 15, 2025, in a 4-4 draw at home to Bournemouth.

Amad Diallo struggled to make an impact against Roma on Tuesday night. It is now 324 days and counting since he last scored a goal for Man United

The best thing for Amad right now would be to take him out of the side, sit him down, and have some honest conversations as to how a player so talented has seen his trajectory plateau at 24

Go back further and, since bagging a hat-trick at Old Trafford against Southampton on January 16, 2025, the same month he was rewarded with a bumper five-year contract, Amad has managed just four goals and five assists in 43 Premier League games.

This season the docket reads no goals and one assist in all competitions, with the latter his pass to Joshua Zirkzee in Como for United’s late consolation in a 4-1 defeat.

Amad likes to do a lot of talking on Instagram – after the 3-2 win over Roma he not-so-subtly posted ‘They're petty and hateful – they'll always have something to say’ – but with Shea Lacey clipping at his heels, he needs to start doing his talking on the pitch.

Since Amad last scored against Bournemouth in December 2025, Bruno Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have both scored nine goals, Benjamin Sesko has 11 and Matheus Cunha, the hero against Roma, has 12.

Amad, through 24 games under Carrick, has delivered zero goals and two assists. It’s simply not good enough.

‘The best years of his career are ahead of him, and we all look forward to helping Amad to reach his immense potential and achieve success at the club in the coming seasons,’ director of football Jason Wilcox said of the winger when he penned his new contract last year.

The truth is, the best thing for Amad right now would be to take him out of the side, sit him down, and have some honest conversations as to how a player so talented has seen his trajectory plateau at 24.

Which is where Lacey, magnificent off the bench and the orchestrator of Cunha’s winning goal last night, comes into all of this.

Shea Lacey's cameo against Roma changed the game and had his boss Michael Carrick purring. 'He gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch,' said Carrick

Lacey inspired the crowd, and his team-mates. His unpredictability had Roma dazed

The 19-year-old scored earlier this season in the Carabao Cup exit to Brighton and has largely been given a watching brief since.

But back under the lights at Old Trafford against Roma, he put in a performance that not only helped take United past their Italian opponents, but one that really ought to take Lacey ahead of Amad when it comes to Carrick's thinking for the team to face Aston Villa on Sunday.

Not only because of the incisive pass to Cunha that led to the winner, but the invention, the daring, the trickery that should have won United a penalty – an inexplicable decision after Lacey was hacked down – and the rest. It was, in Carrick’s own words, a performance full of ‘mischief’.

Lacey, born in Liverpool but a United fan, is a product of the club's famed academy. He has played for England through the age groups up to Under-20s but has yet to start a League match for the Old Trafford club, his only appearance from the first whistle coming in the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat to Brighton.

‘I'm not going too over the top, but at the same point I’m absolutely delighted for Shea,’ Carrick said. ‘We love him to bits. He's a great young man, he's desperate to do well, he's got great ability and so in terms of coming inside and finding the pass, that's not surprising.

‘He's got that little glint in his eye, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like, so he's always looking to have that.

‘I think he gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch, and it was fantastic to see. He made the most of what he had tonight.’

That’s exactly what Lacey did. He lifted the crowd, his team-mates. His unpredictability had Roma dazed. He showed a fearlessness that United badly need if they are to lift themselves out of the mire they are in right now.

‘Amad does some really good things, but it's that end product, that is what takes you to the next level,’ former United striker Wayne Rooney said on Tuesday night.

‘And the glimpses of what I've seen from Lacey when he has come on, especially this season, he has got something in there.’

Match-winner Matheus Cunha thanks Lacey after the 19-year-old set up his decisive goal

It was a cameo that injected so much hope heading into the Villa game. Lacey completed all of his attempted passes, won most of his duels, succeeded in most of his take-ons and laid on a match-winning assist, all in just 15 minutes.

Off the ball Amad does a lot that may – unfairly – get glossed over. His defending has improved considerably since playing as a wing-back under Amorim.

But Amad is playing as United’s go-to right winger and isn’t delivering goals or assists.

To help fulfil the potential of both players, it’s time to start Lacey on Sunday. In the long run, that bold call could be the making of both of them.

Diogo Dalot has revealed Manchester United’s dramatic second-half turnaround against Roma was fuelled by the realisation that their players had ‘nothing to lose’ by going for it.

United have endured an atrocious season so far, struggling in the Champions League and sitting 17th in the Premier League.

They went in 2-0 down at half-time at Old Trafford on Tuesday night but Dalot said the dressing room's acceptance that they had hit rock bottom helped their determination to put things right.

‘If you analyse it, we had nothing more to lose,’ Dalot said after United's 3-2 comeback win. ‘I mean, that's the unfortunate situation that we are in, so we just had to really go at it.

‘You could see in the first five, ten minutes (of the second half) that we were winning duels, we were on the front foot, the crowd came with us and pushed us forward. Once you create that energy inside the stadium, it's really tough for the opponents to even create a chance.

‘That's the biggest thing we need to get out of this game – that when we play like this, when we have the right attitude, when the fans really believe that we are there, we can be a very strong team.’

#1162. How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands

Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

#1158. Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention

Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, especially of bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.

Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.

That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the United States and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.

So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in London.

"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."

But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.

A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.

In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.

In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.

The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.

But since these figures came from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.

"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."

Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.

In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.

Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — had risen among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.

In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.

This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.

A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.

The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.

But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.

Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.

Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.

"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."

Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needed public health policy.

But he also said that young people could lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.

"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."

For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.

#1154. 2026 Nobel Prize winner Anne Carson: Where to start reading

The works of this year's Nobel Prize-winning poet and essayist Anne Carson can feel slightly daunting. Here are some keys to understanding her universe.

This quote is from the long, lyrical poem "The Glass Essay" published in Anne Carson's 1995 collection "Glass, Irony and God" — an entry point into the works of the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature laureate.

In the poem, the narrator explores the burden of memory and obsessive desire after a failed love affair, all while regularly reflecting on Emily Brontë — an author renowned for her intense literary depiction of destructive and passionate love in "Wuthering Heights."

The poem brings several of Carson's recurring obsessions together into one work. She has repeatedly written about desire, abandonment and jealousy, and has often used other literary figures as emotional doubles, as historical anchor points to her ideas.

In a way, "The Glass Essay" encapsulates Carson's method; the Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist has often intellectualized emotional themes by intertwining her personal reflections with analysis, etymology, translation, literary history and philosophical thought.

Another trademark of her work is the genre fluidity found in "The Glass Essay," which — as the title indicates — is partly a literary criticism essay, even though it is also a poem due to its form.

"Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," noted Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel Committee, in his description of the Nobel laureate on October 8.

Born in the Canadian city of Toronto, Carson first developed her fascination for ancient Greek myths as a teenager. She told literary journal The Brick that she spotted a bilingual edition of "Sappho" by Willis Barnstone in the display of a bookstore of a shopping mall in Ontario, and that had led her to ask a high school Latin teacher to teach her ancient Greek.

She went on to publish her doctoral thesis in Classics, entitled "Odi et Amo Ergo Sum" (I hate and I love, therefore I am).

Carson's first book of criticism, "Eros the Bittersweet," was published in 1986. It lays the foundation of her approach, as she draws on ancient Greek writers such as Sappho and Plato to examine how desire — and the obstacles between the lover and the beloved — creates emotional tension.

The book suggests that the ache of wanting is not separate from love; it is one of the things that makes desire so powerful.

Because "Eros the Bittersweet" moves between Greek poetry, philosophy and literary criticism and personal interpretations, it is not considered a conventionally easy read. A more immediately engaging work and good starting point to discover Carson is the verse novel "Autobiography of Red," published in 1998.

"Autobiography of Red" was inspired by the ancient Greek myth of Herakles (or Hercules) and the red-winged monster Geryon, which the hero kills as his 10th task in his series of 12 monumental labors.

An otherwise minor figure from mythology, Geryon is turned into Herakles' lover in Carson's book. She reimagines the myth as a modern, queer coming-of-age story, with the monster experiencing love, jealousy, sexuality and heartbreak.

"We all feel we're monsters most of the time," explained Carson.

The work is accessible, funny and moving, and no deep knowledge of Greek mythology is required to enjoy it.

The key to reading Carson is not to expect every connection to be immediately clear. Her books reward curiosity rather than certainty, and her sprawling, non-linear web of knowledge can be compared to going down a hyperlinked rabbit hole of narrative ideas.

"Men in the Off Hours" (2000) is another intellectually playful collection of poems. Here Carson collides the modern with the ancient, with references to figures as diverse as Beethoven, Virginia Woolf, Emily Dickinson, Jean-Luc Godard, Sigmund Freud, Homer and Hokusai.

The poems bring together fragments of history, mythology and ordinary life, allowing unexpected emotional and intellectual connections to emerge.

In the spoken and sung performance piece "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), Carson similarly brings together classical and pop culture, reimagining the story of Helen of Troy alongside the life and cultural image of Marilyn Monroe.

How do people become the victims of desires they cannot control? This is a core theme Carson explores in "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos," published in 2001.

It features the Canadian author's wry humor in a powerful and moving way, with erotic, painful and heartbreaking scenes from a doomed marriage: a 30-year obsession with a pathological liar whose singular redeeming quality is his sheer physical radiance.

The collection of poetry, which won her the T.S. Eliot Prize, is dedicated to the English Romantic poet John Keats, challenging his famous aphorism, "Beauty is truth."

#1152. Revealed: How Arsenal have used NASA to tackle their injury woes - with Google and Apple joining the fight

Published: 12:00 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 12:08 EDT, 4 November 2026

Mikel Arteta has often stretched the boundaries of quirkiness in his pursuit of excellence at Arsenal - and it can now be revealed that his search for those marginal gains has seen the club quite literally reaching for the stars.

Injuries are once again the focus for Arteta after Bukayo Saka sustained a thigh strain at Bayern Munich two weeks ago. He is expected to be ruled out for four to six weeks. It is the 25-year-old’s 11th injury since September 2024.

Arsenal have been blighted by injury, and Arteta has been fixated on reducing the problem ever since the 2022-23 campaign - where William Saliba’s absence cost them dear in the Premier League run-in.

But what are they doing to fix it? Daily Mail Sport can reveal that Arsenal staff have in recent seasons been tasked with reaching out to blue-chip companies, seeking innovative ways which could help lower the number of injuries and accelerate recovery.

Earlier in Arteta's Arsenal reign, NASA were consulted on their expertise in space physiology, specifically in relation to ACL injuries.

In space, the reduced load on the human body – because of less gravity – contributes to muscle atrophy and bone density loss. As a result, NASA have conducted extensive research into what happens to the body under reduced gravity, and how it responds when back on Earth.

Injuries are the one area that Mikel Arteta has been unable to solve in his quest to find marginal gains

Bukayo Saka went off inside 10 minutes at Bayern Munich last month, having suffered his 11th injury in just over two years

Arsenal believed there could be valuable lessons to apply to their ACL rehabilitation process. This includes exploring areas such as how much weight an injured player should bear at different stages, how quickly that load should be increased, how reduced-gravity exercise can allow players to resume running and loading movements earlier, and how to measure whether a player’s body is actually tolerating those increased demands.

The issue has been particularly pertinent given Arsenal's experiences in recent seasons. Jurrien Timber ruptured his ACL on his Premier League debut against Nottingham Forest in August 2023, ruling him out for nearly nine months, and Gabriel Jesus spent 332 days out when he suffered the same injury in January 2025.

The problem has not been confined to the men’s team. Arsenal women's side have also endured a troubling run of ACL injuries, with several high-profile players affected in recent seasons. Leah Williamson, Beth Mead, Vivianne Miedema and Victoria Pelova all suffered ACL injuries in the 2022-23 season, while Manuela Zinsberger, Michelle Agyemang and Katie Reid have all had the same injury in the past 18 months.

NASA aren’t the only high-tech addition to Arsenal’s crackdown on injuries. It’s understood that Google, one of the club’s official partners, were consulted on data analytics. The company’s expertise in processing vast quantities of information could help identify patterns associated with injury risk, spotting subtle changes in running mechanics or physical output.

Similarly, Apple were consulted about using wearable technology to collect physiological data and build a clearer picture of how players respond to training and rehabilitation. This included the use of Apple Watches to track metrics such as heart rate and exercise intensity.

Arsenal’s global brand helps in these partnerships. It’s ultimately a passport into world-leading organisations, who are often intrigued by the prospect of working with a major sports side.

How effective Arsenal's attempts have been is difficult to measure, as a multitude of factors contribute toinjuries, some of which are out of the club’s control. The number of players injured at Arsenal in recent years, though, have suggested a disproportionate problem compared to other sides.

One noteworthy example, given what has happened since, is the Champions League match against Club Bruges on December 10, 2025. Seven players were out: William Saliba, Gabriel, Cristhian Mosquera, Declan Rice, Kai Havertz, Leandro Trossard and Max Dowman. It took Arsenal’s injury total at that stage to 95 (excluding Rice’s illness) since the start of the 2024–25 Premier League season – only Brighton had more (97).

Jurrien Timber was struck down with an ACL injury in his Premier League debut in August 2023

Gabriel Jesus also suffered an ACL injury in January 2025, ruling him out for almost the entire calendar year

William Saliba's injury in March 2023 proved fatal for Arsenal's title charge, with Rob Holding unable to play in the same high line as Manchester City hunted the Gunners down

The club instigated a mass medical team shake-up last summer kickstarted by the appointment of Spanish physio Joaquin Acedo, a long-term Arteta associate from when he was a Real Sociedad player over two decades ago. Among the other new arrivals are head of medical services Dr Arnaldo Abrantes and physiotherapist Carmen Marquez, who both joined from Aston Villa, head of player rehabilitation Eneko Angulo and fitness coach Jose Jimenez.

A slogan on the wall in Arsenal's medical room which reads: ‘Your best ability is availability’ says it all.

This season, Arsenal have not yet been as badly affected by injuries. Aside from Saliba and Saka, Christos Tzolis, Ben White and Mosquera have all spent time out, while Eberechi Eze recently picked up an unspecified injury.

It is the impact of missing key players at crucial times which has irked Arteta the most. While the 2023 title charge was killed off when Saliba had to be replaced by Rob Holding, who was unable to maintain the same high line and press, the 2024-2025 season fell apart when Jesus and Havertz were injured in January, leaving only midfielder Mikel Merino to play up front.

Last term Havertz started just seven league games after damaging his knee ligaments in the opener at Manchester United.

Perhaps the most Arteta-like thing about all this is that, even after turning to NASA, Google and Apple for answers, the search for an edge never really stops.
